, a former MP, fined $3,000 and put on a year's probation in 1989 after pleading guilty to pocketing $7,463 while he

 resigned as Conservative consumer and corporate affairs minister after pleading guilty to impaired driving in 1989.

title: Beacon of 'moral clarity' Carney names former Supreme Court justice as next governor general
body:
Louise Arbour, the pioneering war crimes prosecutor, human rights commissioner and former Supreme Court 
justice, was named Canada's 31st governor general on Tuesday, when Prime Minister Mark Carney proclaimed 
the need for someone of "judgment" and "moral clarity" in the post.
Describing herself as "serene" and "enthusiastic" about the appointment, Arbour thanked King Charles III for 
accepting her nomination and pledged to stand for all Canadians when she is sworn in as the monarch's 
representative at Rideau Hall in a ceremony expected in early June.
Arbour, 79, was born in Montreal. She will become the third woman from Quebec to assume the role since 2017, 
replacing Mary Simon, who became the first Indigenous governor general in 2021.
"Canada is a wonderful country shaped by its diversity of people, of perspectives and experiences, but I think 
shaped also mostly by a common respect for strong public institutions and for the rule of law," Arbour said, standing 
alongside Carney in the atrium of the National Gallery of Canada near Parliament Hill.
"Above all, we all strive to provide for each other in a spirit of equality and generosity."
While stopping short of describing herself as a monarchist - a term she said is often used as a "pejorative" - Arbour 
defended the institution she will now represent as an essential part of Canada's "constitutional arrangement." She 
noted that as governor general she will also serve as commander-in-chief of the Canadian Armed Forces, an 
institution on which she reported in recent years as a government-appointed commissioner probing widespread 
allegations of sexual misconduct.
Expressing respect for soldiers' "service and professionalism," Arbour said, "Like them, I will strive to serve with 
honour, dedication and integrity."
Carney said in French that it is difficult to predict which crises or challenges might come up during the mandate of a 
governor general, whose duty is to call upon party leaders to form governments and agree - or, more rarely, 
disagree - with prime ministers' requests to prorogue or dissolve Parliaments to trigger an election.
"The most demanding part of that role is rarely seen. It's the duty to ensure the government in Canada is formed, 
sustained and, when the time comes, dismissed in accordance with law and convention. It's a duty that calls for 
sound judgment, deep learning and an unwavering commitment to the rule of law," the prime minister said. 
Page 2 of 3
Beacon of 'moral clarity' Carney names former Supreme Court justice as next governor general
Carney also praised Arbour for her distinguished legal career in Canada and abroad as a champion of human rights 
and international law.
Arbour's legal career began in Quebec and saw her serve as a judge on Ontario's highest court before she entered 
the world of international law as the United Nations' chief prosecutor for the International Criminal Tribunal for the 
former Yugoslavia and Rwanda in the 1990s.
She is known for securing the first conviction under the 1948 Genocide Convention when prosecuting crimes 
relating to the Rwandan genocide.
Arbour also clinched a war crimes indictment for Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic, the first for a sitting 
European head of state, for his role in the wars that erupted during the breakup of Yugoslavia. 
She sat on the Supreme Court of Canada from 1999 until 2004, when she left and became the UN's high 
commissioner for human rights. 
"She gave voice to those whose dignity was denied in places where the powerful preferred silence. She did not 
flinch and she never confused being heard with being safe," Carney said.
More recently, Arbour was appointed to oversee a review of the culture inside the Canadian Armed Forces, amid a 
series of sexual misconduct allegations against high-ranking soldiers. Among her recommendations in 2022 were 
overhauls of military colleges and outsourcing complaints of sexual assault and misconduct from military tribunals to 
the civilian court system.
"In every role she's held, the Honourable Louise Arbour has carried the same conviction that a free society depends 
on institutions properly being held to account, that the law stands between power and the powerless, that the dignity 
of every person should not be a product of the accidents of geography, citizenship or convenience, and that 
Canada's place in the world is to be a country that lives those propositions and helps others to live them as well," 
Carney said. 
Though supposedly above politics, the role of vice-regent comes with close public scrutiny. At her news conference 
Tuesday, Arbour was pressed on her predecessor's lack of ability to speak French - a source of outrage from 
Quebec francophone leaders in recent years. She was also pressed on recent comments to Radio-Canada in 
which she called the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran "pure folly."
Asked whether she is worried about losing her freedom to speak out in her new job, Arbour noted her experience as 
an international figure and judge.
"I'm very, very conscious ... of the privileges and the power that comes with certain jobs and the constraints that we 
need to impose as a consequence," Arbour said in French. "People understand very well the difference between 
private speech and the position that we express in the name of a post."
Arbour was also asked about criticism she received over her statements about Israel in 2008 from the Conservative 
government under Stephen Harper. 
At the time, Tory cabinet minister Vic Toews declared Arbour a "disgrace" after, in her role as the UN's human 
rights commissioner, she warned that the killing of civilians during the Israeli-Lebanon war of 2006 could amount to 
war crimes. She also prompted a backlash over her support of an Arab human rights charter that called for the 
elimination of Zionism, the nationalist movement for a Jewish homeland that has played a role in the Israeli-
Palestinian conflict for decades.

title: Bell: 'Good riddance' - Conservative outrage at turncoat MP's desertion to Liberals
body:
On Wednesday, John Barlow gets a ton of texts about Ontario Conservative MP Marilyn Gladu jumping ship and 
joining Prime Minister Mark Carney's Liberal crew.
This is no inside baseball yarn, only catching the attention of the political talking heads.
People are ticked off, steamed, hot under the collar.
Disgusted.
Barlow is a Conservative member of parliament from southern Alberta's heartland and on this day he is on his way 
to talk to folks in the town of Claresholm.
Gladu was elected as a Conservative less than a year ago and now she's a Liberal( 
https://calgaryherald.com/news/canada/marilyn-gladu-the-conservative-mp-from-sarnia-crosses-the-floor-to-the-
liberals/wcm/9fc2b715-3084-4c00-aa99-cb392bd32c90 ) trying to peddle nonsense about how Carney is a serious 
leader and how she became a turncoat because it was the right thing to do to help the people she represents.
It is mighty tough to swallow that swill. The self-serving rationalization burns the throat and triggers the gag reflex.
The locals in Barlow's neck of the woods are asking what Gladu was offered to abandon her party.
"How much did it cost to sell her integrity, her character, to turn her back on the people who voted for her?" asks 
Barlow, saying it is the question others ask.
For the Alberta Conservative MP, Gladu and the other Conservative defectors to Carney's side obviously didn't 
abandon their party "out of the goodness of their heart."
"This is Mark Carney offering these people something. This is Liberal corruption and dirty politics at its best," he 
says.
People Barlow knows and represents are enraged by how Carney is trying and almost certainly succeeding in 
getting a majority of the MPs in the House of Commons to be Liberals, to get a Liberal majority government.
Page 2 of 3
Bell: 'Good riddance' - Conservative outrage at turncoat MP's desertion to Liberals
It's not by the vote of Canadians, it's by backroom dealing, encouraging Conservative MPs to defect to the Liberals 
and four have done so already.
"In southern Alberta that is not the cowboy way, it's not the honest way of doing things," says Barlow.
Sarnia-Lambton MP Marilyn Gladu in a file photo.
It is then Barlow drops this nugget.
Gladu the defector invited Barlow to a Conservative fundraiser next weekend in her Ontario riding.
She wanted Barlow to meet with local farmers and deliver a speech to local Conservatives.
The Alberta MP says Gladu sent the invitation to Conservative party members in her riding about a week ago.
"This doesn't seem like something she's been mulling over for a long time," says Barlow, referring to Gladu's 
defection Wednesday.
Barlow says he is still going to Ontario.
"I want to show her members and the farmers in her riding it's not the Conservatives who have turned their back on 
them."
There are rumblings, loud rumblings in some quarters, that Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre's days are 
numbered.
Much of the volume comes from those who want the Conservatives nowhere near power in Ottawa.
"I don't see Pierre in trouble whatsoever. If anything I think he's strengthened his support," says Barlow, a strong 
backer of Poilievre.
He says Conservative politicians are behind Poilievre and party members are behind him.
Barlow points to Poilievre's "exceptional performance" in his recent trip to the U.S., including his appearance on Joe 
Rogan's incredibly popular podcast, and adds people have told him they've been impressed with the Conservative 
leader over the last few weeks.
Conservative Party of Canada leader Pierre Poilievre.
As for Carney, Barlow is hopeful more Canadians will catch on to what the prime minister is all about.
"Liberals are the proven masters of the announcement and utter failures at actually following up with the hard work 
to make things come to fruition."
Despite the nasty news of Conservative MPs crossing over to Carney and the Liberals, Barlow is hopeful.
The Alberta Conservative MP says the press in Ottawa makes it sound like Carney has accomplished something 
"when he has accomplished nothing."
"Eventually that comes home to roost, where Canadians will see their life isn't any better.
"If you can't have some action and results, eventually people are going to look at the team offering tangible 
solutions."
The day's story comes full circle, back to Gladu, the latest Conservative defector.
"These people who crossed the floor, they weren't disillusioned with our party or our leader or the Conservative 
movement. They sold their integrity and did this for personal reasons.
Page 3 of 3
Bell: 'Good riddance' - Conservative outrage at turncoat MP's desertion to Liberals
"If they are so easily swayed and manipulated then, good riddance."
In no universe is Barlow, the MP for the riding of Foothills, leaving the Conservative ranks.
"My integrity is not for sale. I would never sell out the people of Foothills. There is no price you could put on that."

title: Bennett apologizes after Wilson-Raybould calls out her 'Pension?' message as racist
body:
OTTAWA - Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Carolyn Bennett has apologized after she was called out for a 
one-word text message to Independent MP Jody Wilson-Raybould, a former cabinet colleague.
Bennett messaged the word "Pension?" in response to a Wilson-Raybould tweet urging the prime minister to quit 
his "selfish jockeying" for an election and focus, as promised, on reconciliation with Indigenous people.
Her tweet was prompted by the announcement Wednesday by a Saskatchewan First Nation that 751 unmarked 
graves have been found on the site of a former Indigenous residential school in that province.
Bennett's pension reference appeared to suggest that Wilson-Raybould is worried she won't be eligible for a 
pension if she should fail to win re-election in a vote this summer or early fall.
Members of Parliament must serve for six years before becoming eligible for a pension and Wilson-Raybould, 
elected in October 2015, would miss that mark if she were not re-elected in an early fall vote.
Wilson-Raybould fired back, publishing Bennett's text on Twitter and calling it both racist and misogynistic.
The pension query reflects the notion that Indigenous Peoples are "lazy & only want $," Wilson-Raybould tweeted.
"Shows disregard, disdain, & disrespect for Indigenous peoples, as in our history," she wrote. "Conveys a strong 
Indigenous woman, is a bad Indig woman."
Bennett issued a swift apology on her Twitter account.
"I let interpersonal dynamics get the better of me and sent an insensitive and inappropriate comment, which I 
deeply regret and shouldn’t have done," she said.
Bennett said she had apologized directly to Wilson-Raybould. Neither politician responded immediately to requests 
for further comment on Thursday.
The apology wasn't sufficient for New Democrat MP Charlie Angus. He took to Twitter to demand that Bennett be 
fired.

Page 2 of 3
Bennett apologizes after Wilson-Raybould calls out her 'Pension?' message as racist
"It is time that @Carolyn_Bennett was sent packing," he said. 
Angus said Bennett's "smear" against Wilson-Raybould demonstrated that Trudeau's commitment to reconciliation 
is really "an agenda of political cynicism and spin."
"This isn't just petty but racist and disrespectful. She needs to go."
The Union of BC Indian Chiefs also called on Bennett to resign, saying it is "deeply disturbed and disgusted by the 
extreme callousness, spite, and ignorance you have shown through the racist message you sent to MP Jody 
Wilson-Raybould."
"This was a cowardly attempt to silence a powerful Indigenous voice calling out for truth, action and justice," the 
union said in an open letter to Bennett.
"With a single word – 'pension' – you not only decided to perpetuate a damaging racial stereotype, that Indigenous 
peoples are lazy and only financially motivated – but dismissed the pressing, overarching issue of residential 
schools, missing and murdered children, and Indigenous rights."
The Prime Minister's Office declined to comment Thursday, referring reporters to Bennett's statement.
Wilson-Raybould was appointed by Trudeau as Canada's first Indigenous justice minister but was booted from the 
Liberal caucus in 2019 after she accused the prime minister of pressuring her to secure a deferred prosecution 
agreement for SNC-Lavalin.
She had earlier resigned as a cabinet minister over the affair.
In August 2019, the federal ethics commissioner concluded that Trudeau violated the Conflict of Interest Act by 
improperly pressuring Wilson-Raybould to halt a criminal prosecution of the Montreal engineering giant on 
corruption charges related to contracts in Libya.
Wilson-Raybould was re-elected as an Independent MP in October 2019.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published June 24, 2021.

title: Boissonnault vows to make amends Liberal MP sorry for confusion over Indigenous heritage
body:
Liberal MP Randy Boissonnault says he is preparing to take legal action against his ex-business partner, insisting 
he had no idea their medical supply company applied for a federal contract while falsely claiming it was Indigenous-
owned. 
Under questioning for two hours Thursday at a House of Commons committee, Boissonnault said he is seeking 
advice from elders and community leaders about how to make amends, and apologized for not being clearer about 
his heritage when he described himself as "non-status adopted Cree." He explained that he used the term because 
he was adopted as a baby into a family in which a great-grandmother was believed to be Cree. 
The former cabinet minister from Edmonton repeatedly denied, however, that he has ever claimed to be 
Indigenous by blood, and said he was not involved when his company, Global Health Imports, applied for a federal 
contract in June 2020 while claiming it was wholly Indigenous-owned - a revelation first reported in the National 
Post. 
The federal government at the time was working to create a target to ensure at least five per cent of government 
procurement contracts were awarded to Indigenous businesses. 
"I have started the process to take legal action against Mr. Anderson now," Boissonnault said, referring to Stephen 
Anderson, with whom he co-founded Global Health Imports in April 2020, after he failed to get re-elected in the 
2019 federal election. 
Boissonnault - who said had no role at the company after he was elected again in 2021 - alleged Anderson used his 
name to advance Global Health Imports's interests without his consent, and said he is exploring options with legal 
counsel on how to clear his name. 
"I have never attempted to leverage my adopted family's history for personal or political gain. I've never identified as 
Indigenous on any application, nor have my businesses ever benefited as a result." 
The Star was unable to reach Anderson for comment on Thursday. 
Earlier this year, Global News reported that Boissonnault remained listed as a director of Global Health Imports, 
and that the company faced a series of lawsuits over unpaid bills and unfulfilled deliveries. Opposition 
Conservatives have since hammered Boissonnault over his ties to the company, and have demanded that 
Page 2 of 3
Boissonnault vows to make amends Liberal MP sorry for confusion over Indigenous heritage
Anderson be hauled before the House of Commons and forced to answer questions after he failed to comply with 
their request to deliver private texts and emails that refer to a person named "Randy." 
Boissonnault denied Thursday that he is the "Randy" referred to in those documents. 
The scrutiny escalated in November, amid reports that the Liberal party advertised Boissonnault as a member of its 
Indigenous caucus in 2016 without noting that he isn't Indigenous. The National Post also reported that Global 
Health Imports applied for a federal contract while claiming to be Indigenous-owned. On Nov. 21, Prime Minister 
Justin Trudeau published a statement that said he and Boissonnault agreed the Edmonton MP should leave cabinet 
while he focuses "on clearing the allegations made against him."
At the committee on Thursday, Boissonnault repeatedly insisted he made sure he was not involved in the 
company's dealings with the federal government and that he didn't know about the application that claimed the 
company was Indigenous-owned. 
"Mr. Anderson should never have ever applied for a federal contract for funds reserved for Indigenous people," 
Boissonnault said. "He did that without my knowledge or consent. I found out about it in the news." 
He also said he has not been contacted by the police, after Global News reported there was a fraud investigation 
involving Global Health Imports. Edmonton police would only confirm to the Star at the time that it was investigating 
a fraud complaint involving a "local medical supply company." 
Regarding his role on the Liberal party's Indigenous caucus, Boissonnault said he joined as an "ally" and because 
he wanted to ensure the group had Alberta representation, as one of the few Liberal MPs from the Conservative-
dominated province. 
Michael McLeod, a Liberal MP from the Northwest Territories who has sat on the party's Indigenous caucus since 
2015, told the committee he never heard Boissonnault claim to be Indigenous. 
"I think one of the first sentences out of his mouth was to state that he was not Indigenous, but he was very keen on 
joining us as part of the caucus," McLeod said. 
NDP MP Lori Idlout, who represents Nunavut and spoke at times in Inuktitut, pressed Boissonnault on how he will 
make amends for harms caused by his lack of clarity about any Indigenous heritage. 
"Pretendianism is not only harmful, it is fraud," Idlout said, using the term for when people pretend to be 
Indigenous. 
Boissonnault responded that he agrees it is a "deeply harmful" and disrespectful thing to do, and that he is seeking 
advice on how to best move forward and listen to people harmed by false claims of Indigenous identity. 
"That's part of my own learning journey here, Ms. Idlout. And I will continue to do that, and I will take your advice as 
well on how I should make amends, because I never intended to be unclear about my history or my family's history. 
And I think that is an important personal act for me when it comes to reconciliation," he said.

title: Boissonnault's departure severs Trudeau cabinet's last link to Alberta and Saskatchewan
body:
OTTAWA - Prime Minister Justin Trudeau finds himself leading a cabinet with zero representation from the 
western provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan after the departure of embattled former employment minister 
Randy Boissonnault on Wednesday.
Boissonnault was the cabinet's sole representative from Alberta and ministerial lead for the rebuilding( 
https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-releases/2024/10/09/prime-minister-announces-new-ministerial-lead-
jasper#:~:text=As%20part%20of%20the%20federal,as%20Ministerial%20Lead%20for%20Jasper. ) of the fire-
ravaged town of Jasper, Alta.
Boissonnault's departure comes at a bad time for the prime minister, who's repeatedly touted the need for a 
unified "Team Canada" approach( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/liberals-reassure-canadians-donald-trump 
) to bilateral relations with the United States, in advance of the looming return of Donald Trump's "America First" 
agenda to Washington.
Trudeau will now need to do this without a single emissary in his cabinet to either Alberta or Saskatchewan, both 
major exporters of energy and agricultural products to the U.S.
Calgary Conservative MP Greg McLean told the National Post on Tuesday that Trudeau has himself to blame for 
the lack of representation.
"There's a reason (the Liberals) don't have good representation in Alberta," said McLean. "It's because they've 
worked against Alberta's interests for a long time."
Boissonnault steps down from cabinet after shifting claims on Indigenous heritage( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/randy-boissonnault-stepping-down-indigenous-heritage )
Boissonnault accused of 'fraud' and 'pretendianism' as calls to resign grow( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/calls-mount-for-randy-boissonnault-to-resign )
Liberal prime ministers Jean Chretien and Paul Martin each tended to promote MPs from the two provinces to 
senior cabinet positions.
Page 2 of 3
Boissonnault's departure severs Trudeau cabinet's last link to Alberta and Saskatchewan
Ex-Alberta MP Anne McLellan and ex-Saskatchewan MP Ralph Goodale, for example, were both senior 
ministers in successive Liberal cabinets in the 1990s and early 2000s.
Justin Trudeau himself tapped Goodale as his second-in-command( 
https://web.archive.org/web/20160305070544/http://www.pco-bcp.gc.ca/oic-ddc.asp?viewattach=31592 ) shortly 
after becoming prime minister in 2015, issuing an order stating that Goodale would become acting prime minister 
in the event of his death or incapacitation.
Goodale was subsequently defeated in the 2019 election, putting an end to his near 26-year run as an MP.
Yet Trudeau now finds himself without an olive branch to extend to the two western provinces, both of which have 
historically leaned conservative.
Boissonnault is one of just two Liberal MPs from Alberta. The other, George Chahal, has had trouble keeping his 
own nose clean( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/liberal-mp-george-chahal-fined-500-for-taking-tory-election-
leaflet-from-front-door ), after being fined $500 for taking an opponent's pamphlet from a front door during the 2021 
federal election.
Chahal told the National Post on Wednesday that Boissonnault had done a "great job" coordinating recovery efforts 
in Jasper but declined to say whether he was prepared to take on the role in the event of Boissonnault's departure.
To make matters even worse, Trudeau has a non-existent talent pool to draw from in Saskatchewan, where the 
Conservative Party has swept all 14 seats in successive elections.

title: Braid: Calgary blanked in Liberal cabinet again; prairies don't do much better
body:
Wednesday's Liberal cabinet shuffle came with a sharp slap in the face for Calgary.
Once again the city has no federal minister, even though there's a local Liberal MP, George Chahal from Skyview.
Chahal dealt himself out of cabinet after the 2021 election. He'd been caught removing a competitor's campaign 
brochure from a doorstep.
Chahal was found in violation of election rules and fined $500( https://calgaryherald.com/news/local-news/calgary-
skyview-mp-george-chahal-pays-500-penalty-for-flyer-removal-incident ).
"It's just a late night on an election campaign," Chahal said afterward. "Call it a dumb mistake or brain fog - it really 
doesn't matter why I did what I did.
"I think what matters is I did it and I acknowledged it fully, openly, publicly."
Dumb it certainly was, but Chahal has done his penance for two years. His offence was relatively minor.
Prime Minister Justin Trudeau has twice been found in formal conflict of interest, for the Aga Khan holiday and 
again in the SNC-Lavalin affair.
On Wednesday, MP Mary Ng kept her job as minister of international trade, export promotion and economic 
development.
Last December, she was ruled to be in conflict for awarding two government contracts to a company owned by a 
friend( https://calgaryherald.com/news/national/trade-minister-mary-ng-hopes-public-sees-her-sincerity-since-
admitting-ethics-error/wcm/fc02f876-cd50-4b46-9519-f9997c2d91e7 ).
Helping family or friends financially is the clearest no-no to any politician with the vaguest notion of ethics rules. But 
Ng is from Markham-Thornhill in the Greater Toronto Area, sacred Liberal land.
Chahal should qualify for sainthood in this company. But he gets no cabinet post, not even a minor chunk of a 
ministry with mixed responsibilities (labour and seniors lumped together, in one odd case.)
Page 2 of 3
Braid: Calgary blanked in Liberal cabinet again; prairies don't do much better
FILE PHOTO: Prime Minister Justin Trudeau was in town to rally with then-candidate George Chahal at the 
Whitehorn Community Centre in Calgary on Thursday, August 19, 2021.
That leaves Randy Boissonnault as the only Alberta voice in cabinet( https://calgaryherald.com/news/local-
news/doubling-down-local-mp-reacts-to-justin-trudeaus-pre-election-cabinet-shuffle/wcm/a8f0c48b-87b0-4c86-
b4f9-c610f60d3b69 ). He gets a promotion from tourism to employment, workforce development and official 
languages.
The workforce part could be significant, and controversial, if it bears on Liberal plans for transition from oil and gas 
to green jobs.
It's unusual for an MP from outside Quebec to get responsibility for official languages. But francophones across the 
prairies will be pleased by this recognition that they exist.
Edmonton will do fine with Boissonnault in cabinet. Mayor Amarjeet Sohi, a former federal energy minister, also 
has heavy-duty connections.
But Calgary is blanked. It's unfathomable that the Liberals would snub one of Canada's most important cities when 
a perfectly serviceable MP is available.
Randy Boissonnault arrives for a cabinet swearing-in ceremony at Rideau Hall in Ottawa on Wednesday, July 26, 
2023.
Nationally, the imbalance is striking.
The prairie provinces, from the eastern border of Manitoba to the west side of Alberta, are home to nearly seven 
million people.
They are represented by exactly two cabinet ministers - Boissonnault and Dan Vandal, from Winnipeg. Vandal is 
responsible for prairie economic development.
Part of the reason for the imbalance, obviously, is that the prairies don't elect many Liberals.
Saskatchewan has no Liberal MPs. Manitoba elected four in 2021.
With Alberta's two Liberals, that's a talent pool of six for the whole prairie region, 1,500 kilometres across.
Trudeau doesn't have much to work with but, still, he could easily have elevated Chahal and picked a second 
minister from Manitoba.
With four regional ministers, at least he'd seem to be trying.
Dan Vandal arrives for a cabinet swearing-in ceremony at Rideau Hall in Ottawa on Wednesday, July 26, 2023.
Nationally, the dominance of Quebec and Ontario in cabinet is almost absolute.
Quebec has 11 ministers, Ontario 17.
B.C. has the next highest provincial total with four, followed by two ministers for Newfoundland and Labrador.
Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick have one each.
Small consolation; the lopsided regional count has been even worse.
In the 1980 election, then-prime minister Pierre Trudeau's comeback, the Liberals won a majority with no seats 
west of Winnipeg.
Page 3 of 3
Braid: Calgary blanked in Liberal cabinet again; prairies don't do much better
Somewhat alarmed, hoping to do better, they held their next party convention in Winnipeg, where I was offered an 
interview with the prime minister.
I don't recall much of what Trudeau said, but do remember vividly that during more than 30 minutes of questions 
and answers about the state of the party in the west, he gazed right past me, never once making eye contact.
That always struck me as weirdly appropriate. Today, even more so.
Don Braid's column appears regularly in the Herald

title: Braid: Trudeau's secret weapon; Axe the Tax means Ruin the Rebate
body:
Albertans receive far higher carbon tax rebates from Ottawa than any other Canadians.
A family of four will get $1,800 annually, up from $1,544 last year.
In Ontario, this year's benefit is $1,120.
Per capita, Albertans burn more fuel and emit more carbon than other Canadians.
That means higher levels of carbon tax - and more money back from what's now called the Canada Carbon 
Rebate.( https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/liberals-announce-new-name-for-carbon-rebates-in-rebrand-
effort/wcm/fff5208a-b2b4-4642-98d8-2ac5d6e20542 )
Weirdly, Albertans are rewarded for doing exactly what Ottawa wants to prevent, emitting carbon.
But how many Alberta families would be thrilled to lose those quarterly political kickbacks if the tax is scrapped 
entirely?
Not many, probably. Rebates are the Liberals' covert weapon in the next election.
Under the Liberal plan, rebates will keep climbing until the carbon price hits $170 per tonne in 2030.
By that time, the Alberta rebate could be more than $4,000 per family. That's a lot of cash to forsake.
Prime Minister Justin Trudeau won't back away from the April 1 carbon tax increase, even though it's opposed by 
seven premiers and 70 per cent of Canadians.
The PM doesn't see the tax as a demerit. In fact, he behaves as if it's his most potent weapon.
Prime Minister Justin Trudeau meets with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith in Calgary on Wednesday, March 13, 
2024.
Trudeau suggested in Alberta this week that his noble duty is to raise the tax so he can send us more cash.
There's little logic to this argument. Historically, however, voters have shown that money is a far more powerful 
motivator than common sense.
Page 2 of 3
Braid: Trudeau's secret weapon; Axe the Tax means Ruin the Rebate
Kill the tax, lose the cash. Simple as that.
The Liberals may look crushed right now, but they are masters at rescuing themselves with such long-term 
calculation, or cynicism.
After Alberta, Saskatchewan gets the highest rebates - or did, until the province stopped collecting and paying tax( 
https://calgaryherald.com/opinion/columnists/braid-smith-sovereignty-act-moe-ottawa-carbon-tax-electricity ) on 
natural gas for home heating.
The Saskatchewan case - as well as the home heating oil exemption - shows what happens when the tax is 
successfully opposed or obligingly reduced.
The Saskatchewan rebate for a family of four is supposed to be $1,504 this year. Last year, it was $1,360.
But the rebate will now diminish because of the tax revolt, the feds say.
Saskatchewan's move is supposed to save the average family $400 annually in carbon tax paid.
Trimmed federal rebates could easily eat up that benefit.
Related
Trudeau says federal government willing to work with Alberta on tailored pharmacare( 
https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/feds-willing-work-with-alberta-tailored-pharmacare-justin-trudeau )
Trudeau stands by environment minister as Smith calls for Guilbeault to be turfed( 
https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/environment-minister-steven-guilbeault-staying-put )
Smith continues to push against carbon tax hike in meeting with Trudeau( 
https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/smith-continues-to-push-against-carbon-tax-hike-in-meeting-with-trudeau )
Trudeau pushes back as Smith and other premiers express concern about carbon tax hike( 
https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/albertas-smith-urges-trudeau-to-heed-concerns-on-carbon-levy )
The Liberals' controversialsuspension of tax on home heating oil( https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/trudeau-
pulls-carbon-tax-from-home-heating-oil/wcm/2790f13b-680f-4f8d-9c3b-63c38d232511 ) carries the same warning.
Because of tax now unpaid, rebates will be significantly lower in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and 
Newfoundland and Labrador.
In the latter, for instance, the rebate will drop from $1,312 to $1,192 for a family of four.
P.E.I. will see a decline from $992 to $880.
Small change, you might say, but the caution is clear - if the carbon tax is abolished, every penny goes away.
People in the Atlantic provinces, especially those who don't use home heating oil, could start to see the carve-out 
as a penalty rather than a benefit.
The federal Conservatives are drawing huge support for their Axe the Tax campaign. They haven't yet faced the 
inevitable Liberal charge that they'd also Ruin the Rebate.
Leader Pierre Poilievre points out that the tax trickles into higher prices for many items, including food.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre
Page 3 of 3
Braid: Trudeau's secret weapon; Axe the Tax means Ruin the Rebate
Standing beside truck cabs in Winnipeg, he said, "Everything transported in these trucks becomes more expensive 
because of the Trudeau tax on carbon and on diesel."
He's not wrong there, but the cost of the tax isn't nearly as visible as the rebate for paying it.
For instance, the April 1 carbon tax hike will raise gasoline prices about three cents per litre.
On the rebate side, that higher tax will bring Alberta families $256 more per year.
You'd have to buy 8,533 litres of gasoline to pay $256 in extra carbon tax - 100 to 150 fill-ups, depending on the 
vehicle.
Is there any real connection between the carbon tax and the rebates? That's not clear, or even likely.
But there's no doubt about the latent political power of Liberal tax math.

title: briefly
body:
A German businessman with Alberta roots is suing the CBC for linking him to the alleged Airbus kickback scheme. 
A lawyer for Karlheinz Schreiber filed a defamation suit Wednesday seeking $ 35 million from the CBC for 
damaging his reputation in its television program The Fifth Estate. The CBC linked Schreiber to a controversy 
surrounding Air Canada's purchase of 34 jetliners in 1988 from Europe-based Airbus for $ 1.8 billion.
Quebec City police livid
at French-only charge
QUEBEC -- Quebec City police said Wednesday they can speak English to suspects, despite claims by two 
arrested Ontario teens who said they couldn't defend themselves because they couldn't speak French. Jason 
Mirlocca and Sean Richards, both 18 and from Pickering, Ont., were charged with assault amid a series of scuffles 
between tourists and Quebec City residents on the weekend. Their lawyer said Tuesday no bilingual officers were 
on duty when the pair was detained. Police chief Normand Bergeron has denied the 18-year-olds' story.
Second candidate joins
race for helm of B.C. NDP
VICTORIA -- A second candidate emerged Wednesday to replace Mike Harcourt as premier of British Columbia. 
NDP backbencher Corky Evans, a popular figure within the party, was to formally announce his candidacy 
Wednesday night. The only other declared candidate is an unknown funeral director named Jack McDonald.
Possible Wells successors
await decision from Tobin
ST. JOHN'S, Nfld. -- Brian Tobin's possible return to Newfoundland politics has prompted senior Liberal cabinet 
ministers to quell their own ambitions of replacing outgoing Premier Clyde Wells. At least five architects of 
government policy long seen as possible successors to Wells are waiting for a decision from the popular federal 
fisheries minister. Tobin has said only he is considering his options. Rex Gibbons, Newfoundland's natural 
resources minister, said Wednesday he will probably run for the job -- if Tobin stays in Ottawa.
Sentencing postponed
in exorcism death
Page 2 of 3
briefly
KITCHENER, Ont. -- The sentencing of a woman who pleaded guilty in what police described as the exorcism 
death of her two-year-old granddaughter was postponed Wednesday while a psychiatric report is completed. Ana 
Maria Canhoto, 43, is to return to court Monday. Although Canhoto pleaded guilty to manslaughter last summer, 
she now believes the girl's death was an act of vengeance by the devil, a psychologist testified.
Use closed military bases
as prisons, Reformer says
VANCOUVER -- Canada should use closed military bases to house low-risk offenders rather than building more 
prisons to solve the overcrowding problem, says Reform MP Randy White. He said he got the idea a few weeks 
ago while touring a new $ 5-million prison for 60 women in Edmonton. The federal government could have used the 
recently closed military base in Calgary, he said Tuesday.
Four leaders absent
from mission to India
Three premiers and one territorial leader will be missing when Prime Minister Jean Chretien leads a mission to 
India, Pakistan, Malaysia and Indonesia on Monday. Saskatchewan Premier Roy Romano, Don Morin, leader of 
the Northwest Territories, Alberta Premier Ralph Klein and Jacques Parizeau will be absent.
Constitutional veto deal
worked out in Maritimes
CHARLOTTETOWN -- Prince Edward Island has cracked a deal to share in the federal government's 
constitutional veto for the Atlantic region. New Brunswick Premier Frank McKenna and Nova Scotia Premier 
John Savage have agreed to extend to P.E.I. full status under the new veto rule. Because of the Island's tiny 
population, it was the only province under the formula that could not invoke the veto with only one other province. 
Under the deal being drafted with New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, P.E.I. automatically gets the support of both 
provinces to invoke the veto if it gets the agreement of either provincial government.
Body of frozen man
identified as Dal student
DARTMOUTH, N.S. -- The frozen body of a man found in Dartmouth was identified Wednesday as that of a 
Dalhousie University student. Shannon Bright, 26, was reported missing after he failed to return from a walk Dec. 
23. Police aided by a tracking dog found his body Wednesday morning in a wooded area after receiving a tip.

title: British Columbians to see limited relief in holiday tax break; Ottawa's cut doesn't extend to PST, putting onus
body:
British Columbians will be saving less than many other Canadians during the federal government's GST-HST tax 
break.
The holiday relief from federal sales tax, announced Thursday, applies to the GST or HST on grocery items, 
restaurant meals, some alcoholic beverages, children's clothing and toys, print newspapers and Christmas trees 
from Dec. 14 to Feb. 15.
The tax break is expected to save Canadians about $1.6 billion over two months.
But British Columbians - who pay five per cent GST and seven per cent provincial sales tax at the till - are going to 
be saving only the GST on qualifying items while still paying the PST. Meanwhile, consumers in the five provinces 
that have an HST will save 13 per cent or 15 per cent on their purchases.
The harmonized sales tax, or HST, is collected by the federal government, which then sends the provincial share to 
the respective provincial governments.
It would be up to the B.C. government to remove its PST if it chooses to do so.
Postmedia News reached out to Premier David Eby's office to ask whether the province plans to cut the PST over 
the holidays, but did not receive a response.
In a news release outlining the savings, the federal Finance Department said a family in B.C. who spent $2,000 on 
qualifying items would save about $100 over the two months.
But a family in Ontario that spent $2,000 on the same basket of goods would get about $260 in savings, more than 
double the B.C. tax break, because Ontario has a 13 per cent HST.
"The issue with the HST is that it would have been very difficult to only charge the provincial component," said 
Steeve Mongrain, an economics professor at Simon Fraser University.
Instead, Ottawa would likely strike a deal with provinces with HST.
Page 2 of 3
British Columbians to see limited relief in holiday tax break; Ottawa's cut doesn't extend to PST, putting onus 
on Eby to follow suit
"In Ontario, for example, I don't know what agreement they have. Would the federal government absorb and remit 
the provincial share to the province, or is the province willing to join in and face the fiscal burden of giving up the tax 
(revenue)?" New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt appeared surprised by the federal announcement, telling CBC 
News the tax cut could cost her province $62 million in revenue. She said she expected Ottawa to "help keep us 
whole."
Carson Binda, B.C. director with the Canadian Taxpayers Federation, said he believes the federal government will 
need to reimburse at least some of the provinces for lost HST revenue after examining its tax agreements with 
them. But B.C. would likely not be reimbursed if it removed its PST.
"That's a problem because B.C. is the epicentre of the affordability crisis," he said.
Five provinces in Canada use the HST: Ontario, Newfoundland and Labrador, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, 
and Prince Edward Island. B.C. adopted the single-tax HST in 2010, but reverted to separate GST and PST three 
years later after a thin majority voted to scrap the HST in a binding provincewide referendum in 2011.
Binda said B.C.'s large deficit may have "eroded the province's ability to be flexible to match the federal tax cut. 
Fiscal irresponsibility has consequences."
He would rather have seen the federal government make permanent tax cuts, or halt expected tax hikes, such as 
the carbon tax increase.
"Tax cuts, not just temporary holidays, are the solution," he said. "This is a Band-Aid."
Prime Minister Justin Trudeau also announced Ottawa will be distributing a $250 cheque next spring to every 
Canadian who earned less than $150,000 a year. The rebate is expected to be distributed to 18.7 million 
Canadians before the next election.
The rebate makes better sense than the temporary GST-HST tax break, Mongrain said.
The tax break is difficult for retailers - who have to adjust till programming, among other things - and opens the door 
to tax evasion by shady businesses who may mislabel items. The selection of items that qualify for the tax break 
also seems arbitrary, he said.
"Garments are fine, but not things exclusively for sports. Beer under seven per cent is exempted, but not if it's more 
than that. Wine is, but not spirits. I'd love to have been in that room when they were trying to decide what's 
exempted."
Many items that will receive a GST break are already exempt from B.C.'s PST, including books, newspapers, 
children's clothing, child car seats, basic groceries and restaurant meals, while others, such as artificial Christmas 
trees and toys, are not.
The B.C. government has promised a $1,000 tax cut for the average family every year, starting with a direct rebate 
next year. chchan@postmedia.com gluymes@postmedia.com !@COPYRIGHT=© 2024 Postmedia Network Inc. All 
rights reserved.

title: Brookfield executive grilled on tax record, ties to prime minister; Ethics committee
body:
O T TAWA . Brookfield chief operating officer Justin Beber appeared at the House of Commons ethics committee 
on Monday, but unlike the Canadian singer with a nearly identical name, his presence did not create waves of 
excitement.
For two hours, Beber was repeatedly grilled by opposition MPs about Prime Minister Mark Carney's potential for 
conflicts of interest with Brookfield, Carney's returns of the global investment funds he helped set up at Brookfield, 
but also Brookfield's tax practices.
"Mr. Beber, you've been, I think, a very patient participant in this late-season fishing expedition," said Liberal MP 
Leslie Church about the opposition's attempts to steer the executive away from his carefully crafted statements to 
the ethics committee.
Beber began his remarks by explaining Carney cut ties with Brookfield on Jan. 16, 2025, the same day on which he 
announced his candidacy to become Liberal leader.
"Since then, at no point has anyone at Brookfield spoken with the prime minister about Brookfield business," he 
said. However, when asked by Conservative MP Michael Barrett when he had communicated with Carney, Beber 
admitted he had met him "only once" to discuss the rise of antisemitism in early October. The meeting took place in 
Carney's office, he said.
Beber said he worked with Carney over five years at Brookfield and said he was an "exceptionally talented 
executive and person of great integrity."
Most of the Conservatives' line of questioning was about the funds Carney is entitled to, as former head of transition 
investing for Brookfield Asset Management.
In this role, Carney co-led efforts to raise capital for two major clean energy funds, Global Transition Fund ("BGTF 
I") and the Second Global Transition Fund ("BGTF II").
He was also in the process of raising money for a new fund, the Catalytic Transition Fund ("CTF"), when he left 
Brookfield.
Page 2 of 4
Brookfield executive grilled on tax record, ties to prime minister; Ethics committee
As previously reported by National Post, Carney acquired Brookfield share options and deferred shared units, but 
also potentially tens of millions in undisclosed "carried interest" - essentially, payments based on a fund's 
performance when it reaches maturity.
Beber said Carney is entitled to carried interest payments for BGTF I - which, Beber explained, is set to reach 
maturity in either 2032 or 2034 - but not for the two other transition funds Carney helped create at Brookfield Asset 
Management.
"The reason for that is we were in the process of setting up those funds when Mr. Carney decided to leave 
Brookfield to pursue the Liberal leadership," Beber said.
Pressed by Conservative MP Michael Cooper if he was disputing that Carney stands to make millions, if not tens of 
millions of dollars from those investments, Beber said it was "certainly not a fact."
Carney put all of his assets, except some money and his personal real estate, into a blind trust when he became 
Liberal leader. He has also disclosed all his potential conflicts to the ethics commissioner, who crafted an extensive 
ethics screen for over 100 entities.
But, in the context of the review of the Conflict of Interest Act which the ethics committee is undertaking, the 
Conservatives are pushing for the law to go even further and require lawmakers such as Carney to sell their assets 
to prevent any potential conflicts.
Current and former senior bureaucrats have advised against going that far to not discourage competent leaders 
from the private sector from entering politics.
But Conservatives say that Carney's situation is unique, as former executive of a company which has financial 
interests in a wide range of sectors - such as modular housing, clean energy and artificial intelligence - that the 
government is taking an active interest in.
They pressed Beber to know whether Carney's latest budget would help Brookfield increase its revenues, with the 
executive responding that his firm has 2,000 businesses under its wing and will assess and react to government 
policy in their best interest.
"What we have isn't a Brookfield problem. The reason that you're here is because the prime minister has a 
financial interest in the performance of this company," said Barrett.
Bloc Québécois MP Luc Thériault tried to grill Beber on allegations of tax avoidance involving Brookfield, but Beber 
insisted his company complies with all tax laws. He even declined to say if tax avoidance exists, saying he can only 
speak to Brookfield.
Thériault appeared visibly frustrated by Beber's lack of answers. "After tax avoidance, we have question 
avoidance," he said in French.
Beber also declined to comment on any changes that should be made to the Conflict of Interest Act. "It's very, 
very hard for me to opine on matters that involve legislation and government apparatus that I'm not very familiar 
with," he said.
Duff Conacher, co-founder of Democracy Watch, said Baber confirmed on Monday what Canadians already knew, 
which is that Carney owns Brookfield stock options and carried interest payments that will not come to maturity for 
many years.
Conacher said Carney's situation is "an ongoing, direct and significant financial conflict of interest" because he 
would profit from any decision he makes or participates in that could help any of Brookfield's many businesses 
make more money.
Page 3 of 4
Brookfield executive grilled on tax record, ties to prime minister; Ethics committee
"The only way to ensure integrity in the federal government's policy-making processes is for him to sell these 
investments."

his Liberal leadership candidacy.;

title: Brown, Charest agree to pull punches
body:
The Conservative leadership race is about to get a whole lot more interesting.
Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown - who is expected to announce his bid Sunday - and former Quebec premier Jean 
Charest - who launches his candidacy Thursday - have forged a pact, sources familiar with the strategy tell the Star. 
Could it lead the party to elect a more moderate leader?
The men have been friends for more than 25 years. Brown credits his involvement with the Conservatives to 
Charest, whom he met as a teenager while visiting his aunt, Charest's next-door neighbour in North Hatley, Que.
The two have spoken at length about the leadership race. I'm told to expect neither will say a bad word about the 
other - a non-aggression pact, if you will - and that they will "publicly" help one another.
Their goals are similarly aligned: a united but more inclusive party that represents the country.
Each anticipates the other's supporters will mark him as their second choice on the party's ranked ballots, and they 
may make that clear when members start receiving their ballots this summer.
Charest will meet party members on Thursday evening in Calgary, the Conservative heartland and home turf of 
former prime minister Stephen Harper. Harper has let it be known that he doesn't want Charest to be the next 
leader, and prefers Carleton MP and former cabinet minister Pierre Poilievre take up the mantle.
Although out of politics for a decade, Charest has deep roots in the Progressive Conservative wing of the party. 
Elected in 1984 in Sherbrooke, Que., he became Canada's youngest cabinet minister at age 28. In 1993, he lost a 
bid for the party's leadership, only to take on the role after becoming one of just two PC MPs to survive a federal 
election later that year. He grew the morsel of what was left of the PCs while facing a popular Reform party until 
1998, when he left federal politics to lead Quebec's Liberal party in its fight against the sovereignists. Charest 
served as premier from 2003 until 2012, when the Liberals were defeated.
As premier, he often butted heads with Harper. Charest opposed the federal Conservative government's 
withdrawal from the Kyoto Protocol on greenhouse gas emissions, and introduced Quebec's carbon cap-and-trade 
system. He demanded increases to equalization payments, then used the money for tax cuts, and criticized the 
Tories during the 2008 federal election campaign for their cuts to culture funding.
Last week, an anti-corruption probe into party financing during Charest's tenure as premier finally concluded, 
without charges, clearing the way for his candidacy.
Page 2 of 3
Brown, Charest agree to pull punches
Similarly, on Wednesday a dark cloud hanging over Brown was removed when CTV acknowledged its 2018 story 
on sexual misconduct allegations - which ended Brown's tenure as Ontario's Progressive Conservative leader - 
contained "factually incorrect" information and "required correction."
Brown is expected to announce his leadership bid Sunday in Brampton. Somewhat of an underdog, Brown has 
proven he shouldn't be underestimated. A three-term Conservative MP who was never appointed to Harper's 
cabinet or chosen as a parliamentary secretary, he surprised many observers when he won the Ontario PC 
leadership in 2015 after out-organizing front-runner Christine Elliott.
Brown brought ethnic communities into the party's fold, as well as firefighters and nurses. He said the party's 
membership didn't represent "modern Ontario," and as leader, he sought to make the party more centrist, 
announcing his support for carbon pricing.
Brown is expected to repeat that strategy federally. He'll need to sign up 200,000 to 300,000 party members if he 
plans to beat Poilievre, the current front-runner. While Brown's network of allies focuses its efforts in Ontario, 
Charest's team plans to ensure his dominance in Quebec.Could Poilievre win the leadership without winning 
Quebec or Ontario? It would be hard, but it's not impossible - in the Conservatives' 2017 leadership vote, Maxime 
Bernier won both provinces in the first round before falling to Andrew Scheer.
To win this time, Charest and Brown need to change the makeup of the party, and dilute the influence of hard-core 
social conservatives, anti-vaxxers, those who harbour western grievances, those fearful of new immigrants, those 
prone to believe conspiracy theories involving the World Economic Forum, and those who don't believe humans 
cause climate change.
But just because organizers ask new party members to support Charest or Brown as their second choice doesn't 
mean they will.
Brown's staunch opposition to Quebec's discriminatory Bill 21, a law that prevents those who wear religious 
symbols from holding certain public-sector jobs, may prove to be too big a challenge for some Charest voters - and 
Quebec caucus members - to overcome. Charest's spokesperson, Michelle Coates Mather, said he is opposed to 
Bill 21 and will argue that if the law comes before the Supreme Court, the federal government should intervene in 
the case. But that's different than asking voters to support a candidate like Brown, who is seen in Quebec as 
meddling in provincial affairs by rallying city councils across the country to donate to legal efforts to fight the law.
Similarly, the tens of thousands of Tamils, Sikhs, Lebanese and Iraqis that Brown may sign up - whose 
communities tend to include many people with more religious and conservative outlooks - could prefer a challenger 
such as Leslyn Lewis, the MP for Haldimand-Norfolk and the favourite of social conservative groups Campaign Life 
Coalition and Right Now, rather than Charest, a pro-choice candidate.
Alliances and endorsements don't always work as planned. Campaign Life Coalition told its members during the 
2020 Conservative leadership race not to support Erin O'Toole. Still, many marked O'Toole's name on their ballots, 
giving him the victory. This time, Campaign Life Coalition is telling its members not to support Poilievre because he 
is "pro-abortion." Will they still mark Poilievre on their ballots, in hopes of avoiding a Charest or Brown win?
It's too easy to paint this Brown-Charest alliance as one involving a stalking horse. Brown will put a lot on the line, 
likely walking away from significant sums of money from CTV in order to put his lawsuit and the controversy behind 
him, and possibly closing the door on running again to become mayor in Brampton. The deadline for nomination 
papers in that contest is Aug. 19. The Conservative party chooses its next leader Sept. 10. Similarly, Charest is in it 
to win.
When Brown was in high school, he used to do his homework in his parents' basement, which was plastered with 
political posters, including one of Charest. Now, it's possible he'll help his political friend become prime minister - 
or maybe it will be Charest who helps him.

title: Cabinet minister toured pot warehouse just before RCMP raid
body:
A New Brunswick provincial cabinet minister toured a cannabis warehouse only a few weeks before RCMP 
raided the facility in Madawaska First Nation that the force said was linked to organized crime, Brunswick News has 
learned.
Luke Randall, the minister responsible for Cannabis NB stores and Opportunities New Brunswick, acknowledged 
on Wednesday he did a friendly tour of Madawaska Warehouse and some pot shops in the Indigenous community 
beside Edmundston on March 30.
The tour was part of back-channel negotiations with First Nations, undisclosed by the Liberal government, about 
finding a way to bring the sale of the recreational drugs into the provincial network.
“What we are exploring at Cannabis NB is how we can ensure safe supply in every community in the province, 
whether that’s an Indigenous community or whether that’s another community,” Randall said in an interview, 
describing Madawaska First Nation as “a really interesting case.”
“They’re the only community in New Brunswick that’s been able to work under the federal act, to create the 
framework and structure for a legal cannabis supply within their community. So, we were very interested to see how 
that was working, how they engaged in that work, and whether there was an opportunity for us to be able to 
collaborate to ensure that safe, legal supply is available in every single community in this province.”
Randall said he and Indigenous Affairs Minister Keith Chiasson had recently sent letters to all 15 First Nations 
chiefs and councils asking to discuss ways they could integrate the cannabis sales in their communities with the 
provincial network.
But those negotiations have been put at risk because of the RCMP raid on Madawaska Warehouse at 4 a.m. on 
April 26.
Randall said no one at Opportunities NB or the Department of Finance and Treasury Board was informed ahead of 
time about the police action, which came as a huge surprise to him.

Page 2 of 4
Cabinet minister toured pot warehouse just before RCMP raid
The Mounties swooped in with more than 20 vehicles at that wee hour, confiscating most of the products at the 
cannabis warehouse. The business acted as a private wholesaler that would ship merchandise to pot shops, mostly 
to other First Nations.
The police also executed a search warrant at the home of Cindy Bernard, who ran the business. She is the niece of 
Madawaska First Nation’s Chief Patricia Bernard and the daughter of John Bernard, the successful businessman 
who owns the Grey Rock casino.
The father, who owns the warehouse but rented the facility to his daughter so she could run her business, told 
Brunswick News in an interview that the RCMP raid was violent, traumatizing and completely uncalled for.
He said his daughter and son-in-law were arrested in front of their two young children, creating panic and fear.
“For God’s sake, the province and its officials, including the minister, were visiting the warehouse just a month 
ago,” John Bernard said. “The province felt horrible after the raid because there had been such a lack of trust 
between the First Nations and the province for so long, and it was finally this new Liberal government that was 
trying to build that relationship back up again. And this did not help. It hurts the relationship.”
Randall met with the Madawaska chief and a couple of First Nations councillors the day he had toured the pot 
facilities with a few government officials in tow.
He and Chiasson also talked to Chief Bernard immediately after the raid, by videoconference.
She has declined comment on the issue, citing the police investigation.
Asked if the provincial Department of Justice and Public Safety knew ahead of time about the raid, Randall said 
he’d leave that question to Robert Gauvin, the public safety minister.
Through a spokesperson, Gauvin told Brunswick News on Thursday he would not comment on an ongoing 
investigation.
The RCMP told Brunswick News last week that it had executed search warrants simultaneously at the cannabis 
distribution centre in Madawaska and five other locations, one in the First Nation, three in Nova Scotia and another 
in Hamilton, Ont.
They did not provide many details but said the operation targeted organized crime, drug trafficking, and money 
laundering. Arrests were made but so far no one has been charged in court.
John Bernard said the other locations were all homes, places where employees of Madawaska Warehouse lived.
Brunswick News asked the Mounties on Thursday if charges were pending.
“We have no further updates,” said Cst. Marie-Pierre Guertin, who works in the RCMP’s eastern region office in 
Montreal. “This file is still under investigation for the time being.”
Cannabis NB, a provincial Crown corporation run like NB Liquor stores, is the only place in New Brunswick people 
can legally buy recreational weed products.
When Ottawa legalized cannabis in 2018, First Nations wanted a cut of the proceeds, arguing they had Aboriginal 
and treaty rights to sell the plant products in their communities. But New Brunswick ignored these wishes and 
monopolized the sale.
Within no time, dozens of pot shops opened in the defiant 15 First Nations in New Brunswick. Up until April, police 
in New Brunswick largely turned a blind eye to these activities as long as they stayed on reserves.
Taking the initiative, Madawaska First Nation passed its own law in 2023 regulating the cannabis and tobacco trade
Page 3 of 4
Cabinet minister toured pot warehouse just before RCMP raid
However, such legislation isn’t granted explicit permission in the federal Cannabis Act and it hasn’t been tested in 
court.
The new regime included inspections of the wholesaler and three pot shops in the community to make sure they 
were abiding by the regulations.
But it did nothing to shield the warehouse from the RCMP raid.
John Bernard said the initial news report of the police raid bothered him because it largely quoted the RCMP, who 
said organized crime groups “exploit situations of vulnerability in certain communities, including Indigenous 
communities, to carry out their criminal activities.”
He scoffed at that characterization.
“Everybody’s thinking, ‘Oh my God, it’s the Hell’s Angels or the mafia or the Sopranos.’ It’s nothing like that.”
Bernard said about a dozen police officers stormed his daughter’s house in the First Nation, where she lives with 
her husband and children, eight and two years old.
“It’s crazy what the RCMP did. At four in the morning, they’re banging on Cindy’s door. They arrest her and her 
husband right in front of their children. Her son, he’s only eight years old, he’s looking down with all the cops there, 
and one of them had a mask on, and the poor little guy was terrified. And they put his parents in handcuffs and led 
them away.”
Bernard said his son-in-law’s mother happened to be visiting at the time, so at least she was there to take care of 
the kids.
The couple were detained briefly at the RCMP’s detachment in St-Leonard, 42 km south, and then released.
The businessman reviewed his security cameras after the raid was over and wasn’t impressed.
The RCMP first surrounded his security guard who was in a truck in the parking lot and arrested him. Then they 
broke down the door of Madawaska Warehouse, where no one was working at the time.
“They saw the license from the First Nation on the wall and they ripped it down. They were all laughing at it. I know 
this because I have footage of the whole thing.”
Bernard said when the police left, they put a piece of plywood across the doorway. The 15 or so people who worked 
there during the day are now out of a job, he added.
Randall, meanwhile, said the Liberal government wouldn’t give up on trying to integrate First Nations pot sales into 
the provincial fold. But he expressed frustration with Health Canada rules and federal legislation that he said made 
it hard to strike a deal.
Cannabis NB’s profits in the last quarter were down a whopping 20 per cent compared to the same time last year. 
CEO Lori Stickles largely blamed the black market for undercutting legal sales.
Randall said it was difficult to know where people were buying all their cannabis, but he didn’t think Indigenous pot 
shops were the main reason behind the drop in legal sales. He pointed the finger at shady foreign sellers who send 
illegal products by mail, using Canada Post.
“Many of those products are packaged as if, you know, they’re a snack good or a candy product. We’re really 
concerned about that product that’s coming from outside of province from websites that we can’t control.”
- with files from Andrew Waugh

The tour was part of back-channel negotiations with First Nations, undisclosed by the Liberal government, about 
finding a way to bring the sale of the recreational drugs into the provincial network.
“What we are exploring at Cannabis NB is how we can ensure safe supply in every community in the province, 
whether that’s an Indigenous community or whether that’s another community,” Randall said in an interview, 
describing Madawaska First Nation as “a really interesting case.”
“They’re the only community in New Brunswick that’s been able to work under the federal act, to create the 
framework and structure for a legal cannabis supply within their community. So, we were very interested to see how 
that was working, how they engaged in that work, and whether there was an opportunity for us to be able to 
collaborate to ensure that safe, legal supply is available in every single community in this province.”
Randall said he and Indigenous Affairs Minister Keith Chiasson had recently sent letters to all 15 First Nations 
chiefs and councils asking to discuss ways they could integrate the cannabis sales in their communities with the 
provincial network.
But those negotiations have been put at risk because of the RCMP raid on Madawaska Warehouse at 4 a.m. on 
April 26.
Randall said no one at Opportunities NB or the Department of Finance and Treasury Board was informed ahead of 
time about the police action, which came as a huge surprise to him.

Page 2 of 4
Cabinet minister toured pot warehouse just before RCMP raid
The Mounties swooped in with more than 20 vehicles at that wee hour, confiscating most of the products at the 
cannabis warehouse. The business acted as a private wholesaler that would ship merchandise to pot shops, mostly 
to other First Nations.
The police also executed a search warrant at the home of Cindy Bernard, who ran the business. She is the niece of 
Madawaska First Nation’s Chief Patricia Bernard and the daughter of John Bernard, the successful businessman 
who owns the Grey Rock casino.
The father, who owns the warehouse but rented the facility to his daughter so she could run her business, told 
Brunswick News in an interview that the RCMP raid was violent, traumatizing and completely uncalled for.
He said his daughter and son-in-law were arrested in front of their two young children, creating panic and fear.
“For God’s sake, the province and its officials, including the minister, were visiting the warehouse just a month 
ago,” John Bernard said. “The province felt horrible after the raid because there had been such a lack of trust 
between the First Nations and the province for so long, and it was finally this new Liberal government that was 
trying to build that relationship back up again. And this did not help. It hurts the relationship.”
Randall met with the Madawaska chief and a couple of First Nations councillors the day he had toured the pot 
facilities with a few government officials in tow.
He and Chiasson also talked to Chief Bernard immediately after the raid, by videoconference.
She has declined comment on the issue, citing the police investigation.
Asked if the provincial Department of Justice and Public Safety knew ahead of time about the raid, Randall said 
he’d leave that question to Robert Gauvin, the public safety minister.
Through a spokesperson, Gauvin told Brunswick News on Thursday he would not comment on an ongoing 
investigation.
The RCMP told Brunswick News last week that it had executed search warrants simultaneously at the cannabis 
distribution centre in Madawaska and five other locations, one in the First Nation, three in Nova Scotia and another 
in Hamilton, Ont.
They did not provide many details but said the operation targeted organized crime, drug trafficking, and money 
laundering. Arrests were made but so far no one has been charged in court.
John Bernard said the other locations were all homes, places where employees of Madawaska Warehouse lived.
Brunswick News asked the Mounties on Thursday if charges were pending.
“We have no further updates,” said Cst. Marie-Pierre Guertin, who works in the RCMP’s eastern region office in 
Montreal. “This file is still under investigation for the time being.”
Cannabis NB, a provincial Crown corporation run like NB Liquor stores, is the only place in New Brunswick people 
can legally buy recreational weed products.
When Ottawa legalized cannabis in 2018, First Nations wanted a cut of the proceeds, arguing they had Aboriginal 
and treaty rights to sell the plant products in their communities. But New Brunswick ignored these wishes and 
monopolized the sale.
Within no time, dozens of pot shops opened in the defiant 15 First Nations in New Brunswick. Up until April, police 
in New Brunswick largely turned a blind eye to these activities as long as they stayed on reserves.
Taking the initiative, Madawaska First Nation passed its own law in 2023 regulating the cannabis and tobacco trade
Page 3 of 4
Cabinet minister toured pot warehouse just before RCMP raid
However, such legislation isn’t granted explicit permission in the federal Cannabis Act and it hasn’t been tested in 
court.
The new regime included inspections of the wholesaler and three pot shops in the community to make sure they 
were abiding by the regulations.
But it did nothing to shield the warehouse from the RCMP raid.
John Bernard said the initial news report of the police raid bothered him because it largely quoted the RCMP, who 
said organized crime groups “exploit situations of vulnerability in certain communities, including Indigenous 
communities, to carry out their criminal activities.”
He scoffed at that characterization.
“Everybody’s thinking, ‘Oh my God, it’s the Hell’s Angels or the mafia or the Sopranos.’ It’s nothing like that.”
Bernard said about a dozen police officers stormed his daughter’s house in the First Nation, where she lives with 
her husband and children, eight and two years old.
“It’s crazy what the RCMP did. At four in the morning, they’re banging on Cindy’s door. They arrest her and her 
husband right in front of their children. Her son, he’s only eight years old, he’s looking down with all the cops there, 
and one of them had a mask on, and the poor little guy was terrified. And they put his parents in handcuffs and led 
them away.”
Bernard said his son-in-law’s mother happened to be visiting at the time, so at least she was there to take care of 
the kids.
The couple were detained briefly at the RCMP’s detachment in St-Leonard, 42 km south, and then released.
The businessman reviewed his security cameras after the raid was over and wasn’t impressed.
The RCMP first surrounded his security guard who was in a truck in the parking lot and arrested him. Then they 
broke down the door of Madawaska Warehouse, where no one was working at the time.
“They saw the license from the First Nation on the wall and they ripped it down. They were all laughing at it. I know 
this because I have footage of the whole thing.”
Bernard said when the police left, they put a piece of plywood across the doorway. The 15 or so people who worked 
there during the day are now out of a job, he added.
Randall, meanwhile, said the Liberal government wouldn’t give up on trying to integrate First Nations pot sales into 
the provincial fold. But he expressed frustration with Health Canada rules and federal legislation that he said made 
it hard to strike a deal.
Cannabis NB’s profits in the last quarter were down a whopping 20 per cent compared to the same time last year. 
CEO Lori Stickles largely blamed the black market for undercutting legal sales.
Randall said it was difficult to know where people were buying all their cannabis, but he didn’t think Indigenous pot 
shops were the main reason behind the drop in legal sales. He pointed the finger at shady foreign sellers who send 
illegal products by mail, using Canada Post.
“Many of those products are packaged as if, you know, they’re a snack good or a candy product. We’re really 
concerned about that product that’s coming from outside of province from websites that we can’t control.”

title: Calgary blanked in federal cabinet; Unfathomable the Liberals would snub one of Canada's most important
body:
Wednesday's Liberal cabinet shuffle came with a sharp slap in the face for Calgary.
Once again the city has no federal minister, even though there's a local Liberal MP, George
Chahal from Skyview.
Chahal dealt himself out of cabinet after the 2021 election. He'd been caught removing a competitor's campaign 
brochure from a doorstep.
Chahal was found in violation of election rules and fined $500.
"It's just a late night on an election campaign," Chahal said afterward. "Call it a dumb mistake or brain fog - it really 
doesn't matter why I did what I did.
"I think what matters is I did it and I acknowledged it fully,
openly, publicly."
Dumb it certainly was, but Chahal has done his penance for two years. His offence was relatively minor.
Prime Minister Justin Trudeau has twice been found in formal conflict of interest, for the Aga Khan holiday and 
again in the SNC-Lavalin affair.
On Wednesday, MP Mary Ng kept her job as minister of international trade, export promotion and economic 
development.
Last December, she was ruled to be in conflict for awarding two government contracts to a company owned by a 
friend.
Helping family or friends financially is the clearest no-no to any politician with the vaguest notion of ethics rules. But 
Ng is from Markham-Thornhill in the Greater Toronto Area, sacred Liberal land.
Page 2 of 3
Calgary blanked in federal cabinet; Unfathomable the Liberals would snub one of Canada's most important 
cities
Chahal should qualify for sainthood in this company. But he gets no cabinet post, not even a minor chunk of a 
ministry with mixed responsibilities (labour and seniors lumped together, in one odd case.)
That leaves Randy Boissonnault as the only Alberta voice in cabinet. He gets a promotion from tourism to 
employment, workforce development and official languages.
The workforce part could be significant, and controversial, if it bears on Liberal plans for transition from oil and gas 
to green jobs.
It's unusual for an MP from outside Quebec to get responsibility for official languages. But francophones across the 
prairies will be pleased by this recognition that they exist.
Edmonton will do fine with Boissonnault in cabinet. Mayor Amarjeet Sohi, a former federal energy minister, also 
has heavy-duty connections.
But Calgary is blanked. It's unfathomable that the Liberals would snub one of Canada's most important cities when 
a perfectly serviceable MP is available.
Nationally, the imbalance is striking.
The prairie provinces, from the eastern border of Manitoba to the west side of Alberta, are home to nearly seven 
million people.
They are represented by exactly two cabinet ministers - Boissonnault and Dan Vandal, from Winnipeg. Vandal is 
responsible for prairie economic development.
Part of the reason for the imbalance, obviously, is that the prairies don't elect many Liberals.
Saskatchewan has no Liberal MPs. Manitoba elected four in 2021.
With Alberta's two Liberals, that's a talent pool of six for the whole prairie region, 1,500 kilometres across.
Trudeau doesn't have much to work with but, still, he could easily have elevated Chahal and picked a second 
minister from Manitoba.
With four regional ministers, at least he'd seem to be trying.
Nationally, the dominance of Quebec and Ontario in cabinet is almost absolute.
Quebec has 11 ministers, Ontario 17.
B.C. has the next highest provincial total with four, followed by two ministers for Newfoundland and Labrador.
Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick have one each.
Small consolation; the lopsided regional count has been even worse.
In the 1980 election, thenprime minister Pierre Trudeau's comeback, the Liberals won a majority with no seats 
west of Winnipeg.
Somewhat alarmed, hoping to do better, they held their next party convention in Winnipeg, where I was offered an 
interview with the prime minister.
I don't recall much of what Trudeau said, but do remember vividly that during more than 30 minutes of questions 
and answers about the state of the party in the west, he gazed right past me, never once making eye contact.
That always struck me as weirdly appropriate. Today, even more so.

cities
