title: FIRST READING: The baggage Mark Carney is bringing to his prime ministerial bid
body:
TOP STORY
As candidates line up to become Justin Trudeau's successor as leader of the Liberal Party of Canada, former 
central banker Mark Carney has arguably been in the running for the position longer than anyone else.
In fact, talk of Carney as Liberal leader goes all the way back to 2012, just after the party's historic defeat in the 
2011 federal election. "Why don't I become a circus clown?" was Carney's riposte to the suggestion at the time.
With Carney expected to officially announce his candidacy this week, he's already wading through a tide of political 
baggage - much of which didn't exist in 2012. Below, a quick summary of how Carney is already on the defensive 
as he begins his campaign to become Canada's next prime minister.
He's in a photo with Ghislaine Maxwell
In a pair of photos captured in 2013, Carney can be seen chatting with Ghislaine Maxwell. Taken at the Wilderness 
Festival - a U.K. music and arts festival that brands itself as a destination for "wholesome hedonism" - it shows a 
smiling Carney standing next to Maxwell along with his wife Diana Fox.
At the time, Maxwell was mostly known as a British socialite seen often in the company of charismatic U.S. financier 
Jeffrey Epstein. Now, she's serving a 20-year jail term for assisting Epstein in running an elaborate pedophile sex-
trafficking ring.
A source close to Carney told the Toronto Sun( https://torontosun.com/opinion/columnists/mark-carney-pushes-
back-on-photos-with-ghislaine-maxwell ) that Maxwell went to the same school as Fox's sister, and that "while they 
have bumped into each other in public settings ... they are not friends."
Feds call on Islamic group to cancel alarming conference while security agencies consider terrorist designation( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/islamic-conference-caliphate-shariah-law-terror-list-2 )
Smith predicts 'national unity crisis' if Liberals block West's energy exports to fight Trump( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/us-tarrifs-alberta-energy-danielle-smith )
He has multiple citizenships
Page 2 of 4
FIRST READING: The baggage Mark Carney is bringing to his prime ministerial bid
There are no rules forbidding Canadian party leaders from holding dual citizenship. Technically, it would even be 
possible for a non-citizen to be prime minister.
But dual citizenship has been a point of controversy for Canadian politicians before, most notably with former 
Conservative leader Andrew Scheer, who held citizenship in both the United States and Canada. Although Scheer 
publicly announced his intentions to renounce his U.S. citizenship, he abandoned the effort after losing the 2019 
election. "Knowing that I won't be prime minister, I discontinued that process," Scheer told CTV at the time( 
https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/scheer-didn-t-follow-through-on-renouncing-u-s-citizenship-1.4941780 ).
Carney is a citizen of three countries. Born a Canadian, he obtained Irish citizenship in the 1980s, and then British 
citizenship in 2018 when he was Governor of the Bank of England.
He's the international face of "net zero"
One of the biggest electoral liabilities for the Liberal Party right now is their climate policy. Although the Trudeau 
Liberals were always very open about their intention to pursue an aggressive policy of emissions reduction, the 
carbon tax very quickly came to rank among their most unpopular policies. With Trudeau announcing his intention 
to resign, party insiders are now openly speaking of ditching the carbon tax altogether.
This would be a harder tack for Carney, given that he's one of the founders of the Net-Zero Banking Alliance, a 
consortium of major financiers pledged to "net-zero" emissions by 2050. Carney was also the UN Special Envoy on 
Climate Action and Finance.
The Net-Zero Banking Alliance is faring about as well as the Liberal Party these days: Just last week, Morgan 
Stanley, Citigroup and Bank of America all defected from the group( https://financialpost.com/fp-finance/morgan-
stanley-quitting-climate-group ).
It also means there's plenty of video around of Carney saying that businesses who do not sign on with centralized 
decarbonization efforts should be punished.
"The companies, and those who invest and lend in them, who are part of the solution, will be rewarded. Those that 
are lagging behind, and are still part of the problem, will be punished," Carney said in one interview( 
https://www.un.org/en/climatechange/mark-carney-investing-net-zero-climate-solutions-creates-value-and-rewards ) 
with the United Nations' Climate Action office.
His tenure as Bank of England governor wasn't all that great
This was something mentioned in a recent column in The Spectator; Carney's last big government job was a bit of a 
fiasco.
There's no obvious black marks on Carney's tenure as Governor of the Bank of Canada; the years 2007 to 2013 
were a pretty stable time for Canadian central banking. Carney also had the prestige of Canada weathering the 
2008 Great Recession better than almost any other peer country.
But it's a different story for his time as Governor of the Bank of England. As British financial columnist Matthew 
Lynn put it, Carney presided over low growth and the decline of London as the world's leading financial centre. "The 
Bank printed way too much money, stoking an asset bubble, and ultimately triggering the highest inflation rate in the 
G7," wrote Lynn.
Carney was also one of the central figures of what the U.K. tabloid press has dubbed "Project Fear"; an organized 
effort warning of dire financial consequences if the U.K. followed through with its exit from the European Union. 
Carney's successor, Andrew Bailey, has now publicly acknowledged( 
https://www.express.co.uk/news/politics/1820237/bank-of-england-dire-warnings-wrong-brexit ) that many of those 
warnings were overblown.
Page 3 of 4
FIRST READING: The baggage Mark Carney is bringing to his prime ministerial bid
'It takes only a cursory glance at Mark Carney's record as Governor of the Bank of England to work out that his 
reputation is completely overblown - and in reality he is not fit to be Canada's next prime minister.'
?? Matthew Lynnhttps://t.co/dcc7y7UreN( https://t.co/dcc7y7UreN )
- The Spectator (@spectator) January 7, 2025( 
https://twitter.com/spectator/status/1876580720170426864?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw )
He's had a Canadian government job at the exact same time his company has been lobbying Ottawa for billions
It was in September when Carney got his first official link to the Liberal government by being named as a senior 
economic advisor to the prime minister. Unusually, though, it was a position with the Liberal Party of Canada 
rather than one with the Prime Minister's Office. As Conservative critics pointed out at the time, this would have 
allowed Carney to take the job without going through the usual conflict-of-interest disclosures required of a prime 
ministerial aide.
He also got the job at the exact same time( https://nationalpost.com/opinion/first-reading-as-mark-carney-takes-up-
pm-advisor-job-his-company-solicits-ottawa-for-10-billion ) that his company, Brookfield Asset Management, was 
lobbying Ottawa on a $50 billion pension fund that would be directed towards Canadian assets. Brookfield was 
asking the federal government to pony up as much as $10 billion for the fund.
IN OTHER NEWS
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith became the latest provincial leader to meet personally with U.S. president-elect 
Donald Trump in an attempt to smooth over his pledge to impose 25 per cent tariffs on Canadian imports. She said 
she engaged in "constructive dialogue and diplomacy," but her meeting with Trump included Canadian 
entrepreneur Kevin O'Leary, who actually sort of supports Trump's plan to erase the Canada/U.S. border. O'Leary's 
not an annexationist. Rather, he favours a kind of economic union with the United States that would erase a hard 
border( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/kevin-oleary-donald-trump-canada-united-states-union ) between the 
two countries. Think of it as a kind of "sovereignty-association." When Quebec held its first separation referendum 
in 1980, the goal wasn't immediate independence, but rather a "sovereignty-association" in which Quebec would 
still use Canadian dollars and have free borders with Canada, but act as an independent entity.
This was NDP Leader Jagmeet Singh's response to repeated threats by U.S. president-elect Donald Trump to 
annex Canada. He recorded a kind of diss video (complete with a beat) in which he says there will be a "price to 
pay" for a trade war with Canada.
The last time a wildly unpopular political party handed the reins to a new leader only a few months before the next 
election, the result was Kim Campbell becoming Canada's first woman prime minister. Now, Nova Scotia MP 
Jaime Battiste (who is Mi'kmaw) appears to be trying the same thing, but as Canada's first Indigenous prime 
minister. In a statement on Monday( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/indigenous-mp-jaime-battiste-liberal-
leadership ), he said he might run for the Liberal leadership, and emphasized that it would make him Canada's first 
Indigenous prime minister. "I am laying the groundwork for an exploratory team that will seek to launch the first 
campaign by an Indigenous candidate for the leadership of the Liberal Party of Canada, and to be the next Prime 
Minister of Canada," he wrote.

title: FIRST READING: The largest government misallocation in Canadian history
body:
First Reading is a daily newsletter keeping you posted on the travails of Canadian politicos, all curated by the 
National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early version sent directly to your inbox every Monday to Thursday at 
6:30 p.m. ET (and 9 a.m. on Saturdays), sign up here( 
http://firstreading.nationalpost.com/p/1?utm_source=Sailthru&;utm_medium=email&;utm_campaign=First%20Readi
ng%20Newsletter%20-%20Mon%20-%20Fri%202021-12-22&;utm_term=PM_Politics_Newsletters ).
This black-ringed toonie will soon be entering circulation to mourn the death of Queen Elizabeth II. According to the 
Royal Canadian Mint, the black outer ring is meant to be "reminiscent of a mourning armband." Meanwhile, we're 
likely still months away from getting coins with King Charles III on them. Charles has to personally approve any 
effigy of himself created by the Royal Canadian Mint, and let's just say that greenlighting Canadian coins hasn't 
been at the top of his priority list.
TOP STORY
A recent Auditor's General's report found that a "minimum" of $27.4 billion in COVID benefits may have been paid 
out to people who were either ineligible or actively scamming the system. Add this to $4.6 billion in confirmed 
government overpayments, and that's more than $32 billion in misappropriated COVID money.
It may not seem like much given the awesome scale of government spending in recent years; $32 billion is only one 
tenth of the $325 billion deficit that Canada racked up in 2020( https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-
quotidien/211122/g-a001-eng.htm ). But if the Auditor General's suspicions are correct, this constitutes the largest 
misappropriation of government funds in the history of Confederation. And frankly, none of Canada's other 
boondoggles, accounting flubs or spending scandals since 1867 even come close.
Below, a guide to just how unbelievably unprecedented it is for a Canadian government to lose $32 billion.
It's enough missing cash to build the Canadian Pacific Railroad 18 times over
Easily the most corrupt era in Canadian history was the decade surrounding the construction of the Canadian 
Pacific Railroad. In the words of historian R.T. Naylor, "the level of corruption in the Canadian political process of 
the period ... is truly astounding even to the cynic." As an example, Sir John A. Macdonald was caught brazenly 
trading sole-sourced railroad contracts for kickbacks, and all it really did was prompt a temporary pause to his 
political career. And yet, even the uber-corrupt Canadian political establishment of the late 19th century couldn't 
dream of coming close to misappropriating $32 billion - the size of government just wasn't big enough. For 
Page 2 of 4
FIRST READING: The largest government misallocation in Canadian history
context, the total cost of the completed Canadian Pacific Railroad (even with all the corruption) came to the 2022 
equivalent of about $1.7 billion - about one eighteenth of $32 billion.

title: FIRST READING: The Liberal scandal that may have just guaranteed a third Quebec referendum
body:
First Reading is a Canadian politics newsletter curated by the National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early 
version sent directly to your inbox, sign up here.( https://nationalpost.com/newsletters/ )
TOP STORY
As Quebec lurches ever closer towards a third separation referendum, an old-fashioned Liberal vote-buying 
scandal might have just removed the last barrier to its occurrence.
Pablo Rodriguez resigned as Quebec Liberal leader this week amid two major corruption allegations against his 
party, one of them involving cash-filled envelopes.
Rodriguez maintains he had nothing to do with either of them, saying, "I regret absolutely nothing."
But the immolation of the Quebec Liberals only solidifies the likelihood that the Parti Québécois will sweep the 
province's 2026 election. Once in power, PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised he will be pulling out 
all the stops to hold a third referendum on secession from Canada.
Quebec's incumbent government, led by the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) under François Legault, is currently 
plumbing new depths of unpopularity. As such, the deeply federalist Quebec Liberals were widely seen as the only 
realistic force to thwart the PQ's ascension.
But under the tenure of Rodriguez, the party's popularity has cratered and given the PQ an overwhelming polling 
lead.
As per a Dec. 17 poll published by the Angus Reid Institute, the PQ is polling at 40 per cent to the Liberals' 18 per 
cent.
It's a far cry from the vote shares the PQ could command in the 1980s heyday of Quebec nationalism, but it would 
still be more than enough for the PQ to secure their most commanding majority in a generation.
In recent weeks, the party has even been rolling out serialized chapters of its "livre bleu," its definitive blueprint for 
what an independent Quebec would look like. Its most recent chapter( https://pq.org/livrebleu/ ) detailed which 
Page 2 of 4

countries would receive Quebec ambassadors and which international sporting events would be contested by 
Équipe Québec.
Rodriguez is best known to the rest of Canada as the champion of some of the most sweeping controls ever 
enacted on the Canadian internet. As heritage minister under then prime minister Justin Trudeau, he helped 
push through both the Online Streaming Act and the Online News Act.
The Online Streaming Act empowers federal regulators to impose content controls on online platforms ranging from 
Netflix to YouTube. The Online News Act is why Canadians can no longer share news articles on Facebook.
Rodriguez resigned from federal politics in September 2024, part of an exodus( 
https://nationalpost.com/opinion/most-telling-indicator-liberals-remain-doomed ) of top Liberals quitting the Trudeau 
government as it lurched towards what was then seen as inevitable electoral oblivion.
He was elected Quebec Liberal leader in June, only for his seven-month tenure to be defined by a string of 
corruption scandals.
The main one being that his very election as leader was secured in an alleged vote-buying scheme, a charge 
currently under investigation( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/upac-quebec-liberals-vote-
buying-allegations ) by Quebec's anticorruption police. Another being that a Rodriguez fundraising event featured 
attendees being handed envelopes full of cash( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-
liberals-rodriguez-cash-envelopes-campaign-allegations ) on the understanding that they would donate it to the 
campaign in their name, thus skirting Quebec law on contribution caps.
Even if this all means that Quebec voters are likely to vote in a PQ government, it's a different story when it comes 
to their desire for separation.
Canada's ongoing trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump has dropped sovereigntist sentiments to historic 
lows, with even many longtime nationalists publicly declaring their allegiance to Ottawa over Washington.
Probably the most noticeable manifestation of this trend was when the Bloc Québécois - the federal voice for 
Quebec independence - spent the 2025 federal election publicly promising not to threaten secession( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/bloc-quebecois-leader-says-he-wont-threaten-to-overthrow-the-government-anytime-
soon-read-more ) until the trade war had subsided.
As of an October Leger poll, a mere 28 per cent of Quebecers favoured full separation of their province from 
Canada( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/30-years-after-quebec-referendum-majority-of-canadians-see-
canada-as-one-nation-poll ). This would be roughly the same as in Alberta, where separatist sentiment was 
hovering at around 24 per cent.
Nevertheless, there are reports that Ottawa is taking this seriously, with federal officials already drafting plans( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/parti-quebecois-fears-ottawa-will-cheat-in-a-third-sovereignty-
referendum ) on how to thwart the "Oui" side if secession once again comes to a vote.
According to Legault, however, there not only won't be a referendum, but the end result of all of this is that he'll get 
to continue being premier.
Although Legault has been quite open in acknowledging his unpopularity, in a year-end interview with Radio-
Canada he predicted that the PQ would ultimately botch their lead so badly that Quebecers would be forced to turn 
back to his CAQ.
Legault used to be a PQ cabinet minister, before founding the CAQ with the explicit goal of attracting Quebec 
nationalists who were tired of organizing and losing referenda. Speaking to Radio-Canada, he predicted that the 
PQ's fever over a third referendum would ultimately prove too much.

"The PQ won't stay where it is in the polls," he said. "People will understand that Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is 
synonymous with a referendum, and we don't want that."
IN OTHER NEWS
The Department of Defence has publicly raised the possibility that it might abandon its order of F-35 fighter jets in 
favour of the Swedish-made Saab Gripen. This is despite the fact that a leaked Canadian Armed Forces scoring 
chart that the F-35 bested the Gripen in every category they tested. But the graph above is from a recent Ekos poll 
finding that a plurality of respondents still like the Gripen anyway.
At the exact same time that two U.S. states are designating the Council on Islamic-American Relations (CAIR) as a 
terror entity, Canada seems to be doing the exact opposite.
The National Council of Canadian Muslims was founded as the Canadian chapter of CAIR, before rebranding in 
2013( https://www.ourcommons.ca/DocumentViewer/en/41-2/SECU/meeting-60/evidence ). In just the last two 
weeks, the NCCM participated in leading a delegation of Canadian MPs( 
https://nationalpost.com/opinion/canadian-mission-to-west-bank-fabricated-a-political-crisis ) to the Middle East, 
and also received an official goodwill visit from Dan Rogers, the director of CSIS, Canada's main spy agency. 
Rogers also just sent a lengthy apology to the NCCM( https://x.com/nccm/status/1999545114931102041/photo/1 ), 
in response to their complaints that he wasn't sufficiently addressing Islamophobia.
Meanwhile, the U.S. states of Florida and Texas just declared CAIR a "foreign terrorist organization." Florida's 
declaration, issued by Governor Ron DeSantis( https://www.flgov.com/eog/sites/default/files/executive-
orders/2025/EO%2025-244.pdf ), stated that it was "founded by persons connected to the Muslim Brotherhood and 
was created, in the words of persons affiliated with CAIR, as 'an official U.S. cover representing the Islamic 
community' to conceal ties to Islamic extremist groups."
Toronto just completed construction of a $3.7 billion LRT line that is so slow that runners have taken it upon 
themselves to race the train by foot. Above is a screenshot from an Instagram video in which a user known as 
514Runner ran the entire length of the line with a time that was 18 minutes faster than the train itself.

buying-allegations ) by Quebec's anticorruption police. Another being that a Rodriguez fundraising event featured 
attendees being handed envelopes full of cash( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/quebec-
liberals-rodriguez-cash-envelopes-campaign-allegations ) on the understanding that they would donate it to the 
campaign in their name, thus skirting Quebec law on contribution caps.

to their desire for separation.

lows, with even many longtime nationalists publicly declaring their allegiance to Ottawa over Washington.

Quebec independence - spent the 2025 federal election publicly promising not to threaten secession(

soon-read-more ) until the trade war had subsided.

Canada( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/30-years-after-quebec-referendum-majority-of-canadians-see-
canada-as-one-nation-poll ). This would be roughly the same as in Alberta, where separatist sentiment was 
hovering at around 24 per cent.

https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/parti-quebecois-fears-ottawa-will-cheat-in-a-third-sovereignty-
referendum ) on how to thwart the "Oui" side if secession once again comes to a vote.
According to Legault, however, there not only won't be a referendum, but the end result of all of this is that he'll get 
to continue being premier.

Canada he predicted that the PQ would ultimately botch their lead so badly that Quebecers would be forced to turn 
back to his CAQ.
Legault used to be a PQ cabinet minister, before founding the CAQ with the explicit goal of attracting Quebec 
nationalists who were tired of organizing and losing referenda. Speaking to Radio-Canada, he predicted that the 
PQ's fever over a third referendum would ultimately prove too much.

"The PQ won't stay where it is in the polls," he said. "People will understand that Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is 
synonymous with a referendum, and we don't want that."

favour of the Swedish-made Saab Gripen. This is despite the fact that a leaked Canadian Armed Forces scoring 
chart that the F-35 bested the Gripen in every category they tested. But the graph above is from a recent Ekos poll

terror entity, Canada seems to be doing the exact opposite.

2013( https://www.ourcommons.ca/DocumentViewer/en/41-2/SECU/meeting-60/evidence ). In just the last two

https://nationalpost.com/opinion/canadian-mission-to-west-bank-fabricated-a-political-crisis ) to the Middle East,

title: FIRST READING: The unglamorous life that awaits an ex-prime minister Trudeau
body:
First Reading is a daily newsletter keeping you posted on the travails of Canadian politicos, all curated by the 
National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early version sent directly to your inbox, sign up here( 
https://nationalpost.com/newsletters/ ).
TOP STORY
Rarely in Canadian history has there been such unanimity in the notion that an incumbent prime minister 
shouldn't be prime minister anymore.
A recent Abacus Data poll found that 57 per cent of Canadians living in a Liberal riding wanted their MP to "call on 
Justin Trudeau to resign and not run again."
As far back as June, an Ipsos poll found more than two thirds of Canadians wanted Trudeau to step down - a rate 
pollsters characterized as "close to rock bottom." And it is now rare that a sit-down interview with the prime 
minister doesn't end with queries about why he's still prime minister.
But if Trudeau intends to delay his exit as long as humanly possible, one reason might be that he has a unique 
insight into the unglamorous afterlife that awaits him.
The classic post-politics job for a Canadian prime minister is to take up an ambiguous position in a major law 
office.
This was the route taken by Trudeau's father, Pierre Elliott Trudeau. Within months of his 1984 resignation, the 
elder Trudeau accepted a job as counsel for the Montreal law firm Heenan Blaikie.
In a press conference convened at his modest new office (described as being just four square metres), Trudeau 
described his job as hanging around the office and answering questions from the other lawyers.
"If occasionally my colleagues want to ask my advice on certain subjects, I'll be happy to give it to them," he said, 
offering the example of nuclear issues, civil liberties and other "things like that."
Gone were the official limousines and VIP jets; the elder Trudeau now commuted to work by foot from his Montreal 
mansion.
Page 2 of 4
FIRST READING: The unglamorous life that awaits an ex-prime minister Trudeau
Pierre Trudeau seen walking to his office in Montreal in 1992.
Brian Mulroney similarly took up a job at Norton Rose Fulbright within weeks of his own 1993 resignation. Like 
Trudeau, his role was similarly that of a consultant.
A desk at a law firm would also await Jean Chrétien, first at Heenan Blaikie, and then Dentons after the former firm 
dissolved in 2014.
As recently as December, Chrétien was reporting that he still works there basically full-time. "I leave my home every 
morning at 9:00 o'clock for the office four mornings a week," the 90-year-old said in an interview( 
https://www.policymagazine.ca/policy-qa-jim-munson-with-jean-chretien-on-loving-canada-hating-no-one-and-
turning-90/ ) with Policy Magazine.
All-purpose consulting can also describe what Stephen Harper has been up to since leaving politics. Although, 
rather than take a salary with a law firm, he's run it through his own shop, Harper &; Associates, a firm that 
promises the "global network, experience and insight of a G-7 Leader to create value for clients."
One of those clients is the Government of Saskatchewan. Starting in 2019, they started paying Harper &; 
Associates $240,000 per year to target "specific geographic regions of importance" for commodity exports.
There are also a wide variety of ambiguous jobs in academia and the non-profit sphere.
That's been the primary pursuit of Kim Campbell; her resume includes a fellowship at Harvard University's John F. 
Kennedy School and a four-year stint( https://www.ualberta.ca/en/lougheed-leadership-college/about-us/kim-
bio.html ) as founding principal of the University of Alberta's Peter Lougheed Leadership College.
Trudeau has rarely acknowledged a life after his premiership, but he did say in a recent interview with the 
Freakonomics podcast that "when I leave politics I will look to teach again in one way, shape or form."
Trudeau's life outside politics will also likely see him re-enter the speaking circuit.
Almost every ex-prime minister has enlisted a speaking fee agent in retirement. The group APB Speakers 
manages Kim Campbell; her official booking site offers one of four speeches, ranging from "Gender &; Power" to 
"We're Already in World War III: Examining the Social &; Political Dimensions of Climate Change."
Joe Clark is managed by the National Speakers Bureau( https://www.nsb.com/speakers/joe-clark/ ). His booking 
page gives clients the choice of "Managing Diversity," "Canada and the USA" and "How we lead: Canada in a 
century of change."
Joe Clark giving a dinner lecture in 2015.
Stephen Harper, represented by Worldwide Speakers Group, offers four speeches: "Foreign Policy Leadership," 
"Growing Global Trade," "Living in a Low-Growth World" and "21st Century Trends: Erosion of Global Stability."
Where Trudeau might differ from all the other ex-PMs, however, is that he's the only prime minister who was 
already raking in high speaking fees even when he was just a Montreal MP.
Between his election as a Papineau MP in 2008 and when he won the Liberal leadership in 2013, Trudeau has 
disclosed that he collected $277,000 in appearance and speaking fees paid out by 17 organizations. He stopped 
accepting paid appearances after deciding to run for the Liberal leadership.
Before his election as Liberal leader, Trudeau was easily pulling down five figures per appearance. In the summer 
of 2012, for instance, the New Brunswick-based Grace Foundation paid Trudeau $20,000 to headline a hospital 
fundraiser. Controversially, the event would lose money - prompting Trudeau to offer to repay the fee once it 
became a public scandal.
Page 3 of 4
FIRST READING: The unglamorous life that awaits an ex-prime minister Trudeau
EXCLUSIVE: Trudeau government to slash immigration levels( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/trudeau-
government-lower-immigration-2025 )
Nova Scotia woman was asked if she knew about assisted dying before mastectomy surgery for breast cancer( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/medical-assistance-in-dying-nova-scotia )
IN OTHER NEWS
Canadian French has just been added to Google Translate. Canada's version of the language is famously the 
more archaic version; it's a linguistic time capsule of the kind of French that was spoken at the time New France 
was settled. As shown above, it also continues to employ French words for things that speakers in much of the rest 
of the Francophonie have abandoned in favour of English words, such as "faire du shopping." Above is a sample 
translation, with French on the top and Canadian French on the bottom.
The attempted coup of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau wasn't quite as decisive as might have been expected, but 
ominously gave him five days to decide what to do( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/liberal-mps-ottawa-
justin-trudeau ). A three-and-a-half-hour Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday featured about 25 to 30 MPs airing 
their grievances against the Liberal leader, and he was also presented with a letter that very delicately hinted at the 
same (according to National Post reporting, the letter "recognized Trudeau's accomplishments in office" and was 
framed as MPs sharing "feedback from constituents" that he's not wanted anymore). The letter reportedly said that 
if Trudeau was still Liberal leader by Monday, the dissident MPs would take unspecified actions.
Meanwhile, in addition to the dissident MPs, a coterie of Liberal Party insiders have begun circulating a "Code Red 
Petition" urging the party's national executive to conduct a party-wide leadership vote via secret ballot.
Get all of these insights and more into your inbox by signing up for the First Reading newsletter here( 
https://nationalpost.com/newsletters/ ). !@COPYRIGHT=© 2024 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

title: FIRST READING: There's not actually anything to stop Canadian MPs working for foreign governments
body:
First Reading is a Canadian politics newsletter curated by the National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early 
version sent directly to your inbox, sign up here.( https://nationalpost.com/newsletters/ )
TOP STORY
After former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland got a job with the Ukrainian government while still serving as 
an MP, she was lambasted by the opposition for serving two masters.
Roman Baber, who represents the nearby riding of York Centre, called it a "blatant conflict of interest." Michael 
Chong, the Conservative foreign affairs critic, wrote in a statement "one cannot be a Canadian MP and an advisor 
to a foreign government. She must do one or the other."
But the criticisms against Freeland are all based on alleged impropriety, because while it's unusual for MPs to take 
foreign government postings, she didn't actually break any rules.
Canada doesn't have any restrictions against foreign government actors serving in its parliament. In fact, if a sitting 
MP ever wanted to take up a side job as a foreign head of state, there's not really anything in Canadian law to stop 
them.
On Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that he had appointed Freeland as an "Advisor 
on Economic Development." She was already in Ukraine as a special envoy appointed by Prime Minister Mark 
Carney.
And although Freeland resigned her position in cabinet in mid-2025, she remains the MP for the Toronto area riding 
of University-Rosedale. She was still voting( https://openparliament.ca/politicians/chrystia-freeland/ ) in the House of 
Commons as recently as Dec. 11. Most notably, she helped to narrowly pass( 
https://www.ourcommons.ca/members/en/votes/45/1/50 ) the Liberals' 2025 budget, which included generous civil 
and military assistance for Ukraine.
After the appointment by Zelenskyy, Freeland said she would step down immediately from the special envoy job, 
but would keep her MP job pending a departure in "the coming weeks."
Page 2 of 4
FIRST READING: There's not actually anything to stop Canadian MPs working for foreign governments
Under the Canada Elections Act, the only requirements to be an MP is that the candidate must be a Canadian 
citizen who is not in jail and is at least 18 years old.
While the candidate cannot be a "member of the legislative assembly of a province," it doesn't say anything about 
working for foreign governments, or even sitting in a foreign parliament.
This is markedly different than the conditions for sitting in the Senate.
Canada's founding document, the 1867 British North America Act, made clear that a senator could be fired if they 
ever made any kind of "Declaration or Acknowledgement of Allegiance, Obedience, or Adherence to a Foreign 
Power."
But no such condition was attached to members of the House of Commons.
Although the Conflict of Interest Act assigns parliamentarians a "cooling off" period under which they can't work 
with businesses or organizations in which they had "direct and significant official dealings," it doesn't cover foreign 
governments.
Among some of Canada's peer countries, the issue of foreign entanglements is sometimes dealt with via controls 
on joint citizenship.
The Australian constitution, for instance, bars anyone holding citizenship in a "foreign power" from sitting in their 
parliament.
Japan, India and South Korea all maintain tight controls on any of their nationals holding joint citizenship, which 
necessarily makes for parliaments full of representatives who would have trouble meeting the qualifications for 
foreign political appointments.
This was also true of Ukraine until only a few months ago. Ukraine did not recognize dual citizenship following its 
1991 independence, but relaxed the provision last year to allow Ukrainians to obtain joint citizenship in Canada, the 
United States, Germany, Poland, and the Czech Republic.
Freeland is not a Ukrainian citizen, and is accepting the post in Kyiv as a Canadian national. However, if she was a 
parliamentarian in the U.S. or several European countries, her acceptance of a job offer from a foreign president 
would likely bring her into conflict with rules designed to prevent foreign interference.
In the United States, a Congressperson accepting a position with a foreign government would potentially fall afoul of 
the Emoluments Clause, a section of the U.S. Constitution that bars federal office-holders( 
https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S9-C8-3/ALDE_00013206/ ) from accepting "any present, 
Emolument, Office, or Title, of any kind whatever, from any King, Prince, or foreign State."
It was only in 2024 that Canada was scandalized by allegations that parliamentarians were actively working for 
unspecified foreign governments. In a March 2024 report( https://www.nsicop-cpsnr.ca/reports/rp-2024-06-
03/special-report-foreign-interference.pdf ) that employed classified intelligence information, the National Security 
and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians declared that some MPs were "wittingly assisting foreign state 
actors."
IN OTHER NEWS
This was the statement put out by Prime Minister Mark Carney after the United States pulled off an operation to 
capture Venezuelan leader Nicholas Maduro and fly him to New York City to face drug trafficking charges. The 
Carney government is no fan of Maduro, but it's standard practice that Liberal governments will respond with muted 
reprobation to U.S. military adventurism, particularly when it involves close neighbours. That, and Ottawa is actively 
trying not to enrage the White House in hopes of reigniting trade talks. The statement above is what all those 
intersecting and contradictory demands look like in textual form.
Page 3 of 4
FIRST READING: There's not actually anything to stop Canadian MPs working for foreign governments
Canada's not-insubstantial Venezuelan diaspora is mostly happy about the helicopter ouster of Maduro (one of 
those diaspora happens to be the wife of Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre). But economists quickly took note 
that a liberated and prosperous Venezuela may not be great for Canada( https://nationalpost.com/opinion/adam-
pankratz-venezuelan-oil-could-put-canada-out-of-business ). Both countries are major oil producers located right 
next to the United States, except that Venezuela has largely removed itself from the global oil market due to 
mismanagement.
So if that mismanagement stops, there's suddenly an ocean of new oil to compete with the Canadian oil servicing 
the U.S. The good news, however, is that Canadian blends of oil are still among the cheapest in the world, 
preserving their attractiveness for American buyers. Also, the system of pipelines transferring Alberta oil to U.S. 
refineries is extremely efficient, and would remain competitive even if convoys of oil tankers started being 
dispatched out of Caracas.
It's been a few months since U.S. President Donald Trump has made any kind of high-profile annexation threat 
against Canada. This might be because he's shifted his attention east to Greenland. In the wake of the successful 
U.S. capture of Venezuelan leader Nicholas Maduro, Trump told a Sunday press conference "we need Greenland 
from the standpoint of national security." To this, both the Greenlandic and Danish prime ministers (both pictured) 
told the White House that the U.S. already has wide access to Greenland, and can basically do whatever they want 
militarily without annexation. In prior decades, this has even meant that Greenland was occasionally hit with 
accidental American nuclear bombings, although fortunately none of the bombs ever detonated.

Freeland is not a Ukrainian citizen, and is accepting the post in Kyiv as a Canadian national. However, if she was a 
parliamentarian in the U.S. or several European countries, her acceptance of a job offer from a foreign president 
would likely bring her into conflict with rules designed to prevent foreign interference.
In the United States, a Congressperson accepting a position with a foreign government would potentially fall afoul of 
the Emoluments Clause, a section of the U.S. Constitution that bars federal office-holders( 
https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S9-C8-3/ALDE_00013206/ ) from accepting "any present, 
Emolument, Office, or Title, of any kind whatever, from any King, Prince, or foreign State."
It was only in 2024 that Canada was scandalized by allegations that parliamentarians were actively working for 
unspecified foreign governments. In a March 2024 report( https://www.nsicop-cpsnr.ca/reports/rp-2024-06-
03/special-report-foreign-interference.pdf ) that employed classified intelligence information, the National Security 
and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians declared that some MPs were "wittingly assisting foreign state 
actors."
IN OTHER NEWS
This was the statement put out by Prime Minister Mark Carney after the United States pulled off an operation to 
capture Venezuelan leader Nicholas Maduro and fly him to New York City to face drug trafficking charges. The 
Carney government is no fan of Maduro, but it's standard practice that Liberal governments will respond with muted 
reprobation to U.S. military adventurism, particularly when it involves close neighbours. That, and Ottawa is actively 
trying not to enrage the White House in hopes of reigniting trade talks. The statement above is what all those 
intersecting and contradictory demands look like in textual form.

Canada's not-insubstantial Venezuelan diaspora is mostly happy about the helicopter ouster of Maduro (one of 
those diaspora happens to be the wife of Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre). But economists quickly took note 
that a liberated and prosperous Venezuela may not be great for Canada( https://nationalpost.com/opinion/adam-
pankratz-venezuelan-oil-could-put-canada-out-of-business ). Both countries are major oil producers located right 
next to the United States, except that Venezuela has largely removed itself from the global oil market due to 
mismanagement.
So if that mismanagement stops, there's suddenly an ocean of new oil to compete with the Canadian oil servicing 
the U.S. The good news, however, is that Canadian blends of oil are still among the cheapest in the world, 
preserving their attractiveness for American buyers. Also, the system of pipelines transferring Alberta oil to U.S. 
refineries is extremely efficient, and would remain competitive even if convoys of oil tankers started being 
dispatched out of Caracas.
It's been a few months since U.S. President Donald Trump has made any kind of high-profile annexation threat 
against Canada. This might be because he's shifted his attention east to Greenland. In the wake of the successful 
U.S. capture of Venezuelan leader Nicholas Maduro, Trump told a Sunday press conference "we need Greenland 
from the standpoint of national security." To this, both the Greenlandic and Danish prime ministers (both pictured) 
told the White House that the U.S. already has wide access to Greenland, and can basically do whatever they want 
militarily without annexation. In prior decades, this has even meant that Greenland was occasionally hit with 
accidental American nuclear bombings, although fortunately none of the bombs ever detonated.

title: FIRST READING: We are in a new golden age of Canadian boondoggles
body:
First Reading is a Canadian politics newsletter curated by the National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early 
version sent directly to your inbox, sign up here( https://nationalpost.com/newsletters/ ).
TOP STORY
It's no secret that Canada is in an era of incredibly high deficit spending, with the interim Parliamentary Budget 
Officer recently telling a House of Commons committee that the current rate of federal debt accumulation is 
"stupefying" and "shocking." And, just like other periods of high deficit spending, this one is yielding plenty of white 
elephants, boondoggles and spending scandals.
But if the boondoggles of recent years are different, it's that they don't seem to be turning heads nearly as much as 
they used to. Historically, if an ill-advised public project managed to rack up nine-figure losses it would bring down 
governments, define political eras and enter Canadian lore as a cautionary tale against institutional hubris. But 
now, it's possible to disappear billions of dollars without even making the front page.
Below, a gallery of five famous Canadian boondoggles, contrasted with a modern equivalent that is not only more 
egregious, but hasn't yielded nearly the same public furor.
The original: The Bricklin SV-1
The Bricklin SV-1 remains one of the most famous Canadian government boondoggles, if only because it's still 
possible to see the occasional Bricklin on a Canadian highway. In the 1970s, U.S. auto entrepreneur Malcolm 
Bricklin convinced the government of New Brunswick to put up the money for a "safety sports car" that would be 
manufactured in the small town of Minto, N.B. Much like the Delorean and Cybertruck that were to follow, Bricklin 
overestimated the demand for an expensive boutique, and production stopped after just 3,000 models. The New 
Brunswick government took a bath on the project of about $23 million ($128 million in 2025).
In this 1974 photo, then New Brunswick Premier Richard Hatfield and car designer Malcolm Bricklin show off the 
Bricklin SV-1, an ultimately doomed automobile that was manufactured outside of Fredericton with heavy provincial 
assistance.
The modern equivalent: ArriveCan
Page 2 of 4

ArriveCan was the much-maligned smartphone app that for months was a mandatory requirement for travellers 
entering Canada. The raw losses from the app are admittedly not quite at the level of the Bricklin SV-1; the best 
estimates of the Auditor General of Canada is that the app ultimately cost the federal government $59.5 million( 
https://www.oag-bvg.gc.ca/internet/English/parl_oag_202402_01_e_44428.html ). But the scandal is arguably far 
more egregious given the product that was delivered. Rather than manufacturing an automobile from scratch in the 
hinterlands of New Brunswick, ArriveCan's builders delivered an app of such simplicity that its entire coding could 
be duplicated( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/in-two-days-a-single-programmer-duplicated-arrivecan-an-
app-that-cost-ottawa-54-million ) by a single programmer over the course of a weekend.
The ArriveCan app.
The original: The B.C. "FastCat" Ferries
This was a fleet of three catamaran car ferries whose 1999 rollout was so catastrophic that they'd come to loom like 
a phantom over the next two decades of B.C. politics. They were the brainchild of the NDP government of then 
premier Glen Clark, and the idea was to use B.C. shipbuilders to construct a fleet of ultra-modern "fast" ferries that 
would cut down travel times between Vancouver Island and the Mainland. Delivered at more than double their 
projected cost, design issues and breakdowns meant that the Pacificats never really delivered on their core promise 
of faster travel, and they were pulled from service within months. An inquiry later pegged the total cost of the fiasco 
at $463 million, about $800 million in 2025 dollars.
The PacifiCat Discovery, pictured in 2003 shortly before it was auctioned off as surplus.
The modern equivalent: Quebec hemorrhaging money on Northvolt and Airbus
In just the last two months, the Quebec government of François Legault has acknowledged $670 million in bad 
industrial investments. Last week, the Quebec government wrote down a loss of $400 million( 
https://www.ctvnews.ca/montreal/article/quebec-writes-off-400-million-of-its-investment-in-airbus/ ) on provincial 
assistance to the Airbus A220, a wide-bodied airliner being assembled in Mirabel, Que. The month prior, Quebec 
wrote off a $270 million loss on its equity stake in Northvolt, a Swedish battery company that was handed a 
generous package of government assistance in 2023( https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-
releases/2023/09/28/making-worlds-cleanest-batteries-quebec ), only months before the company would descend 
into bankruptcy. "This venture has proved unsuccessful, and we are obviously disappointed," Quebec Economy 
Minister Christine Frechette declared at the time. And in both cases, the total losses may climb still higher, with 
hundreds of millions in additional government money still hanging in the balance.
The original: The 1976 Montreal Olympics
It was a major news item when, in 2006, the Government of Quebec finally paid off the last of its debt stemming 
from the 1976 Montreal Olympics. Canada had won the bid for the 1976 games with the full confidence that the 
event wouldn't incur a cent of public debt. "The Montreal Olympics can no more lose money than a man can have a 
baby," was the infamous prophecy of then Montreal mayor Jean Drapeau. Instead, the official tally is that the 
games racked up $990 million in government debt( https://www.olympics.com/ioc/news/the-economics-of-montreal-
1976 ), the inflation-adjusted equivalent of about $5 billion. The infamy of the bill was driven in part by the fact that 
the Olympic stadium and accompanying tower is one of Montreal's most visible landmarks, ultimately earning the 
nickname of "The Big Owe."
The Olympic Stadium looming over Montreal.
The modern equivalent: Cumulative losses on the Phoenix pay system
The Phoenix payroll system was conceived during the tenure of the government of Stephen Harper, but 
implemented shortly after the swearing-in of the government of then prime minister Justin Trudeau. The system 
never worked as intended, and was soon yielding thousands of botched payments that all had to be manually 
investigated and remedied. While the total losses will never be quite as easy to calculate as the 1976 Olympics, at

least one bureaucrat at the centre of the fiasco has estimated that the cost is about the same: $5.1 billion. That's 
according to June testimony( https://torontosun.com/news/national/fixing-problems-with-phoenix-payroll-system-
cost-taxpayers-5-1b-official ) by Alex Benay, associate deputy minister at Public Services and Procurement 
Canada.
The original: Montreal-Mirabel Airport
Mirabel Airport quite literally remains the textbook case( https://www.editionsjfd.com/en/shop/the-saga-of-mirabel-
and-dorval-airports-11672 ) for the perils of incompetent government infrastructure planning. Conceived in the 
1960s, the idea was to expropriate a block of Quebec farmland the size of Montreal itself, and use it to build a 
massive, palatial airport that would serve as the singular Canadian air hub for the jet age. But airlines never saw 
the sense in sending their international flights to a sprawling airport in the middle of nowhere, and Mirabel was 
almost immediately rendered obsolete. The cost of Canada's most pointless airport came to $500 million in 1975, 
roughly $2.8 billion in 2025 dollars.
A long-abandoned Mirabel Airport terminal, pictured in 2014.
The modern equivalent: $3.5 billion in misallocated COVID-19 loans.
Governments around the world utterly blew out their public debt to cover the various lockdowns and strictures of the 
COVID-19 pandemic. But Canada still managed a rate of pandemic spending( 
https://www.taxpayer.com/newsroom/canada-was-a-big-pandemic-spender,-but-didn%E2%80%99t-achieve-top-
results-report-en_ca ) that put most of the industrialized world to shame. Early analyses by the Fraser Institute have 
estimated that as much as 25 per cent( https://www.fraserinstitute.org/commentary/ottawa-and-washington-wasted-
many-billions-during-covid ) of this went to places it shouldn't have gone. One of the worst single examples was 
$3.5 billion in Canada Emergency Business Account loans that, according to a December report by Auditor General 
Karen Hogan, were distributed to "ineligible" applicants.
The original: Newfoundland's Sprung Greenhouses
Newfoundland's disastrous 1980s attempt to diversify into the cucumber trade is now such a part of provincial lore 
that it even has its own dedicated writeup( https://www.heritage.nf.ca/articles/politics/sprung-greenhouse.php ) on 
the website of Heritage Newfoundland and Labrador. In 1987, then Progressive Conservative premier Brian 
Peckford signed on to a plan hatched by Calgary businessman Philip Sprung to fill the island with greenhouses and 
turn "Newfoundland cucumbers" into a profitable export industry. The economics never worked out, and the project 
lost the province $22 million ($48 million in 2025 dollars) and ended Peckford's political career.
The modern equivalent: The Aspire Food Group cricket factory
This didn't burn up quite as much government money as the Sprung greenhouses. In 2022, Aspire Food Group, a 
company founded by five McGill University students, used financing from several government sources to build the 
world's largest cricket factory outside London, Ont. The idea was to establish Canada as a world leader in edible 
cricket protein, but the demand for powdered crickets never really kept up with production. According to an analysis 
by Farmers Forum( https://farmersforum.com/cricket-factory-sold-taxpayers-poured-35-million-into-massive-failure/ 
), the now-vacant factory consumed $35 million in federal agriculture and climate change grants.
A 2021 photo showing the world's largest cricket farm under construction in London, Ont. Crickets were to be 
hatched and grown on-site and be processed into a tasteless, odourless protein powder that could be sold as a 
food additive.

title: FIRST READING: Why Canada lets prime ministers opportunistically call elections whenever they want
body:
First Reading is a Canadian politics newsletter curated by the National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early 
version sent directly to your inbox, sign up here.( https://nationalpost.com/newsletters/ )
TOP STORY
There is now open speculation that Prime Minister Mark Carney could be poised to exercise what is arguably the 
single greatest privilege of his office.
Namely, the ability to call a snap election the moment the polls are in his favour.
On Tuesday, Conservative MP Michelle Rempel Garner accused Carney of deliberately provoking U.S. President 
Donald Trump with an anti-American speech in Davos with an eye towards a "snap spring election."
As Rempel Garner wrote in a social media post, the idea was to allegedly reignite Trump's ire for Canada and 
"restart the same narrative they had in the campaign last year."
Carney would certainly not be the first prime minister to opportunistically call an early election. Similarly, the tactic 
has been used at the provincial level by politicians of every conceivable political stripe.
Most recently, Ontario Premier Doug Ford called a snap election in early 2025 just as opinion polls showed his 
Progressive Conservatives enjoying a near-unprecedented 20 point lead( https://innovativeresearch.ca/wp-
content/uploads/2025/01/CTM2501-ON-Politics-Web-Post-Deck-Public-Release.pdf ).
But while it's a normalized part of Canadian politics for incumbents to call elections whenever it's to their personal 
advantage, it's a power shared by few other G7 leaders.
The U.S. president holds no power whatsoever over the timing of elections.
In Germany, the chancellor can't unilaterally trigger an election, but must instead seek a vote of non-confidence in 
the Bundestag, the federal parliament of Germany.
The French president can call snap elections for the National Assembly, but not for his own office, which must 
adhere to five-year terms bookended by fixed election days.
Page 2 of 3
FIRST READING: Why Canada lets prime ministers opportunistically call elections whenever they want
Italy's system is notorious for constant snap elections, but the prime minister's power to unilaterally dissolve 
parliament is checked somewhat by the fact that the Italian president will sometimes deny the request.
It was the U.K. that gave Canada its system of a prime minister able to unilaterally dissolve Parliament, of course. 
But even the Brits have been much more skeptical of the measure, and have experimented with plans to rescind it.
The U.K. passed the Fixed-term Parliaments Act in 2011, which set fixed election dates and bound British prime 
ministers to a system of triggering early elections only after a two-thirds vote of non-confidence.
Nick Clegg, the then deputy prime minister who championed the bill, said it would stop general elections from 
being "a play thing of governments."
However, the measure was repealed in 2022( https://consoc.org.uk/the-intention-behind-the-repeal-of-the-fixed-
term-parliaments-act-is-to-strengthen-the-executive-and-the-conservative-party/ ) by then prime minister Boris 
Johnson, after he argued that his inability to call an election was hindering his ability to facilitate the U.K.'s 
withdrawal from the European Union.
There's nothing in the Canadian constitution that specifically empowers the prime minister to unilaterally trigger 
elections at any time. Rather, it's just worked out that way as a consequence of the centuries-long process of 
gradually transferring power from the Crown to Parliament.
As a write-up by the Centre for Constitutional Studies puts it, it's one of many things in the Canadian system relying 
on "unwritten rules."
Since the beginning, the power has always given an incumbent advantage to Canadian prime ministers, who 
could use a snap election to head off a looming scandal or capitalize on a weak opposition.
But in modern times, the value of the snap election prerogative has only gone up with the advent of public opinion 
polling and mass media.
Critics of Carney, for instance, are accusing him of engineering a temporary surge in the polls in order to ride it to a 
majority government.
In a recent appearance on CBC's Power and Politics, Conservative political analyst Kate Harrison cited Carney's 
recent boost to the GST credit, and Ottawa's new "well-manicured" Buy Canada ad campaign.
"There are a lot of breadcrumbs still being left by the Liberals, I would observe, in terms of leaving themselves open 
to the prospect of pulling the plug and having an early election," she said.
The one major check against the snap election prerogative is that there is a bit of a history of prime ministers being 
punished by the electorate if their snap election call is seen as particularly cynical.
An analysis of Canada's 2021 snap election published in the Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties, for 
instance, concluded that then prime minister Justin Trudeau was likely denied his hoped-for majority due to voter 
perceptions that the campaign was an attempt to use the COVID pandemic to consolidate power.
An earlier paper on Canada's 2000 snap election similarly concluded that then prime minister Jean Chrétien was 
also punished for electoral opportunism. Although in that case, it didn't matter, and Chrétien cruised to a majority 
anyway.
Carney, for his part, said he has no plans to use the snap election prerogative. "Of course we're not," he said in 
response to a question about whether he was angling for a spring election.

Title: FIRST READING: Why Canada lets prime ministers opportunistically call elections whenever they want

Body: First Reading is a Canadian politics newsletter curated by the National Post's own Tristin Hopper. To get an early 
version sent directly to your inbox, sign up here.( https://nationalpost.com/newsletters/ )
TOP STORY
There is now open speculation that Prime Minister Mark Carney could be poised to exercise what is arguably the 
single greatest privilege of his office.
Namely, the ability to call a snap election the moment the polls are in his favour.
On Tuesday, Conservative MP Michelle Rempel Garner accused Carney of deliberately provoking U.S. President 
Donald Trump with an anti-American speech in Davos with an eye towards a "snap spring election."
As Rempel Garner wrote in a social media post, the idea was to allegedly reignite Trump's ire for Canada and 
"restart the same narrative they had in the campaign last year."
Carney would certainly not be the first prime minister to opportunistically call an early election. Similarly, the tactic 
has been used at the provincial level by politicians of every conceivable political stripe.
Most recently, Ontario Premier Doug Ford called a snap election in early 2025 just as opinion polls showed his 
Progressive Conservatives enjoying a near-unprecedented 20 point lead( https://innovativeresearch.ca/wp-
content/uploads/2025/01/CTM2501-ON-Politics-Web-Post-Deck-Public-Release.pdf ).
But while it's a normalized part of Canadian politics for incumbents to call elections whenever it's to their personal 
advantage, it's a power shared by few other G7 leaders.
The U.S. president holds no power whatsoever over the timing of elections.
In Germany, the chancellor can't unilaterally trigger an election, but must instead seek a vote of non-confidence in 
the Bundestag, the federal parliament of Germany.
The French president can call snap elections for the National Assembly, but not for his own office, which must 
adhere to five-year terms bookended by fixed election days.
Page 2 of 3
FIRST READING: Why Canada lets prime ministers opportunistically call elections whenever they want
Italy's system is notorious for constant snap elections, but the prime minister's power to unilaterally dissolve 
parliament is checked somewhat by the fact that the Italian president will sometimes deny the request.
It was the U.K. that gave Canada its system of a prime minister able to unilaterally dissolve Parliament, of course. 
But even the Brits have been much more skeptical of the measure, and have experimented with plans to rescind it.
The U.K. passed the Fixed-term Parliaments Act in 2011, which set fixed election dates and bound British prime 
ministers to a system of triggering early elections only after a two-thirds vote of non-confidence.
Nick Clegg, the then deputy prime minister who championed the bill, said it would stop general elections from 
being "a play thing of governments."
However, the measure was repealed in 2022( https://consoc.org.uk/the-intention-behind-the-repeal-of-the-fixed-
term-parliaments-act-is-to-strengthen-the-executive-and-the-conservative-party/ ) by then prime minister Boris 
Johnson, after he argued that his inability to call an election was hindering his ability to facilitate the U.K.'s 
withdrawal from the European Union.
There's nothing in the Canadian constitution that specifically empowers the prime minister to unilaterally trigger 
elections at any time. Rather, it's just worked out that way as a consequence of the centuries-long process of 
gradually transferring power from the Crown to Parliament.
As a write-up by the Centre for Constitutional Studies puts it, it's one of many things in the Canadian system relying 
on "unwritten rules."
Since the beginning, the power has always given an incumbent advantage to Canadian prime ministers, who 
could use a snap election to head off a looming scandal or capitalize on a weak opposition.
But in modern times, the value of the snap election prerogative has only gone up with the advent of public opinion 
polling and mass media.
Critics of Carney, for instance, are accusing him of engineering a temporary surge in the polls in order to ride it to a 
majority government.
In a recent appearance on CBC's Power and Politics, Conservative political analyst Kate Harrison cited Carney's 
recent boost to the GST credit, and Ottawa's new "well-manicured" Buy Canada ad campaign.
"There are a lot of breadcrumbs still being left by the Liberals, I would observe, in terms of leaving themselves open 
to the prospect of pulling the plug and having an early election," she said.
The one major check against the snap election prerogative is that there is a bit of a history of prime ministers being 
punished by the electorate if their snap election call is seen as particularly cynical.
An analysis of Canada's 2021 snap election published in the Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties, for 
instance, concluded that then prime minister Justin Trudeau was likely denied his hoped-for majority due to voter 
perceptions that the campaign was an attempt to use the COVID pandemic to consolidate power.
An earlier paper on Canada's 2000 snap election similarly concluded that then prime minister Jean Chrétien was 
also punished for electoral opportunism. Although in that case, it didn't matter, and Chrétien cruised to a majority 
anyway.
Carney, for his part, said he has no plans to use the snap election prerogative. "Of course we're not," he said in 
response to a question about whether he was angling for a spring election.

title: Five Conservative Candidates offer distinct choices for party Voters; As race comes down to last few weeks,
body:
After three debates, the candidates for the B.C. Conservative leadership have sorted themselves into five distinctive 
campaigns, each with its own identity, strengths, and weaknesses.
Iain Black, the tax cutter. The former B.C. Liberal cabinet minister and ex-head of the Vancouver Board of Trade 
says experience in government and business makes him the most ready to take office as premier.
He promises "seismic change" on the fiscal front, starting with a 20 per cent cut in income taxes and phasing out 
the employer health tax.
Critics say that means a $7 billion-plus hit on revenues to a budget already $13 billion in the red. Black notes the 
Gordon Campbell B.C. Liberal government (where he served two terms) used a big tax cut to jump-start economic 
recovery in 2001. Opponents say that government also brought in the carbon tax and the HST.
Caroline Elliott, the antiwokester. She makes much of being anti-DRIPA before it was politically safe to do so. She'd 
clean out the education curriculum, eliminating "activist fads" linked to gender identity and decolonization, while 
teaching pride in province and country.
She also wants to scrap Clean B.C., citing a report that showed it was exacting a $110 billion hit on the economy 
over four years, twice the impact of U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs.
The political staffer, policy analyst and pundit has taken hits of her own, for her lack of experience in elected office 
and for recruiting high-profile organizational talent from Ontario.
Note that Campbell endorsed Elliott over Black, who served in his cabinet. Kerry-Lynne Findlay, the true blue Tory. 
The former federal cabinet minister and MP boasts the most endorsements from current and former Conservative 
MLAs and MPs. She reminds opponents that being party leader and premier "is not an entry-level job."
On DRIPA, she cites her experience as a lawyer, leaseholder and spokesperson for the Musqueam Park Residents 
Association. She fought the Musqueam nation all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada and won a split decision 
against its excessive rent hikes.
Page 2 of 3
Five Conservative Candidates offer distinct choices for party Voters; As race comes down to last few weeks, 
challenge for next leader remains unity
Findlay is accused of mounting a political "purity test" against opponents with links to federal and provincial 
Liberals. Yet she acknowledges supporting the B.C. Liberals when they were the vehicle of choice to defeat the 
NDP.
Yuri Fulmer, the deal-maker. Business leader Fulmer says the other candidates talk big about uniting the right, but 
he's the only one who has done anything about it.
He cut a unique deal with OneBC Leader Dallas Brodie where she agreed not to run candidates in 88 of 93 
provincial ridings and Fulmer agreed the Conservatives would leave five free for her party. Opponents question the 
wisdom of surrendering five seats in a province where the 2017 and 2024 elections were decided by one seat.
The most aggressive candidate on economic growth and resource development, Fulmer says it is time to "put a 
business person in the premier's office."
He vows to end voluntary transfers of land and money to Indigenous nations until they come to an understanding 
with B.C. on expedited development. He'd sign permits in the premier's office in his own hand if that is what it takes 
to get resource development moving.
Fulmer's freedom charter would enshrine property rights, restore merit-based hiring, strengthen parental rights, and 
end land acknowledgments.
Findlay is probably the closest to Fulmer ideologically, but even she thinks he's gone too far with the OneBC deal.
Peter Milobar, the realist. The former Kamloops mayor is the only candidate with a legislature seat. He asks the 
other four if they intend to persuade a current MLA to step down should they be elected leader.
As his party's finance critic, Milobar was the first to flag the fiscal implications of Black's tax cuts. He argues the Eby 
deficits can only be eliminated by more modest tax cuts, major reductions in spending and measures to promote 
growth over a period of years.
On DRIPA, Milobar favours repeal, same as the other four. But he warns that it won't be accomplished without 
major difficulties in Indigenous relations. He says the other candidates seem to be engaged in a contest over "who 
can attract the biggest protest on the front lawn of the legislature."
Fulmer blasted Milobar as the voice of the status quo during Saturday's debate on Global TV.
Milobar's words of caution on Indigenous relations may have been what provoked Findlay to accuse him of a 
"conflict of interest" because his wife and children are Indigenous.
Milobar responded with restraint ("that's ridiculous"). Black came to his defence with a scorching posting on social 
media that accused Findlay of "playing the race card."
Ironically, at the end of the second debate, Milobar had briefly misinterpreted Black's comment about "divided 
loyalties" as a reference to him. Black clarified that he was referring to Fulmer's deal with OneBC.
Findlay's shot and Black's response provided the most bitter exchange of the campaign so far.
A reminder that holding this fractious party together will be one of the biggest challenges for whoever wins the 
leadership. vpalmer@postmedia.com !@COPYRIGHT=© 2026 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Five things to watch out for as Quebec 's legislature resumes ahead of fall election
body:
QUÉBEC - Quebec's legislature is back in session May 5, and new Premier Christine Fréchette has five weeks to 
push through her political agenda before the summer break — and October's general election.
Here are five things to watch out for at the national assembly in Quebec City:
1. A law to protect victims of domestic violence
Fréchette’s Coalition Avenir Québec has promised to table a bill that would allow people to obtain their intimate 
partner's criminal record history relating to conjugal violence. A few Canadian provinces have adopted similar 
legislation, including Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
Domestic Security Minister Ian Lafrenière said last week the party is working on a draft of the bill, and Fréchette 
campaigned on the idea during her successful bid to become party leader. She has also promised additional 
resources for women’s shelters.
Nine women have been killed in what are believed to be incidents of domestic violence in Quebec since Jan. 1, 
according to advocates.
2. Trying to adopt ‘as many bills as possible’
Former premier François Legault abruptly prorogued the national assembly in early April during the final sprint of 
CAQ's leadership race to replace him. Following Fréchette's win, the legislature is returning Tuesday and the CAQ 
is bringing back all the bills that had died on the floor — including legislation introduced by the opposition, says 
François Bonnardel, the CAQ's government house leader.
Bonnardel told journalists last week the government wants to “adopt as many bills as possible” in the next five 
weeks.
Another new bill the CAQ plans on tabling would prevent the province's electoral commission from eliminating a 
riding in Montreal and on the Gaspé Peninsula.
3. Will Quebec have a constitution?

Page 2 of 3
Five things to watch out for as Quebec 's legislature resumes ahead of fall election
Among the bills being considered is a draft constitution introduced by Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette, who 
had supported Fréchette's rival in the leadership race, Bernard Drainville.
Jolin-Barrette's approach to moving his bill through the legislature has been described by opposition parties as ill-
conceived, divisive and authoritarian. Nonetheless, Fréchette has said she would “pull out all the stops to get this 
important text adopted.”
But even though the CAQ has a majority — and can pass bills into law on its own — Fréchette has said she wants 
the support of at least one other party before adopting the constitution, a document the justice minister says will 
protect Quebec’s identity and culture.
4. Can the Conservatives make their mark in the national assembly?
The only opposition party to have shown openness to Jolin-Barrette’s constitution is Éric Duhaime’s Conservatives, 
who until March did not have a seat in the national assembly despite winning just under 13 per cent of the popular 
vote in the 2022 election. In comparison, the Liberals won 21 seats with just over 14 per cent of the vote.
The party made its entry into the legislature when former CAQ minister Maïté Blanchette Vézina — who had been 
shuffled out of Legault's cabinet — officially joined the Conservatives in late March.
Before the member from Rimouski joined his party, Duhaime had to be invited by a sitting member to hold news 
events at the legislature. Now, it remains to be seen whether Duhaime and Blanchette Vézina can raise the party's 
profile enough to give the Conservatives the momentum and energy they need to win seats in the Oct. 5 election.
Poll aggregator Qc125.com indicates Duhaime's party would win 10 out of 125 seats if an election were held today.
5. Leadership changes
Two of Quebec’s five parties have held leadership races earlier this year: the governing CAQ and the Liberals.
Charles Milliard, a pharmacist, was acclaimed Liberal leader in February after Pablo Rodriguez stepped down 
following a series of scandals. Milliard, like Duhaime, does not have a seat at the legislature. The Liberal leader 
has said his priorities are to support small and medium-sized businesses and revitalize Quebec’s economy.
Fréchette has been busy since she was sworn in on April 15. She reached a tentative agreement with Quebec’s 
specialist doctors, cut taxes for 75,000 small- and medium-size businesses, and announced a holiday for the 
welcome tax for new homeowners. She also flew to Washington to meet with influential members of U.S. President 
Donald Trump’s administration.
Fréchette has until October to turn the ship around for the CAQ, which Qc125.com says would win zero seats if an 
election were held today.
--- With files from Erika Morris, Thomas Laberge, Patrice Bergeron and Frédéric Lacroix-Couture
This report by The Canadian Press was first published May 5, 2026.
