title: Michael Taube: Andrew Scheer gets the political comeback he deserves
body:
The Conservative caucus announced( https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/poilievre-conservative-caucus-meeting-
1.7527562 ) on Wednesday that Andrew Scheer will serve as interim Opposition leader during the spring 
parliamentary session. It's not only an incredible political comeback for the former party leader, but it's also led to a 
hilarious amount of pearl-clutching from political critics and foes alike.
Filling the Opposition leader's role in the House of Commons was unavoidable.
Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre led the party to a solid second-place finish and its highest share of popular 
support (41.3 per cent) since( https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/article/poilievre-pledges-to-listen-after-election-loss-
as-conservative-mps-opt-for-power-to-remove-leader/ ) former prime minister Brian Mulroney in 1988. Alas, he 
unexpectedly lost his seat in the Ontario-based riding of Carleton to Liberal candidate Bruce Fanjoy. Conservative 
MP Damien Kurek has agreed to step aside( https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/damien-kurek-poilievre-byelection-
1.7526895 ) from his extremely safe Alberta-based seat in Battle River-Crowfoot to trigger a byelection. The 
earliest( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/andrew-scheer-interim-leader-conservative-party ) that Kurek can 
resign is late June, meaning Poilievre won't be able to rejoin Parliament until mid-September.
This opened the door to Scheer's return to political leadership, albeit on a temporary basis. While Conservative 
colleagues and supporters congratulated him, a brigade of rabid lefties began to freak out right on cue.
Scheer was called a "clown," "loser," "irrelevant," "snivelling," "misogynistic," "unserious" and far worse on social 
media. He was labelled an "American" and "goofy and immature." One person was "creeped out" by his "perma-
smile." There was also this offensive albeit creative insult, "Andrew Scheer said he's confused, he thought they 
nominated him Pope."
Putting this left-wing disdain for Scheer aside, why are some Canadians so irritated by the prospect of his brief 
sojourn as Opposition leader? People get triggered by almost anything these days, so that's part of the equation. 
The other component? They remember how much they opposed his fiscal and social conservative beliefs and 
values.
Scheer has been in politics for over two decades. He was first elected( 
https://lop.parl.ca/sites/ParlInfo/default/en_CA/People/Profile?personId=9276 ) in 2004 as a Conservative MP for 
the Saskatchewan riding of Regina-Qu'Appelle. (One of the members of that particular freshman class was, as it 
happens, Poilievre( https://lop.parl.ca/sites/ParlInfo/default/en_CA/People/Profile?personId=16312 ).) He's never 
Page 2 of 3
Michael Taube: Andrew Scheer gets the political comeback he deserves
been a cabinet minister, but served as Deputy Speaker of the House and became the youngest-ever( 
https://www.ourcommons.ca/heritage/en/collection/27925 ) House Speaker in 2011 at age 32.
His defining career moment was serving as Conservative party leader from May 2017 to August 2020. Scheer was 
effective in this role from the get-go. He fought for lower taxes, smaller government, private enterprise and more 
individual rights and freedoms with enthusiasm. He was called( 
https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=1526480840718996 ) "Stephen Harper with a smile," which gave him the 
ability to be compared to the well-respected former prime minister while still ensuring that his own personality and 
leadership would continue to shine.
Scheer led( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opinion_polling_for_the_2019_Canadian_federal_election ) in most polls 
against then-Liberal Prime Minister Justin Trudeau starting around February 2019. He took advantage of 
Trudeau's declining popularity in the midst of some of his worst scandals, including three older instances of 
wearing blackface. When the election was called, it seemed as if he was going to win.
Things soon began to fall apart. Scheer was hurt by several controversies of his own. These included questions( 
https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/andrew-scheer-insurance-broker-accreditation-1.5302093 ) about his previous 
work in the insurance industry in Saskatchewan as well as the revelation that he actually held( 
https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-conservative-leader-andrew-scheer-holds-dual-canadian-us-
citizenship/ ) dual Canadian and American citizenship.
Moreover, he got dragged down for his social conservative values by his critics in politics and the media. Scheer 
has a strong Catholic faith. He supports religious freedom, family values and the rights of the unborn. That being 
said, he recognized that his private views had to always remain separate from his political ambitions. He also stood 
for a big tent philosophy in the Conservative party and movement. Those who differed from his own position on 
abortion and gay marriage would continue to have their views respected and heard in every corner of this country.
This was a fair and level-headed approach to these contentious issues. Anyone who knows Scheer on a political or 
personal level could vouch for its authenticity.
The problem was that he consistently struggled to convey those long-held positions with the right words and tone to 
ease people's concerns. This became problematic when a 2005 video was unearthed in which he spoke out against 
gay marriage. He said( https://macleans.ca/politics/ottawa/what-andrew-scheer-believes-about-same-sex-marriage/ 
) that same-sex couples "have many of the collateral features of marriage, but they do not have its inherent feature, 
as they cannot commit to the natural procreation of children. They cannot, therefore, be married." Although he 
acknowledged( https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/andrew-scheer-gay-marriage-lgbtq-goodale-1.5256095 ) his views 
on this subject had evolved and he would not reopen this debate in Parliament as prime minister, many doubted 
his words all the way to election day.
That was then, and this is now.
Scheer has worked hard to successfully rebuild his name and public image. He's been Opposition House leader 
since September 2022. He's one of the party's main faces and voices to get out( 
https://www.ctvnews.ca/video/politics/2025/04/30/he-led-our-party-to-historic-highs-andrew-scheer-on-poilievres-
future-as-conservative-leader/ ) important political messaging and set the tone for policy initiatives. He's well-
respected by his leader, colleagues and peers. He's earned the right to be leader of the Opposition until Poilievre 
returns to Ottawa.
Will pearl-clutching Canadians think differently about Scheer's improbable political comeback once the House 
reconvenes? No. The world of politics may be his oyster, but they're not going to let go of the shell.

This opened the door to Scheer's return to political leadership, albeit on a temporary basis. While Conservative 
colleagues and supporters congratulated him, a brigade of rabid lefties began to freak out right on cue.
Scheer was called a "clown," "loser," "irrelevant," "snivelling," "misogynistic," "unserious" and far worse on social 
media. He was labelled an "American" and "goofy and immature." One person was "creeped out" by his "perma-
smile." There was also this offensive albeit creative insult, "Andrew Scheer said he's confused, he thought they 
nominated him Pope."
Putting this left-wing disdain for Scheer aside, why are some Canadians so irritated by the prospect of his brief 
sojourn as Opposition leader? People get triggered by almost anything these days, so that's part of the equation. 
The other component? They remember how much they opposed his fiscal and social conservative beliefs and 
values.
Scheer has been in politics for over two decades. He was first elected( 
https://lop.parl.ca/sites/ParlInfo/default/en_CA/People/Profile?personId=9276 ) in 2004 as a Conservative MP for 
the Saskatchewan riding of Regina-Qu'Appelle. (One of the members of that particular freshman class was, as it 
happens, Poilievre( https://lop.parl.ca/sites/ParlInfo/default/en_CA/People/Profile?personId=16312 ).) He's never 
Page 2 of 3
Michael Taube: Andrew Scheer gets the political comeback he deserves
been a cabinet minister, but served as Deputy Speaker of the House and became the youngest-ever( 
https://www.ourcommons.ca/heritage/en/collection/27925 ) House Speaker in 2011 at age 32.
His defining career moment was serving as Conservative party leader from May 2017 to August 2020. Scheer was 
effective in this role from the get-go. He fought for lower taxes, smaller government, private enterprise and more 
individual rights and freedoms with enthusiasm. He was called( 
https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=1526480840718996 ) "Stephen Harper with a smile," which gave him the 
ability to be compared to the well-respected former prime minister while still ensuring that his own personality and 
leadership would continue to shine.
Scheer led( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opinion_polling_for_the_2019_Canadian_federal_election ) in most polls 
against then-Liberal Prime Minister Justin Trudeau starting around February 2019. He took advantage of 
Trudeau's declining popularity in the midst of some of his worst scandals, including three older instances of 
wearing blackface. When the election was called, it seemed as if he was going to win.
Things soon began to fall apart. Scheer was hurt by several controversies of his own. These included questions( 
https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/andrew-scheer-insurance-broker-accreditation-1.5302093 ) about his previous 
work in the insurance industry in Saskatchewan as well as the revelation that he actually held( 
https://www.theglobeandmail.com/politics/article-conservative-leader-andrew-scheer-holds-dual-canadian-us-
citizenship/ ) dual Canadian and American citizenship.
Moreover, he got dragged down for his social conservative values by his critics in politics and the media. Scheer 
has a strong Catholic faith. He supports religious freedom, family values and the rights of the unborn. That being 
said, he recognized that his private views had to always remain separate from his political ambitions. He also stood 
for a big tent philosophy in the Conservative party and movement. Those who differed from his own position on 
abortion and gay marriage would continue to have their views respected and heard in every corner of this country.
This was a fair and level-headed approach to these contentious issues. Anyone who knows Scheer on a political or 
personal level could vouch for its authenticity.
The problem was that he consistently struggled to convey those long-held positions with the right words and tone to 
ease people's concerns. This became problematic when a 2005 video was unearthed in which he spoke out against 
gay marriage. He said( https://macleans.ca/politics/ottawa/what-andrew-scheer-believes-about-same-sex-marriage/ 
) that same-sex couples "have many of the collateral features of marriage, but they do not have its inherent feature, 
as they cannot commit to the natural procreation of children. They cannot, therefore, be married." Although he 
acknowledged( https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/andrew-scheer-gay-marriage-lgbtq-goodale-1.5256095 ) his views 
on this subject had evolved and he would not reopen this debate in Parliament as prime minister, many doubted 
his words all the way to election day.
That was then, and this is now.
Scheer has worked hard to successfully rebuild his name and public image. He's been Opposition House leader 
since September 2022. He's one of the party's main faces and voices to get out( 
https://www.ctvnews.ca/video/politics/2025/04/30/he-led-our-party-to-historic-highs-andrew-scheer-on-poilievres-
future-as-conservative-leader/ ) important political messaging and set the tone for policy initiatives. He's well-
respected by his leader, colleagues and peers. He's earned the right to be leader of the Opposition until Poilievre 
returns to Ottawa.
Will pearl-clutching Canadians think differently about Scheer's improbable political comeback once the House 
reconvenes? No. The world of politics may be his oyster, but they're not going to let go of the shell.

title: Michael Taube: Chrystia Freeland, failed white knight of the Liberal party
body:
The federal Liberals will pick a new party leader and prime minister on March 9. Former Bank of Canada and 
Bank of England governor Mark Carney has a significant lead over his closest rival, former deputy prime minister 
and finance minister Chrystia Freeland. He's been ahead by double digits since late January. A Feb. 11 Leger poll 
suggested the gap( https://leger360.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Leger-x-Canadian-Press-Federal-
Politics_VF.pdf ) was an eye-popping 54 points (68 to 14 per cent).
Freeland has soldiered on. She's attempting to defy the odds and make a miraculous comeback, but some of her 
comments have been unusual as of late. More than her usual fare, in fact.
"I intend to win on Sunday, and when I win, I will invite Mark to serve as finance minister in my government. I think 
we'll make a great team," Freeland triumphantly said( https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/article/chrystia-freeland-
wants-mark-carney-to-be-finance-minister-if-she-becomes-pm/ ) during Wednesday's media scrum in Vaughan, 
Ont. Being positive and upbeat is one thing. Since she's trailing badly against Carney, the acknowledged 
frontrunner, any suggestion that she'll put him in her cabinet makes her look delusional.
Nevertheless, it's a tame comment compared to the bizarre statement she recently made about U.S. President 
Donald Trump.
During the Feb. 25 English-language leadership debate, Freeland said she wanted to build stronger ties with 
European allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). That's fine, but she also stated,( 
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/us/politics/2025/03/03/british-nuclear-weapons-canada-trump-chrystia-freeland/ ) "I 
would be sure that France and Britain were there, who possess nuclear weapons." Why does this matter? "I would 
be working urgently with those partners to build a closer security relationship ... in a time when the United States 
can be a threat."
Wait, what?
That's right. Freeland went nuclear against Trump and seemingly called for nuclear protection against him. She 
suggested the president is "clearly threatening our sovereignty" with calls to annex Canada, and stronger NATO 
ties would "guarantee our security."
I'm sorry, but that's completely nuts.
Page 2 of 3
Michael Taube: Chrystia Freeland, failed white knight of the Liberal party
Tensions between Canada and the U.S. have escalated for months. They went over the edge when Trump's 25 per 
cent tariffs took effect( https://apnews.com/article/trump-tariffs-mexico-canada-
b19e004dddb579c373b247037e04424b ) on Tuesday (only to pause them for some goods for another month two 
days later( https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/economics/trump-administration-floats-exemptions-tariffs-canadian-
mexican-goods-rcna195110 )). Freeland's analysis, which was shared before the tariffs became a reality, made her 
seem hysterical, unstable and unworthy of Canada's next prime minister. All the qualities she likely associates 
with Trump.
What caused Freeland to go rogue?
One possibility is that she doesn't want to become another casualty in political history. Those who bring down party 
leaders and governments, or attempt to become political white knights, are rarely rewarded with the riches they feel 
they're owed.
Here are two examples.
Michael Heseltine, a longtime( https://www.gov.uk/government/people/michael-heseltine ) British Conservative MP 
from 1966 to 2001, helped bring down( 
https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://www.gov.uk/government/people/michael-
heseltine__;!!MtWvt2UVEQ!GbXALzK4gevnh829wOg3xdEmcsvsPnWf0McJbav8hgHetRSKhS7KkZJP7jNlQeYTDo
PsdU4GZK0y2HSgyqg$ ) Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher's leadership in 1990. He had previously served in 
Thatcher's cabinet, but was sitting in the backbenches due to opposition to her economic views and 
Euroscepticism. When the deputy prime minister at the time, Geoffrey Howe, stunningly resigned on Nov. 13, 
1990 in Parliament, Heseltine seized upon this opportunity. He challenged Thatcher for the party leadership, 
winning 152 votes (41 per cent) on the first ballot while she received 204 votes (55 per cent). It looked like Heseltine 
had enough momentum to beat her. Humiliated and embarrassed, Thatcher resigned( 
https://www.nytimes.com/1990/11/23/world/change-britain-thatcher-says-she-ll-quit-11-1-2-years-prime-minister-
ended-party.html ).
Ironically, Heseltine received blowback on the second ballot from Conservative MPs who had supported him. He 
dropped to 131 votes, with many shifting to Chancellor of the Exchequer John Major. Realizing he couldn't win, 
Heseltine withdrew( https://www.theguardian.com/fromthearchive/story/0,12269,1095402,00.html ). He went on to 
become deputy prime minister and first secretary of state in Major's cabinet, but was never completely forgiven by 
Thatcher's supporters for his betrayal.
There's also Grace McCarthy( https://www.leg.bc.ca/learn/watv/biographies/grace-mccarthy ), the grand dame of 
British Columbia's Social Credit Party. She was first elected in 1966, and helped rebuild the Socreds after their 
devastating loss in the 1972 election. She worked tirelessly and increased membership( 
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_McCarthy ) from 5,000 to 70,000. She was a senior cabinet minister under 
then-Premier Bill Bennett when the Socreds returned to power in 1975. She helped bring Expo 86 to Vancouver, 
established the SkyTrain and initiated Canada's first toll-free helpline for abused children.
For all the good work McCarthy did, her party never seemed to reciprocate. She lost the 1986 Socred leadership 
race( https://whistlermuseum.org/tag/1986-socred-leadership-convention/ ) to Bill Vander Zalm and finished third. 
When he resigned after a series of scandals in 1991, McCarthy was viewed as the frontrunner to replace him. Yet, 
she shockingly lost this leadership race to Rita Johnson( https://www.leg.bc.ca/learn/discover-your-legislature/1991-
first-woman-premier-in-canadian-history ), a Vander Zalm loyalist.
After the party was decimated in the 1991 election, Johnson resigned and McCarthy became( 
https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://books.google.ca/books?id=jdIPs9zun7AC&;dq=*22linda*reid*22**A22allan*warn
ke*22&;pg=PA369&;redir_esc=y*v=onepage&;q=*22linda*20reid*22*20*22allan*20warnke*22&;f=false__;JSslKyUr
JSMlJSUlJSUl!!MtWvt2UVEQ!GbXALzK4gevnh829wOg3xdEmcsvsPnWf0McJbav8hgHetRSKhS7KkZJP7jNlQeYT
DoPsdU4GZK0yREJEu-w$ ) Socred leader in 1993. She would never become premier. Instead, she lost in a 
byelection to Liberal Mike de Jong in the historically safe Socred riding of Matsqui the following year. Four of the six 
Page 3 of 3
Michael Taube: Chrystia Freeland, failed white knight of the Liberal party
Socred MLAs defected to B.C.'s Reform Party, wiping out the Socreds' party status. McCarthy resigned in May 
1994 and exited politics for good.
Freeland played a major role in forcing Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's resignation after he decided to shuffle her 
out as finance minister in favour of Carney. She was applauded for her efforts and even served as a white knight 
(of sorts) since the Liberals had been well behind Pierre Poilievre and the Conservatives for two years.
Alas, many of Freeland's longtime colleagues have turned against her and supported the politically inexperienced 
Carney. This impending failure and forthcoming loss has clearly hit her hard. Maybe that's why she chose to utilize 
the nuclear option.

title: Michael Taube: Mark Carney should opt for civility over snide remarks
body:
Politicians in Canada, like those in most countries, have had their moments of behaving badly in public. We've 
witnessed backbenchers all the way to prime ministers willing to either speak out, criticize, or occasionally swear at 
opponents. Many of these inappropriate comments were made in the hallowed halls of Parliament or provincial 
legislatures, which protected them from being sued in court.
Yet, something odd has happened recently. There's been a noticeable rise in the vexatious and noxious behaviour 
of some of our public officials. It's led to an increase in the "snide side" of Canadian politics, and that's not a good 
thing for this venerable institution.
Liberal Prime Minister Mark Carney was recently asked by a reporter when he last spoke with U.S. President 
Donald Trump. His immediate answer( https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FsH2FvpbmK8 ) - "Who cares?" He 
continued with his runaway train of thought thusly, "I mean, it's a detail. It's a detail. I spoke to him... I'll speak to him 
again when it matters."
Oh, it's much more than a detail. When the relationship with our greatest friend, ally, and trading partner is so badly 
frayed, every word matters.
Carney has since apologized( https://globalnews.ca/news/11543425/mark-carney-donald-trump-trade-who-cares-
response/ ) for his "poor choice of words."
Ontario Progressive Conservative Premier Doug Ford joined the apologies fray, too. Just before Bill 60( 
https://www.ola.org/en/legislative-business/bills/parliament-44/session-1/bill-60 ), also known as the Fighting 
Delays, Building Faster Act, easily passed its third and final reading, several protesters chanted( 
https://www.ctvnews.ca/toronto/politics/queens-park/article/doug-ford-tells-heckler-to-find-a-job-as-protest-erupts-
over-ontario-law-critics-say-will-speed-up-evictions/ ) "people over profit," "shame" and "you're putting people on 
the streets." As one protester was being ejected from the legislature, Ford quipped( 
https://x.com/TinaYazdani/status/1993004158832800231 ), "go find a job, buddy." He doubled down by suggesting( 
https://globalnews.ca/news/11543088/doug-ford-find-a-job-comment/ ) that the protesters "do have a job, by the 
way, they're getting paid by the groups" that oppose his government and leadership.
Whether you agree or disagree with the premier's comments, that's not what a political leader should be saying 
about or to a member of the public.
Page 2 of 3
Michael Taube: Mark Carney should opt for civility over snide remarks
Meanwhile, Ontario NDP leader Marit Stiles was recently expelled( https://globalnews.ca/video/11535359/ontario-
ndp-leader-marit-stiles-calls-ford-government-corrupt-gets-expelled-from-legislature ) from the legislature for 
calling Ford's government "corrupt." This occurred during a heated
tête-à-tête with Labour Minister David Piccini related to the Skills Development Fund controversy involving donors 
and lobbyists friendly to the government. After suggesting( https://globalnews.ca/news/11533297/marit-stiles-ford-
government-corrupt-skills-development-fund-claim/ ) this was part of the "endless grift of an anti-democratic and 
yes, corrupt government," Stiles was asked to apologize by House Speaker Donna Skelly. She refused, leading to 
her expulsion.
Stiles, much like Ford, has doubled down on her assessment. "Goddamn right they're corrupt," she wrote( 
https://x.com/MaritStiles/status/1991237098964197605 ) on X on Nov. 19, and said( 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q-i-MUwz958 ) "I think that is corruption, and I'm going to call it what it is... and 
I'm not allowed to say that word in the Chamber" to City News reporter Caryn Ceolin on Nov. 21. Regardless of her 
personal feelings, it's still wrong for the Opposition leader to make these sorts of allegations in a public space.
Some observers might suggest these remarks are fairly tame compared to other historical examples. Former Prime 
Minister Pierre Trudeau's infamous "fuddle duddle" remark( https://www.cbc.ca/archives/fuddle-duddle-when-the-
pm-denied-saying-the-f-word-in-the-house-1.4668000 ) in 1971, for instance, when it seemed pretty clear to former 
Progressive Conservative MPs Lincoln Alexander and John Lundrigan that he mouthed an obscenity. There was 
also former Reform Party, Canadian Alliance, and Conservative MP Darrel Stinson's small collection of infamous 
remarks. The most notorious was when he told( https://x.com/MBrant75/status/1993763855038607394?s=20 ) 
former Liberal MP John Cannis, "Do you have the fortitude or the gonads to stand up and come across here and 
say that to me, you son of a b-ch?," after the latter called him a racist in the House of Commons. Cannis shouldn't 
have called him a racist either.
To say nothing of comments made in other countries.
Then-U.S. President John Adams depicted( https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/are-presidential-
campaigns-getting-nastier-not-
really#%3A~%3Atext=The%20Detroit%20Free%20Press%2C%20late%2Cas%20brainless%20as%20his%20saddl
e.%E2%80%9D ) Alexander Hamilton as the "bastard brat of a Scotch pedler" to Benjamin Rush in an 1806 letter. 
Kenneth Rayner, a former North Carolina Congressman, infamously described then-President Franklin Pierce as 
the "pimp of the White House" in an 1855 speech. Then-Alabama Senator Thomas Heflin made critical remarks in 
1928 about Alfred E. Smith, the first Catholic presidential candidate, suggesting if the "wet, Romish, East Side, 
Tammany Hall candidate, is nominated it will be on account of the Roman influence." We'll also toss in then-Italian 
Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi's cringeworthy 2008 remark( https://nationalpost.com/wp-admin/post-new.php ) 
about then-U.S. President Barack Obama being( https://www.theguardian.com/world/2008/nov/06/italy-
barackobama ) "young, handsome and tanned."
Yes, these remarks were more creative and entertaining than "who cares," "go find a job" and "corrupt." So what? 
This isn't a contest about who can make the vilest comment about a political opponent who is perceived to be thin-
skinned. That's easy to achieve. None of these insults were necessary or called for, however.
Some Canadians will be enthralled with this surge in outrageous and outlandish remarks. They shouldn't be. Public 
officials must be held to a higher standard of civility as representatives of the people. Attacking opponents and 
critics, using schoolyard tactics, and appealing to the lowest common denominator isn't something to be admired or 
emulated. Politicians, like leaders in other industries, should use their intelligence and take the high road instead of 
relying on inappropriate language inside and outside of a legislature.
If the "snide side" of politics maintains its current trajectory, it will further weaken the institution and discourage even 
more people from running for public office. That doesn't benefit anyone.

continued with his runaway train of thought thusly, "I mean, it's a detail. It's a detail. I spoke to him... I'll speak to him 
again when it matters."
Oh, it's much more than a detail. When the relationship with our greatest friend, ally, and trading partner is so badly 
frayed, every word matters.
Carney has since apologized( https://globalnews.ca/news/11543425/mark-carney-donald-trump-trade-who-cares-
response/ ) for his "poor choice of words."
Ontario Progressive Conservative Premier Doug Ford joined the apologies fray, too. Just before Bill 60( 
https://www.ola.org/en/legislative-business/bills/parliament-44/session-1/bill-60 ), also known as the Fighting 
Delays, Building Faster Act, easily passed its third and final reading, several protesters chanted( 
https://www.ctvnews.ca/toronto/politics/queens-park/article/doug-ford-tells-heckler-to-find-a-job-as-protest-erupts-
over-ontario-law-critics-say-will-speed-up-evictions/ ) "people over profit," "shame" and "you're putting people on 
the streets." As one protester was being ejected from the legislature, Ford quipped( 
https://x.com/TinaYazdani/status/1993004158832800231 ), "go find a job, buddy." He doubled down by suggesting( 
https://globalnews.ca/news/11543088/doug-ford-find-a-job-comment/ ) that the protesters "do have a job, by the 
way, they're getting paid by the groups" that oppose his government and leadership.
Whether you agree or disagree with the premier's comments, that's not what a political leader should be saying 
about or to a member of the public.
Page 2 of 3
Michael Taube: Mark Carney should opt for civility over snide remarks
Meanwhile, Ontario NDP leader Marit Stiles was recently expelled( https://globalnews.ca/video/11535359/ontario-
ndp-leader-marit-stiles-calls-ford-government-corrupt-gets-expelled-from-legislature ) from the legislature for 
calling Ford's government "corrupt." This occurred during a heated
tête-à-tête with Labour Minister David Piccini related to the Skills Development Fund controversy involving donors 
and lobbyists friendly to the government. After suggesting( https://globalnews.ca/news/11533297/marit-stiles-ford-
government-corrupt-skills-development-fund-claim/ ) this was part of the "endless grift of an anti-democratic and 
yes, corrupt government," Stiles was asked to apologize by House Speaker Donna Skelly. She refused, leading to 
her expulsion.
Stiles, much like Ford, has doubled down on her assessment. "Goddamn right they're corrupt," she wrote( 
https://x.com/MaritStiles/status/1991237098964197605 ) on X on Nov. 19, and said( 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q-i-MUwz958 ) "I think that is corruption, and I'm going to call it what it is... and 
I'm not allowed to say that word in the Chamber" to City News reporter Caryn Ceolin on Nov. 21. Regardless of her 
personal feelings, it's still wrong for the Opposition leader to make these sorts of allegations in a public space.
Some observers might suggest these remarks are fairly tame compared to other historical examples. Former Prime 
Minister Pierre Trudeau's infamous "fuddle duddle" remark( https://www.cbc.ca/archives/fuddle-duddle-when-the-
pm-denied-saying-the-f-word-in-the-house-1.4668000 ) in 1971, for instance, when it seemed pretty clear to former 
Progressive Conservative MPs Lincoln Alexander and John Lundrigan that he mouthed an obscenity. There was 
also former Reform Party, Canadian Alliance, and Conservative MP Darrel Stinson's small collection of infamous 
remarks. The most notorious was when he told( https://x.com/MBrant75/status/1993763855038607394?s=20 ) 
former Liberal MP John Cannis, "Do you have the fortitude or the gonads to stand up and come across here and 
say that to me, you son of a b-ch?," after the latter called him a racist in the House of Commons. Cannis shouldn't 
have called him a racist either.
To say nothing of comments made in other countries.
Then-U.S. President John Adams depicted( https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/are-presidential-
campaigns-getting-nastier-not-
really#%3A~%3Atext=The%20Detroit%20Free%20Press%2C%20late%2Cas%20brainless%20as%20his%20saddl
e.%E2%80%9D ) Alexander Hamilton as the "bastard brat of a Scotch pedler" to Benjamin Rush in an 1806 letter. 
Kenneth Rayner, a former North Carolina Congressman, infamously described then-President Franklin Pierce as 
the "pimp of the White House" in an 1855 speech. Then-Alabama Senator Thomas Heflin made critical remarks in 
1928 about Alfred E. Smith, the first Catholic presidential candidate, suggesting if the "wet, Romish, East Side, 
Tammany Hall candidate, is nominated it will be on account of the Roman influence." We'll also toss in then-Italian 
Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi's cringeworthy 2008 remark( https://nationalpost.com/wp-admin/post-new.php ) 
about then-U.S. President Barack Obama being( https://www.theguardian.com/world/2008/nov/06/italy-
barackobama ) "young, handsome and tanned."
Yes, these remarks were more creative and entertaining than "who cares," "go find a job" and "corrupt." So what? 
This isn't a contest about who can make the vilest comment about a political opponent who is perceived to be thin-
skinned. That's easy to achieve. None of these insults were necessary or called for, however.
Some Canadians will be enthralled with this surge in outrageous and outlandish remarks. They shouldn't be. Public 
officials must be held to a higher standard of civility as representatives of the people. Attacking opponents and 
critics, using schoolyard tactics, and appealing to the lowest common denominator isn't something to be admired or 
emulated. Politicians, like leaders in other industries, should use their intelligence and take the high road instead of 
relying on inappropriate language inside and outside of a legislature.
If the "snide side" of politics maintains its current trajectory, it will further weaken the institution and discourage even 
more people from running for public office. That doesn't benefit anyone.

title: Michelle Rempel-Garner: Randy Boissonnault is Trudeau's embarrassment
body:
Why was embattled former Liberal cabinet minister Randy Boissonnault allowed to linger in the federal Liberal 
government as scandal after scandal emerged about his conduct?
The answer to this question can be found in the most recent issue that came to light. While it's tempting to dismiss 
the discovery that Boissonnault falsely claimed Indigenous identity - and that a company he formerly co-owned 
claimed Indigenous ownership( https://nationalpost.com/news/randy-boissonnault-indigenous-claims ) - simply as 
the latest plot twist in a scandal worthy of immortalization in a made-for-Netflix docudrama, the issue underscores a 
broader problem with the federal Liberal government.
Boissonnault and his (allegedly) former business associates have made a legion of fantastical headlines over the 
past year. A scandal-plagued company formerly co-owned by the minister coincidentally received government 
contracts( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/ethics-commissioner-to-look-into-employment-ministers-dealings-
with-company ) as he sat in cabinet. Then came stories of shady allegedly former business partners, 
doppelgangers( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/randy-boissonnault-business-associate-contempt-other-
randy-saga ), pushing the technical capabilities of autocorrect beyond the boundaries of known science, corporate 
mailboxes shared with people adjacent to cocaine busts( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/cabinet-ministers-
firm-shared-mailing-address-with-person-held-in-cocaine-busts ), and allegations of corporate fraud( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/one-more-firm-alleges-it-was-defrauded-by-liberal-cabinet-ministers-partner 
). Throughout, he kept his plum government appointment.
And the fact that Boissonnault remained in Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's cabinet for days after news broke that 
he had fabricated his claims of Indigenous ancestry - on top of all these other scandals - belies an unfixable 
problem within Canada's Liberal government: they operate under a culture that replaces substantive action with fluff 
and hypocrisy, and Canadians suffer the consequences.
Take, for example, the issue at the heart of Boissonault's latest scandal - the inability of the Liberals to 
meaningfully address reconciliation with Indigenous and First Nations people.
Instead of doing the hard work required of such a sensitive and monumental task, the Liberals have oozed 
unctuous sanctimony every time there's an opportunity to take a photo, but have turtled any time there's a need to 
make hard decisions. Trudeau's vocal support for creating a statutory holiday to solemnize reconciliation only to 
take a surfing holiday on its first observance( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/first-reading-trudeaus-tofino-
Page 2 of 3
Michelle Rempel-Garner: Randy Boissonnault is Trudeau's embarrassment
truth-and-reconciliation-adventure ) is but one of a litany of examples of his government's prioritization of fluff over 
substance. Boissonnault politically dining out for years on false claims of Indigenous heritage is another.
So after nine years of government, it's easy to call the Liberals hypocrites and tough for them to seriously make any 
claim that the lives of First Nations and Indigenous persons have improved due to their efforts. Communities remain 
under long-term boil water advisories( https://www.sac-isc.gc.ca/eng/1506514143353/1533317130660 ), crime is 
increasing - particularly against Indigenous women( https://www.justice.gc.ca/eng/rp-pr/jr/jf-pf/2019/may01.html ), 
and Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's government has actually worked against some First Nations communities( 
https://financialpost.com/commodities/energy/disappointment-fear-and-anger-indigenous-communities-blindsided-
by-tecks-decision-to-pull-frontier-project ) as they embark upon various economic development opportunities. There 
are countless other examples just like this, across every area of government, where the Liberals signal one thing 
but do the opposite.
Canadians should view these types of scenarios as a binary: either the Liberals are serious about fixing meaningful 
problems, or they are incompetent hypocrites who reward those like Randy Boissonnault. That Trudeau had an 
opportunity to publicly chastise his hot mess of a minister's actions at a G20 press conference but chose not to do 
so should settle any doubts on the matter. At time of writing, he has yet to say anything of substance about the 
wrongness of what Boissonnault did.
This issue came to a head in the House of Commons Tuesday as Conservative Members of Parliament called for 
Boissonnault's resignation in light of his false claims. I know - I was one of them. Upon making a statement that 
stemmed from Cree lawyer and Sixties-Scoop survivor Leah Ballentine's earlier comments in National Post, in 
which she rightly said, "Identity fraud is fraud( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/randy-boissonnault-
indigenous-claims-5 )," I was expelled from the House of Commons. That I was chastised for this action while 
Boissonneault remained in the cabinet is an indictment on the functionality of both the government and the Liberal 
party as a whole.
The federal Liberal's parliamentary dance partners, the New Democratic Party, shouldn't escape blame on this front 
either. That they continue to express confidence in a government that allows many questionable cabinet ministers 
to linger should cause suspicion as to whether they place a greater priority on supporting their leader's quest to 
reach his February 2025 pension-vesting eligibility date or actions related to their commitment to social justice 
causes they routinely wave their fists in the air about.
Justin Trudeau should not have taken months to remove Mr. Boissonnault from his cabinet. There are several 
others who should be given the boot too, yet remain with car and driver, and hands on the federal purse strings. 
That arrogance is the common denominator behind many of the systemic problems facing Canadians across the 
country right now: a federal government who allows harmful people and ideologies to linger when the courage to 
change is needed.
But Canadians aren't stupid - they know a phoney when they see one. And so in return for Trudeau's charitability 
towards his incompetent and scandal plagued ministers, he shouldn't expect Canadians to allow him to linger in 
his job come the next federal election.
Michelle Rempel-Garner is a Conservative MP for the Alberta riding of Calgary Nose Hill. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2024

title: Miller named new culture minister; Liberals bring Trudeau-era minister back into cabinet as Carney fills gaps
body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney retooled his federal cabinet Monday with an eye on trying to shore up his Quebec 
flank after losing a key minister who resigned in protest over Carney's controversial Alberta energy deal.
To replace Steven Guilbeault - the environmental activist once recruited as a star Liberal candidate in Quebec - 
Carney split Guilbeault's various ministerial roles and responsibilities into three, and gave two of the bigger jobs to 
two other Quebecers.
But he did not undertake a bigger shuffle that many political observers believe is still in the works to deal with those 
the prime minister views as underperformers.
Guilbeault quit cabinet Thursday because he could not defend Carney's agreement to roll back so many of the 
environmental regulations and climate change policies he had once led, after the prime minister signed a deal to 
back a future new oil pipeline with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.
The fluently bilingual Marc Miller, a longtime confidante of Justin Trudeau and former minister of immigration, 
Crown-Indigenous relations and Indigenous services, had been left out of Carney's first two cabinets despite being 
one of the earliest ministers to endorse Carney for Liberal leader.
Now, Miller, 52, who represents the Montreal riding of Ville-Marie-Le Sud-Ouest-Île-des-S\x9Curs, becomes 
Carney's minister of Canadian identity and culture (formerly styled heritage) and of official languages at a critical 
time when a provincial election looms next year in Quebec and there are signs of trouble for the federalist standard-
bearing party.
The provincial wing of the Liberals, the Quebec Liberal Party, is in disarray amid allegations a vote-buying scandal 
marred the selection of its latest leader - Pablo Rodriguez - and the rival separatist Parti Quebecois is on the rise, 
as the governing Coalition Avenir Quebec party plunges in polls. PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has vowed 
to hold a referendum on Quebec sovereignty before 2030 if he wins power in 2026. 
Miller, a bilingual anglophone, will be part of Ottawa's response as that public debate unfolds.
Page 2 of 3
Miller named new culture minister; Liberals bring Trudeau-era minister back into cabinet as Carney fills gaps 
left by Guilbeault
In a second move, the prime minister chose Joël Lightbound, a Quebec City-area minister in charge of 
government transformation, public services and procurement, to take on additional duties as Carney's Quebec 
political lieutenant.
It's a job that requires a deft political antenna, knowledge of the electoral landscape, the skills to attract political 
talent, and the ability to grow a voting base.
Lightbound, 37, was once critical of what he said was Trudeau's political weaponization of divisive vaccination 
mandates during the 2021 mid-pandemic federal election campaign. He was removed as chair of the Quebec 
Liberal caucus after voicing his criticisms publicly. He now takes on the job of politically wielding Liberal policies to 
gain more traction - or at least, resist losing ground - in Quebec. He'll be on the front line as well in the fight to push 
back the separatist sentiment in his home province.
Lightbound recently steered the federal Liberal move to allow Canada Post to close rural post offices and end home 
delivery - something the Bloc Québécois fiercely opposed.
The MP for the Quebec City riding of Louis-Hebert retains his other ministerial responsibilities as Carney seeks to 
expedite government procurement and services through more use of artificial intelligence, and streamlining of the 
federal public service and use of outside consultants.
Carney handed off Guilbeault's ministerial title of "minister of nature" to Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, who 
replaced him in the portfolio in May after the federal election.
In his first public comments on Radio-Canada's French-language talk show "Tout le monde en parle," Guilbeault 
said on Sunday night that while he still believes Carney is the right prime minister for the country, he objected to 
Carney's decisions to exempt Alberta from clean electricity regulations, to lift the oil and gas emissions cap, to 
negotiate a $130 a tonne industrial carbon price lower than the federal benchmark of $170 a tonne, and to 
potentially lift the oil tanker ban on the coast of northern B.C. to facilitate construction of a new oil pipeline.
Guilbeault believes it will be impossible for Canada to meet its greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets for 
2020 in light of the changes, and said Smith "will never be happy" with the concessions made and will demand 
more. "She is not a reliable partner, in my opinion, in this negotiation," he said. 
"Talk about an unwilling and hostile partner," Smith responded Monday. "I'm quite happy, glad to see him go and 
not have the influence in caucus that he clearly had under the previous administration."
She said the deal reached last week with Carney was "possible under prime minister Justin Trudeau, but it was 
impossible because of an obstructionist environment minister named Steven Guilbeault, and I think that the fact 
that he has left is going to be good for Alberta, good for the country, and allow for us to continue working 
constructively together."

title: Minister tied to funding recipient; Summer Jobs Diab a member of church that received money
body:
When Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab dropped by a church kids camp this summer, she posed for photos 
to highlight the funding that came from the Canada Summer Jobs program.
It might not have seemed unusual: members of Parliament have a hand in helping organizations in their riding get 
the summer-job subsidies in the first place. MPs get lists of organizations in their ridings that apply for the subsidy, 
and recommend who should get it.
But Metlege Diab had a more personal relationship with this particular Lebanese parish church in Halifax than just 
representing it as an MP. She has been a parishioner there since the 1980s.
The situation does not seem to violate either the Conflict of Interest Act or codes that public office holders must 
follow, but one government ethics specialist said it touches on issues around perceptions of conflict, as well as what 
questions the department responsible for administering the money asks of MPs who may have ties to the 
organizations whose requests they review.
"Do I think that the minister, in this case, has broken the Act or code? No," said Ian Stedman, who previously 
worked for Ontario's integrity commissioner and now teaches as an associate professor at York University.
"Do I think that the program may want to protect itself by having a higher bar or a higher standard than the Act or 
code? Yes."
The Canada Summer Jobs program offers a wage subsidy for employers to hire those aged 15 to 30 each summer. 
This year, the government announced it would spend $25 million more to create another 6,000 spots to combat the 
country's high youth unemployment rate.
How it works is simple: An organization, including religious ones, applies for the subsidy. The department that 
administers it assesses the application to ensure it meets the criteria and then asks MPs for their feedback based 
on a recommended list, which, according to the program's website, is to ensure "local priorities" are met.
Their feedback, it says, is then used to inform the government's final decisions.
Page 2 of 3
Minister tied to funding recipient; Summer Jobs Diab a member of church that received money
In Metlege Diab's case, a spokeswoman in her Halifax West constituency office said she provided her feedback 
back in March, two months before Prime Minister Mark Carney promoted her to cabinet. She has represented the 
riding federally since 2021.
"The final funding decisions by (Employment and Social Development Canada) were made during the writ period," 
the spokeswoman wrote, referring to the period during the spring federal election.

family member, or where they have a "private interest."

recommendations on funding, should also ask whether they have any personal connections to the organizations on

title: MLA Melanie Mark resigns, says B.C. Legislature felt like a "torture chamber"
body:
Citing a colonial institution that felt like a "torture chamber," Melanie Mark, B.C.'s first First Nations cabinet 
minister, has resigned her Vancouver-Mount Pleasant seat in the Legislature.
Wearing her grandfather's tan beaded jacket and holding an eagle feather, Mark delivered an emotional speech in 
the Legislature Wednesday that charted her rise to a B.C. NDP cabinet minister from her difficult upbringing in the 
East Vancouver "projects", the child of two parents who struggled with addiction and homelessness.
"There was a lot that I'm proud of but this journey has been challenging and has come at a significant personal toll," 
said the 47-year-old.
Mark expressed frustration with colonial institutions like the Legislature that "fundamentally resist the urge to do 
things differently."
"This place felt like a torture chamber," Mark said in her speech. "I will not miss the character assassination," 
although she did not specify who directed those attacks.
"I'm not quitting. If anything I'm standing up for myself," she said.
Mark, a single mother who is Nisga'a, Gitxsan, Cree and Ojibway, also revealed she has attention deficit 
hyperactivity disorder. She said she wants to focus on raising her "baby eagles", her two daughters, Makayla, 12, 
and Maya, 19.
Mark's speech carried similarities to the resignation of 27-year-old Nunavut NDP MP Mumilaaq Qaqqaq who, in a 
powerful farewell speech, said Canada is a country "stained with blood" that was "created off the backs, trauma 
and displacement of Indigenous people."
Jody Wilson-Raybould, Canada's first Indigenous attorney general, left the Trudeau government amid the SNC-
Lavalin scandal and wrote a book, Indian in the Cabinet, which criticized the prime minister over a lack of 
progress on Indigenous reconciliation and criminal justice reform.
Mark has been sitting in the NDP caucus backbench since September when she stepped down as tourism 
minister. At the time, she said she needed to focus on "urgent personal matters."
Page 2 of 3
MLA Melanie Mark resigns, says B.C. Legislature felt like a "torture chamber"
As tourism minister she faced criticism for the now-scrapped $800-million plan to shutter the Royal B.C. Museum, 
tear it down and rebuild it by 2030. Public backlash forced former premier John Horgan to announce the 
government was reversing course and keeping the museum open.
Mark was elected in a 2016 byelection to replace Jenny Kwan, who quit her seat to run federally.
Mark has been open about her difficult childhood which was marred by sexual abuse, an alcoholic mother and a 
father who deserted their family.
Despite that, Mark pursued a career in advocacy, working with Indigenous counselling groups and conducting 
research into sexually exploited Indigenous children. She served as deputy representative at B.C.'s Office of the 
Representative for Children and Youth.
Mark's departure will trigger byelection in the Vancouver-Mount Pleasant riding, one of the safest NDP seats in the 
province.
When the New Democrats were decimated in the 2001 election, Vancouver-Mount Pleasant was one of the two 
seats they retained with the election of Jenny Kwan.
It will be one of two byelections this year, including the one in former Premier John Horgan's riding( 
https://vancouversun.com/news/politics/former-bc-premier-john-horgan-to-step-down-as-mla-in-march ), Langford-
Juan de Fuca.
Eby must set a date for a byelection within six months of the MLA stepping down.

title: MP opts to abandon 'more toxic' House
body:
OTTAWA Independent MP Jody Wilson-Raybould will not seek re-election in the next federal campaign, saying in a 
letter to her constituents on Thursday that Parliament has become "toxic and ineffective" during her time in politics.
"I have not made this decision in order to spend more time with my family or to focus on other challenges and 
pursuits," the former Liberal cabinet minister who represents Vancouver Granville wrote in her letter posted to 
Twitter.
"From my seat over the last six years, I have noticed a change in Parliament, a regression. It has become more 
toxic and ineffective while simultaneously marginalizing individuals from certain backgrounds."
Wilson-Raybould went on to deride an "increasingly disgraceful triumph of harmful partisanship over substantive 
action," and promised to carry on her previous work on Indigenous reconciliation, climate change and other issues 
outside Parliament.
She said she will share more details later.
Prime Minister Justin Trudeau appointed Wilson-Raybould as Canada's first Indigenous justice minister in 2015, 
but she was booted from the Liberal caucus four years later after she accused the prime minister of pressuring her 
to secure a deferred prosecution agreement for SNC-Lavalin.
The former regional chief of the B.C. Assembly of First Nations had earlier resigned as a cabinet minister over the 
affair.
In August 2019, the federal ethics commissioner concluded that Trudeau violated the Conflict of Interest Act by 
improperly pressuring Wilson-Raybould to halt a criminal prosecution of the Montreal engineering giant on 
corruption charges related to contracts in Libya.
Wilson-Raybould was re-elected as an Independent MP in October 2019.
News of Wilson-Raybould's decision not to seek re-election was greeted with sadness from other members of 
Parliament.
Page 2 of 2

NDP MP Randall Garrison wrote in a message to Wilson-Raybould on Twitter: "Some departures diminish the 
House. This is one of those. Your absence will leave a gap on principle, on policy, and for many of us personally."

title: MP urges Hockey Canada officials to resign positions Organization's interim board chair quit on weekend
body:
A member of Parliament says that more members of Hockey Canada's leadership group should resign.
Sébastien Lemire said Andrea Skinner made the right decision to resign as Hockey Canada's interim board chair 
Saturday.
Lemire, a Bloc Québécois MP who sits on the standing committee on Canadian Heritage, tweeted in French on 
Sunday that "for the good of all" Hockey Canada must continue to clean house.
Skinner and her predecessor Michael Brind'Amour were grilled by the parliamentary committee last week over 
Hockey Canada's handling of an alleged group sexual assault involving members of the 2018 men's national junior 
team, and how it has paid out money in lawsuit settlements.
Members of Parliament demanded to know why Hockey Canada president and chief executive officer Scott Smith 
had not yet been fired.
Skinner vigorously defended Hockey Canada's executives.
She insisted hockey shouldn't be made a "scapegoat" or "centrepiec" for toxic culture that exists elsewhere in 
society, and referred to politicians who have been accused of sexual misconduct.
Fallout from Skinner and Brind'Amour's testimony came quickly.
Nike suspended corporate sponsorship of Hockey Canada on Friday to join three other premier partners - Tim 
Hortons, Esso and Telus - in pausing support for hockey's governing body.
More provincial hockey associations began withholding player fees from Hockey Canada.
Hockey N.L. and Hockey New Brunswick both withdrew their $3-per-player fees Friday following Quebec, Ontario 
and Nova Scotia.
"Upon reflection, it is clear to me from recent events that it no longer makes sense for me to continue to volunteer 
my time as Interim Chair or as a Director of the organization," Skinner said in her Saturday statement.
The Toronto lawyer said she has been "gratified" for the opportunity to work with people in the organization, 
"despite recent challenges."
Page 2 of 2

"I sincerely appreciate the support I have received from many Canadians, particularly women, who also seek to 
positively influence the game and sport," Skinner wrote.

title: MPP defends NDP leader after ejection from legislature
body:
THUNDER BAY — NDP and Opposition Leader Marit Stiles was ejected from Ontario’s legislative chamber for 
calling it like it is, New Democrat MPP Lise Vaugeois said Wednesday.
“Absolutely,” Vaugeois, the member for Thunder Bay-Superior North, told Newswatch a few hours after her party 
leader’s ejection.
“The minister of labour is a great talker,” she continued. “You know, he can spin a story with the best of them.
“But there is clearly corruption in how those grants were given out.”
Vaugeois was referring to grants the provincial Skills Development Fund has handed to clients of lobbying firms 
with ties to the governing Progressive Conservatives.
In questioning Labour Minister David Piccini about controversy in the fund Wednesday morning, Stiles described 
Premier Doug Ford’s government as “corrupt” and “anti-democratic.”
She said Piccini won’t “take responsibility for the mess he has created” and that the “corrupt” government engages 
in “endless grifting.”
Speaker Donna Skelly said those remarks were unparliamentary and asked Stiles to withdraw them. When Stiles 
refused, the speaker ordered her removed from the chamber.
Ontario’s auditor general said in a special report earlier this fall that the Skills Development Fund often chose 
applicants ranked low by bureaucrats and did not provide sufficient justification for those decisions.
The Trillium reported in October that clients of a lobbying firm owned by the premier’s campaign manager have 
received more than $100 million from the fund.
Six clients of another Progressive Conservative Party-connected firm received almost $38 million from the training 
fund, according to the Trillium.
The Trillium further reported in early November that the fund gave millions of dollars to partners in a Toronto “adult 
entertainment” venue “where strippers give lap dances and scantily clad aerialists hang in the air by their teeth.”

Page 2 of 2
MPP defends NDP leader after ejection from legislature
The nightclub’s main partner has a long history with Ford and the PC Party, according to the Trillium.
Vaugeois told Newswatch her party is focused on only some recipients and “it’s not the program itself that we are 
criticizing — it is how the decisions are being made.”
The minister has “inserted himself” and corrupted the selection process, she said from Toronto.
Newswatch reached out to regional PC MPPs Greg Rickford (Kenora-Rainy River) and Kevin Holland (Thunder 
Bay-Atikokan) for comment.

body:
Charles Milliard had an extremely effective launch to his leadership over the weekend. He has breathed some life 
into the moribund Quebec Liberals, who managed to show that they still had some management skills and political 
reflexes.
For example, Milliard came out four-square in favour of a new bridge or tunnel in Quebec City. It helps that he grew 
up in Lévis, right across the river from the provincial capital. It also helps that he has very good instincts.
The greater Quebec City area has over a dozen seats. It propelled François Legault to his first victory as premier 
and helped keep him there for a second term. There was such a backlash against Legault's betrayal of his promise 
on this issue that the Parti Québécois took animplausible byelection win( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/quebec/jean-talon-byelection-results ) in a staunchly federalist riding there.
Now the hard part begins, with polling numbers for the Liberals( https://leger360.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/01/Rapport-Intentions-de-vote-29-janvier-2026.pdf ) remaining depressingly weak outside of 
greater Montreal.
Milliard says he plans to run in Orford riding, which is plausibly rural. He took pains to distance himself from the 
Pablo Rodriguez debacle by placing integrity at the top of his list of priorities. But will any of this allow him to 
connect with the Quebec heartland and forget the era of the Charbonneau Commission( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/local-news/the-5-ws-of-the-charbonneau-commission ) into collusion and 
corruption in the Quebec construction industry?
Across the floor of the National Assembly, the Coalition Avenir Québec has gone from bad to worse.
This week's brutal assessment of the Gallant Commission( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial_politics/saaqclic-public-inquiry-report-legault-caq ) into the SAAQclic 
scandal says it all. It's doubtful Legault convinced anyone with his histrionics about suing those who he said lied to 
his government.
The No. 1 rule in our form of parliamentary democracy is ministerial responsibility, and Legault is the top minister. 
He can't blame anyone but himself. For a guy who boasted about forming a "government of accountants," it's 
terribly humiliating.
Page 2 of 3
Mulcair: Quebecers might be dealt two elections, one wild card
By all indications Legault is about to be replaced by the exceptionally competent Christine Fréchette, who polls 
show is making short work of the flailing Bernard Drainville, her only adversary.
With her remarkable administrative and communications skills, will Fréchette be able to make voters forget eight 
years of CAQ mismanagement? That will depend on the "ballot question": What will people be thinking when they 
cast their vote? What's the priority issue?
I believe it will be: "Who stands the best chance of beating the PQ"?
Polls show around two-thirds of Quebecers don't want a referendum, much less sovereignty. Milliard is a hard "No." 
Fréchette is much more: "Not now." Her position reminds one of Robert Bourassa's famous speech that Quebec is 
and will always remain master of its own destiny.
Milliard's approach will solidify the current Liberal seats west of Atwater Ave. Fréchette's will play well up and down 
the St. Lawrence. The wild card could be the Quebec Conservatives with their able leader, Éric Duhaime.
The Conservatives sit on a large chunk of votes, around 15 per cent. That will get them zero seats but incredible 
influence (and a senior ministerial portfolio) if Duhaime makes a deal with Milliard or Fréchette. Will any of them put 
the future of the federation above their partisanship?
Lest we think that the only election this year will be provincial, it would be wise to keep an eye on Prime Minister 
Mark Carney.
The Supreme Court just cancelled last year's Liberal election win( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/canada_news/canadian_politics/supreme-court-of-canada-annuls-single-vote-
win-in-terrebonne-riding-vacating-seat ) in Terrebonne riding. The Liberals have little chance of holding on to it. 
There's a lot of bad feeling there, and the federal Liberals have failed to give more profile to their outgoing MP, 
Tatiana Auguste.
Carney remains popular in Quebec and will do well if there's an early election. However, if he were to lose that 
byelection, it would send a negative message about Liberal fortunes here. That would weigh heavily in the decision 
to go to the polls early against a personally unpopular Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre.
Tom Mulcair, a former leader of the federal NDP, served as minister of the environment in the Quebec Liberal 
government of Jean Charest.

title: Murray joins cabinet as fisheries minister; Fellow B.C. MPs Sajjan, Wilkinson land new roles, Qualtrough
body:
There were few surprises for B.C. members of Parliament in Tuesday's cabinet shakeup, as they ended up at the 
helm of four government ministries, including those related to the critical issue of climate change.
Prime Minister Justin Trudeau ousted Vancouver-South MP Harjit Sajjan from his post as defence minister after 
allegations of sexual misconduct in the military led to repeated calls for his removal. Sajjan was given the portfolio 
of minister of international development.
The move was a demotion, according to Richard Johnston, a professor emeritus in the department of political 
science at UBC. "He had clearly become a liability. He had been there a long time and things were getting worse."
Johnston said the real question remains why Sajjan remained in cabinet at all, and suggested geographical balance 
and the need to keep at least four ministries in B.C. could have played a role.
Sajjan will be replaced by former procurement minister Anita Anand, the MP for Oakville, Ont., who has been 
widely credited for the success of Canada's vaccine rollout. Other shifts in cabinet among B.C. MPs signal 
Trudeau's commitment to climate and the environment, said Johnston.
North Vancouver MP Jonathan Wilkinson was moved out of the environment portfolio and appointed to the ministry 
of natural resources. Former Greenpeace member Steven Guilbeault of Quebec replaces him as minister of the 
environment.
Guilbeault represents the Montreal riding of Laurier-Sainte-Marie. The appointment of Guilbeault to the 
environmental portfolio, and Wilkinson, who has a background in clean energy, to the natural resources portfolio 
signals a tangible commitment to the climate agenda, and is "absolutely related" to coming summits at the G20 in 
Rome and the United Nations climate change conference (COP26) in Glasgow, said Johnston.
The appointment of longtime Vancouver-Quadra MP Joyce Murray as minister of fisheries, oceans and the 
Canadian Coast Guard was a surprise, said Johnston, but could herald a "transferring focus from the east coast to 
the west coast fisheries."
Murray replaces Bernadette Jordan, who lost her re-election bid in her Nova Scotia riding.

maintains post
Delta MP Carla Qualtrough remains as minister of employment, workforce development and disability inclusion. 
She is one of only 10 ministers to retain her position. dryan@postmedia.com !@COPYRIGHT=© 2021 Postmedia

title: Nakedly partisan, despite the fig leaf; Trudeau's reforms did little to alter our cushy Senate
body:
The Senate expenses affair in the run-up to the 2015 election was a very Canadian scandal - there was no sex 
and no one was found guilty of doing anything wrong.
Then-senator Mike Duffy was charged with 31 offences by the RCMP over expense claims he made but was 
exonerated by the Ontario Superior Court.
Charges against two other senators over allegedly questionable expenses were subsequently dropped.
However,the Senate's reputation as an ermine-lined soft landing for party hacks was established and the Red 
Chamber's credibility was further impaired by a broader investigation by then-auditor general Michael Ferguson, 
who found 30 senators had claimed expenses that were not in accordance with Senate rules.
Stephen Harper's government had already tried to reform the Senate by introducing term limits for senators but 
had been foiled by a Supreme Court ruling that said Ottawa could not act without provincial consent.
As a result, Harper all but washed his hands of the Senate, leaving 22 vacancies in the upper house by the time he 
left office in 2015.
Justin Trudeau's response to the discredited Senate's lack of accountability and transparency had more to 
commend it - at least on paper.
Without warning on the morning of Jan. 29, 2014, he gathered all 32 Liberal senators - many of whom were friends 
and contemporaries of his father - and told them they were out, expelled from the caucus.
At the same time, he said that if elected prime minister, he would inaugurate a non-partisan appointment process.
In the run-up to the 2015 election, he unveiled a 32-point plan to "restore democracy in Canada" that included 
introducing electoral reform (2015 would be the last election under the first-past-the-post system), overhauling the 
access to information regime and creating a nonpartisan Senate.
In government, he instituted a Senate advisory board to nominate new senators that has since made 86 
"independent" appointments to the 105-seat chamber.
Page 2 of 3
Nakedly partisan, despite the fig leaf; Trudeau's reforms did little to alter our cushy Senate
The dynamics of the Red Chamber were altered irrevocably from the adversarial structure of government and 
opposition typical of Westminster institutions. There remains a small core of Conservatives and three other loose 
parliamentary groups that may or may not vote together.
Critics have long made the claim that the new senators are Liberal in all but name. As former Harper deputy chief 
of staff Howard Anglin and Cardus cofounder Ray Pennings wrote recently: "Without casting aspersions on the 
integrity of any senator, Trudeau's appointments are not representative of a cross-section of 'independent'political 
perspectives. They are a relatively cohesive ideological conformity that is mostly aligned with the current Liberal 
party."
Yet, at least initially, you didn't need to be a card-carrying party member to be considered, as now seems to be the 
case for the majority of new senators.
There have been occasions over the past 81/2 years when the independent Senate has bitten back. In 2017, the 
Red Chamber refused to pass the government's budget as written, with some senators unhappy that the Trudeau 
Liberals had stuffed the plan with legislation for its new infrastructure bank and included an escalator tax on beer 
that would have seen prices rise in perpetuity.
The Liberal-dominated House vetoed Senate amendments and the senators were forced to back down, but not 
before reiterating their powers under the Constitution to amend legislation.
The problem is that the Senate's attempts to assert the independence to which Trudeau paid lip service has 
encouraged the prime minister to make a mockery of his promise to "restore democracy."
This summer has seen the appointment of five new senators - Victor Boudreau in New Brunswick, who is a 
former interim leader of the province's Liberal party; Tracy Muggli in Saskatchewan, who is a former federal Liberal 
candidate; Charles Adler in Manitoba, a former conservative broadcaster who professes his dislike of Pierre 
Poilievre; and last weekend in Alberta, Daryl Fridhandler, a corporate lawyer and businessman who was once a 
regional fundraiser for the federal Liberals, and Kristopher Wells, a professor who has been a vocal critic of 
Premier Danielle Smith's gender policies.
The last two are perhaps the most egregious appointments, given that Alberta held Senate elections in 2021 and 
chose three Conservatives, with one candidate, Pam Davidson, garnering 382,000 votes.
The government's fig leaf response is that all new senators were recommended by an advisory board chaired by 
former University of Ottawa chancellor Huguette Labelle. But the appointments are ultimately made by the prime 
minister. We have no idea how many recommendations he passed over before agreeing to candidates who fit his 
partisan demands.
Milton Friedman's assertion that it is a great mistake to judge policies by their intentions, rather than their results, is 
a criticism that could be applied to this government in almost every circumstance, but it is particularly apt in this 
case.
If Trudeau had in good faith named a bipartisan advisory board and chosen senators who were representative of a 
cross-section of Canadian society, he could have fudged an acceptable compromise.
But he seems determined to stack the Red Chamber with ideological fellow travellers, with the intent of frustrating 
an incoming Conservative government.
Anglin and Pennings were concerned that this could foreshadow a Constitutional crisis, where senators breach the 
convention that they can oppose the government "vocally, but not politically."
That seems to me to be an unlikely development. Senators know their legitimacy depends on them backing down.
Canada's Constitution is judged the world's most difficult democratic constitution to change by formal amendment - 
major reforms are virtually impossible and killing the Senate requires unanimous consent of all the provinces.
Page 3 of 3
Nakedly partisan, despite the fig leaf; Trudeau's reforms did little to alter our cushy Senate
But if a "Liberal" Senate tried to impede a Conservative-dominated House, Poilievre could go to the people and call 
a Senate-abolition referendum, as the late senator Hugh Segal proposed twice when he served in the Red 
Chamber.
If Canadians were suitably outraged, a 50-per-centplus-one vote for abolition in every province, if unlikely, may not 
be an impossible outcome.
There remain four vacancies in the Senate. If there are more overtly partisan appointments, we really will be back to 
the days when, at roll-call, senators don't know whether to shout "present" or "not guilty."

title: national briefs
body:
Calgary
 E. Coli outbreak at daycares over
 Alberta Health Services says an E. coli outbreak that infected hundreds of children at numerous Calgary daycares 
is over, eight weeks after it started. The health authority said in an update on its website Tuesday that the final three 
affected sites came off outbreak status last week and there are no children left in hospital. The outbreak, which was 
declared on Sept. 4, was linked to a central kitchen used by the daycares.
 Ottawa
 Five Atlantic senators named
 Former Liberal MP Rodger Cuzner has been named a senator for Nova Scotia. Three new senators for New 
Brunswick include Joan Kingston, a nurse and former Liberal member of that province's legislative assembly; John 
McNair, a lawyer and public servant; and Krista Ross, a business and non-profit leader. Réjean Aucoin, a lawyer 
and francophone leader, is joining Cuzner as a new senator for Nova Scotia.
 Fortin retires from military
 Dany Fortin, who recently settled a lawsuit over how the Canadian military and federal government handled an 
allegation of sexual misconduct, has retired from the Armed Forces. Fortin, who had reached the rank of major-
general, was removed as head of Canada's COVID-19 vaccine rollout campaign in May 2021. 
 Star wire services

title: NDP minister was at centre of bingo scandal
body:
NANAIMO - One of the central figures in the Bingogate political scandal of the early 1990s died Wednesday.
Dave Stupich, the former B.C. NDP cabinet minister and one-time MP for Nanaimo-Cowichan, was 84. The cause 
of his death was not released.
Once revered as one of the most powerful politicians in Canada, Stupich was shamed publicly after masterminding 
the Nanaimo Commonwealth Holding Society bingo scam.
The scandal led to the resignation of premier Mike Harcourt, though he was not implicated.
Stupich was elected to the B.C. legislature as MLA for Nanaimo-Cowichan in 1963 and spent the better part of the 
next 30 years serving as an MLA or MP for the Nanaimo region.
Provincially, he held two cabinet posts, serving as minister of agriculture and minister of finance. He did not seek 
re-election in the 1993 federal election.
Dale Lovick, who was the NDP MLA for Nanaimo from 1986 through 2001 and shared a constituency office with 
Stupich, heard of his death with sadness.
"When I think in terms of Dave and his career, I think in terms of great tragedy," he said. "Here was a guy who, until 
a series of events late in his political career, was universally admired and respected. How sad his career ended as it 
did. He did more good than bad, that's for sure."
Former Ladysmith-Cowichan NDP MLA Jan Pullinger said that, apart from his troubles with Bingogate, Stupich

title: Nelson: Federal Tories left Danielle Smith no choice but to deal with Carney
body:
It's the hope that kills you. That's why the constant failure of the federal Conservative Party is the true driver of 
separation sentiment here in Alberta.
Let's face it - we don't trust the Liberals in this part of the world. We haven't since they tried to dupe us more than a 
century ago by pretending to bring telephone service to rural Alberta. In reality, they were just dumping thousands 
of wooden poles in prominent small-town locations right before a provincial election.
When this hoax was discovered, it was the upstart United Farmers of Alberta party that roared to victory, replacing 
the ruling Liberals. Following that scandal, the Grits have been shut out in provincial and national elections in 
Alberta ever since. (Premier Danielle Smith better hope the memorandum of understanding on future energy 
development( https://calgaryherald.com/business/energy/despite-rare-agreement-alberta-ottawa-pipeline-familiar-
battle-lines ) she recently signed with Prime Minister Mark Carney isn't a Liberal rerun of that great telephone 
scandal of 1921.)
If the desire to go it alone were due simply to the mistrust the Liberals engender in Albertans, this province would 
have separated long ago. But what really spurs feelings of alienation and humiliation is waiting patiently for the 
Liberals' political demise, repeatedly turning out in droves to back the opposition Tories, only to find we've staked 
our futures yet again on a bunch of losers.
We did our bit, returning all those Conservative MPs, but the national party still messed up.
Do that long enough, and frustration turns to desperation, and desperation can make people do risky things, such 
as imagining a landlocked province in the middle of a huge continent can push the various surrounding powers to 
do its bidding by helping us sell our plentiful resources without taking a massive haircut.
Twelve months ago, separation chatter was somewhat muted. Albertans believed the Justin Trudeau regime in 
Ottawa was finally and mercifully coming to its end.
The federal Conservatives looked certain to finally form a majority government in 2025 and bring relief from the 
barrage of laws, regulations and Central Canada sentiment that has handcuffed Alberta from developing its own 
natural resources - despite the Constitution's pledge that they belong to us.
Page 2 of 3
Nelson: Federal Tories left Danielle Smith no choice but to deal with Carney
But we forgot the Liberal party has always been willing to devour its own to keep power. So, Trudeau was dumped, 
and former central banker Carney parachuted in as prime minister. The Conservatives soon began falling apart, 
with the Ontario provincial Tories acting more like opponents than supporters during the election campaign.
When, for the fourth time in a row, they failed - with leader Pierre Poilievre losing his own seat - Albertans were 
crushed. They'd voted Tory in droves, but it was in vain, and another decade of Grit power loomed. Is it any wonder 
that separation sentiment soared?
Related
Despite quibbles with Conservative pipeline motion, Danielle Smith endorses Poilievre ahead of leadership review( 
https://calgaryherald.com/news/canada/despite-quibbles-with-conservative-pipeline-motion-danielle-smith-
endorses-poilievre-ahead-of-leadership-review/wcm/13404f4b-6501-4cb7-91cf-78058b7806a7 )
Tasha Kheiriddin: The Conservatives who could replace Pierre Poilievre( https://calgaryherald.com/opinion/the-
conservatives-who-could-replace-pierre-poilievre/wcm/ffd2af66-2c90-45fe-ba99-cb3c407f8f34 )
For Smith and the UCP, the choice became clear - waiting for a federal Conservative government was off the table, 
so all that remained was wholeheartedly backing separation from Canada or seriously trying to do a deal with this 
new prime minister. It chose the latter.
Was it wrong to give up on a Conservative government? Well, nothing that has happened since suggests so.
In fact, Poilievre himself is struggling to hold things together, as the party approaches its annual convention in 
Calgary next month.
Ontario MP Michael Ma( https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/conservative-mp-michael-ma-crosses-floor-to-
liberals/wcm/48708d32-1ae0-40fb-a595-3a2be8b4a205 ) announced last week he's jumping ship and leaving the 
Conservative fold for the Liberals. This follows an earlier defection by Nova Scotia MP Chris d'Entremont( 
https://calgaryherald.com/news/politics/mp-chris-dentremont-out-of-federal-conservative-caucus/wcm/757feff5-
e33f-4523-ac0f-195ff5a8ccd5 ).
There are rumblings that more Tories could follow. With Carney's government now only one MP short of a majority, 
it's no wonder Poilievre's leadership is in jeopardy, as his party faces another decade in opposition.
It is a shame. But doing the same thing in awaiting a national Tory government and expecting a different outcome 
would indeed be political insanity.
So, it's a deal with the Grits or eventual separation for Alberta.
Chris Nelson is a regular columnist. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2025 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.
