title: Tory zealots and an ex-separatist; Appointees will get $130,400 a year to sit in upper house
body:
He vowed to reform the Senate, denouncing it as a "dumping ground for cronies" that was far too often used as a 
patronage plum to reward party organizers and fundraisers.
But three of the four people Prime Minister Stephen Harper named to the Senate yesterday from Quebec are Tory 
supporters who have worked as either campaign organizers or fundraisers for the party in Quebec.
One has served as a Conservative MP, while two ran unsuccessfully for the Canadian Alliance.
And despite statements by officials in the prime minister's office that Harper had no intention of naming 
"separatists" to the Senate, one of his appointees is a former Parti Québécois MNA who publicly fought in the 1995 
referendum to take Quebec out of Canada. Another has a track record as a strong Quebec nationalist who was as 
likely to agree with the Bloc Québécois as she was to agree with her own party in her final time in office.
Yesterday, however, Harper's office defended its decision to appoint someone who once fought to separate 
Quebec from Canada, saying "people are allowed to change their beliefs."
The comments come as the Conservative government announced yesterday that four Quebecers were among the 
18 Canadians who will be appointed to $130,400-a-year jobs in the Senate early in the new year.
Among those named yesterday by Harper is Michel Rivard, 67, a businessman who was elected as a PQ MNA in 
1994 after a stint in municipal politics. Defeated in 1998, Rivard ran for the Canadian Alliance in 2000.
Since April 2001, he has worked as an organizer for the Conservative Party in Quebec and has been named as 
one of those involved in the "in and out" campaign financing scheme that is under investigation by Elections 
Canada.
Also named to the Senate yesterday was Suzanne Fortin Duplessis, co-chairperson of the Conservative Party's 
campaign in Quebec in the last election.
A teacher by profession, Duplessis, 68, served as Conservative MP for the Quebec City area riding of Louis Hébert 
from 1984 to 1993.
Page 2 of 4

As an MP, she developed a reputation as a strong Quebec nationalist, and in 1990 she angered Conservative

title: Tourists urged not to visit as 21,000 people flee wildfires More than 300 firefighters battling blazes throughout
body:
Manitoba is urging tourists to reconsider visiting as it works to find shelter for a flood of wildfire evacuees now 
reaching 21,000.
"This is one of the largest evacuations in our province's history," Lisa Naylor, the Manitoba cabinet minister in 
charge of emergency management, said Monday.
"The government anticipates there may be a need for more hotel rooms as the wildfire season continues. For that 
reason, we are urging Manitobans and Canadians to reconsider non-essential travel and event plans within 
Manitoba."
She added: "There are thousands of evacuees currently displaced and the provincial government along with its 
partners have been working quickly to find accommodation that fits their comfort, medical and family needs."
Naylor acknowledged it was a difficult announcement to make.
"We absolutely know how important tourism is to Manitoba and we are very mindful of the many workers whose 
livelihoods depend on a strong tourism sector."
The Manitoba Hotel Association estimates there are about 15,000 hotel rooms in the province.
The province has set up four congregate shelters for wildfire evacuees, with reception centres in Winnipeg, 
Brandon and Thompson.
Manitoba has more than 300 firefighters battling blazes from the remote northwest down through the southeast. 
Crews have come from other provinces and the United States, with more U.S. crews expected Monday.
There are 28 active wildfires, 10 of which are out of control.
That firefighting work, along with a little bit of weekend rain, has kept the fires from overwhelming evacuated 
communities.
The largest fire, menacing the city of Flin Flon and surrounding communities, sits at more than 3,000 square 
kilometres. All 5,000 residents of Flin Flon and thousands more in the area are out.
Page 2 of 3
Tourists urged not to visit as 21,000 people flee wildfires More than 300 firefighters battling blazes throughout 
the province
In north-central Manitoba, fires have forced 6,700 out of Pimicikamak Cree Nation.
In total, there are 27 communities under evacuation orders.
The province is under a state of emergency, making it easier for various levels of government to co-ordinate 
coverage.
Kristin Hayward, with the Manitoba Wildfire Service, said 74 charges and 28 warnings have been issued for those 
breaking the fire rules.
She referred to two arson charges laid by RCMP last month, but said arson is not a widespread problem.
"Many of our fires remain under investigation, (but) I wouldn't say people are out deliberately setting fires on a 
large scale," said Hayward. "The majority of what we see are fires that start because of carelessness."
Thousands also remained out of their homes in Saskatchewan and Alberta, including between 10,000 and 15,000 
in Saskatchewan alone.
Some residents of Pelican Narrows, Sask., in the province's remote north, can return home provided they are 
healthy and they have access to their own vehicles.
The fires have forced about 7,000 out the area around La Ronge.
Premier Scott Moe has resisted Opposition calls to bring in the military. Moe has said they talk with the federal 
government daily, but notes the military provides air evacuation and so far the province has been able to get people 
out by road.
The Canadian Press

title: Trial of former Calgary city councillor Joe Magliocca on fraud and breach of trust allegations underway
body:
Former Calgary city councillor Joe Magliocca is opposed to the Crown calling more than two dozen witnesses 
scattered across the country and beyond via video link on criminal charges.
Defence counsel Aryan Sadat said Monday he only learned this past weekend that Crown prosecutor Aaron Rankin 
intends to call much of his case through remote witness testimony.
But Rankin said the list of witnesses, mostly people allegedly falsely named as recipients of booze or food paid for 
by Magliocca, should not be inconvenienced by having to come to Calgary to give brief evidence.
Rankin told Justice Gord Wong that many of the proposed 27 witnesses are currently serving politicians who don't 
want their schedules interrupted by a trip to Cowtown.
"Mr. Sadat advised me his client would not consent to remote testimony for any witness," Rankin told the Calgary 
Court of Justice judge.
Among the proposed witnesses are current Halifax Mayor Mike Savage, former Quebec City council member and 
current Quebec provincial cabinet minister Jonatan Julien and former Peterborough, Ont. council member 
Stephen Wright, who now resides in Australia.
The remainder of the 27 proposed witnesses reside across Canada.
Magliocca, 59, faces charges of breach of trust by a public officer and fraud over allegations he was reimbursed 
for expenses at out-of-town functions that weren't actually incurred.
Rankin said the witnesses aren't expected to give lengthy testimony when they do give evidence during the trial, 
which is set to run over 11 days until Sept. 26.
"These people attended municipal government conferences not located in Calgary," he said.
Rankin said the witnesses were interviewed by police and asked regarding a specific date and time, "Were you the 
guest of Mr. Magliocca?"
"They will give evidence on that point. The expectation is the answer will be 'no.'"

https://calgaryherald.com/news/crime/calgary-judge-will-hear-fraud-and-breach-of-trust-trial-of-former-city-council-
member-joe-magliocca )
RCMP charge Coun. Joe Magliocca with fraud, breach of trust( https://calgaryherald.com/news/local-news/rcmp-
charge-coun-joe-magliocca-with-fraud-breach-of-trust )
But Sadat argued there was no evidence any of the witnesses were reluctant to travel to Calgary and suggested the 
prosecutor should have filed affidavits supporting that contention.
Instead, Rankin called lead investigator, RCMP Const. David Mitchell, who went over several short transcripts of 
interviews with the proposed witnesses showing their statements were brief.
Mitchell said several of the proposed witnesses, such as current Ontario Liberal Party leader Bonnie Crombie, 
brought up the issue of interrupting their busy schedules.
"Many have expressed frustration with the idea ... of taking time to come to testify," he said.
Wong will hear further submissions from Sadat on whether to allow the remote testimony on day two of the trial this 
Friday.
Rankin said he still has other witnesses who can give evidence before Wong hands down a ruling on his 
application.
Magliocca was a two-time member of Calgary city council from October 2013 to October 2021, when he lost his bid 
for a third term just days after charges were laid.

title: Trudeau cabinet shuffle: Harjit Sajjan out as defence minister, replaced by Anita Anand
body:
OTTAWA - Prime Minister Justin Trudeau is starting his third term in office with a major overhaul of his cabinet, 
removing several long-term ministers and shuffling almost all of his government's senior positions.
In one of the biggest changes, long-time Defence Minister Harjit Sajjan is being replaced by Procurement Minister 
Anita Anand.
Anand handled the government's vaccine rollout and is seen as one of the standouts in Trudeau's last cabinet. 
Sajjan, a former soldier and police officer, leaves Defence as the military deals with a sexual misconduct crisis 
with several top generals facing accusations and concerns the department has done little to make women feel safe 
in the forces.
The new cabinet maintains gender balance and has 39 members including Trudeau.
Anita Anand is sworn in as the minister of National Defence during the presentation of Prime Minister Justin 
Trudeau's new cabinet at Rideau Hall in Ottawa, October 26, 2021.
Patty Hajdu, who has been health minister throughout the pandemic, is being moved to become the minister of 
Indigenous services as former treasury board president Jean-Yves Duclos gets moved to the Health portfolio.
The Health portfolio is being split with Carolyn Bennett, who takes on a newly created Ministry of Mental Health and 
Addictions. Marc Miller, the previous Indigenous services minister, replaces Bennett as minister of Crown 
Indigenous Relations.
Jonathan Wilkinson, the environment minister, will move to Natural Resources, while Steven Guilbeault, a former 
climate activist, takes on the job of environment minister. Karina Gould becomes the new minister of families, 
children and social development.
Foreign Affairs Minister Marc Garneau is being shuffled out of cabinet with Melanie Joly taking on his job. Usually a 
more stable post, the Foreign Ministry has gone through five politicians in the Trudeau government's six years in 
office.
Bardish Chagger and Jim Carr are also being shuffled out of cabinet entirely.
Conservative Leader Erin O'Toole said the new cabinet is ill-prepared to address the real economic challenges 
Canada faces.
Page 2 of 3
Trudeau cabinet shuffle: Harjit Sajjan out as defence minister, replaced by Anita Anand
"It is clear from today's appointments that the Trudeau government is not serious about addressing Canada's 
economic challenges," said O'Toole in a statement. "Today's changes to cabinet represent just another example of 
the prime minister continuing to reward ministers who have consistently demonstrated incompetence and a lack 
of accountability."
Prime Minister Justin Trudeau arrives with his wife Sophie Gregoire to attend the swearing-in ceremony of his new 
cabinet at Rideau Hall in Ottawa, October 26, 2021.
Pablo Rodriguez returns to his former job as minister of Canadian heritage, a post he held in the first Trudeau 
term. Ajax MP Mark Holland takes over for Rodriguez as government house leader, a post that involves 
negotiations with opposition parties and is particularly important during a minority government.
Mona Fortier becomes the president of the Treasury Board. She had been the minister of middle class prosperity 
in the previous government, but that position is being eliminated. The minister of digital government position was 
also eliminated with its former occupant, Joyce Murray, moving to minister of fisheries.
Ahmed Hussen becomes minister of housing, and diversity and inclusion. Dominic LeBlanc remains minister of 
intergovernmental affairs and takes on the infrastructure portfolio.
Marco Mendicino becomes the minister of public safety and Bill Blair, who did hold that role, will become the new 
minister of emergency preparedness and president of the Queen's Privy Council. Seamus O'Regan becomes the 
minister of labour and Filomena Tassi who was on the labour file, becomes minister of public services and 
procurement, taking over for Anand. Mary Ng stays at international trade, but adds small business to her portfolio.
Ginette Petipas Taylor, who was briefly minister of health during Trudeau's first term in office, is returning to 
cabinet to become the minister of official languages. Dan Vandal remains in charge of northern affairs.
The Liberals have also taken all of the federal government's economic development agencies and attached them to 
ministers from those regions. First-time cabinet minister Helena Jaczek from Toronto's York Region is the 
minister responsible for the federal economic development agency of southern Ontario and Pascale St.-Onge, a 
freshly elected Quebec MP, will be the minister of sport and responsible for Quebec's economic development 
agency.
There are a few other new faces: Edmonton MP Randy Boissonnault becomes minister of tourism and an 
associate minister of finance; Sean Fraser from Nova Scotia becomes minister of immigration; Gudie Hutchings 
becomes minister of rural economic development; Marci Ien, the former Canada AM host and Toronto Centre MP, 
will serve as minister for women, gender equality and youth; and Kamal Kherea becomes the new minister of 
seniors.
Some cabinet ministers are staying put: Chrystia Freeland remains the minister of finance and deputy prime 
minister; David Lametti stays as justice minister and attorney general; Diana Lebouthillier as minister of national 
revenue; Omar Alghabara as transport minister; Marie-Claude Bibeau as agriculture minister; Carla Qualtrough as 
employment, workforce development minister; and Lawrenece MacAulay as veterans affairs minister.
FranÃ§ois-Philippe Champagne is minister of innovation, science and commerce, a new name for his post at 
industry.
Trudeau has previously said Parliament will not resume until Nov. 22, nearly two months after the election.

title: Trudeau has been swift to dole out discipline Is PM treating himself as he treated other Liberals caught up in
body:
OTTAWA-Liberal Leader Justin Trudeau has asked Canadian voters for forgiveness after being exposed for 
wearing blackface makeup on at least three separate occasions.
But have other Liberals under his leadership received the same benefit of the doubt?
Since becoming Liberal leader in 2014, Trudeau has had a track record of being decisive when members of his 
team have been caught on the wrong side of a scandal. But facing one of the largest controversies of his own 
making Wednesday, Trudeau appealed to Canadians' for forgiveness.
"I think there are people who have made mistakes in this life, and you make decisions based on what they actually 
do, what they did, and on a case-by-case basis," Trudeau said in a press conference Wednesday night.
Here's a look at some of his case-by-case decisions as Liberal leader.
Liberal senators
Trudeau's decisive streak was first widely apparent when he decided to expel Liberal senators - important 
organizers, fundraisers and the institutional memory of his party - from the Liberal caucus at the height of the 
Senate expense scandal.
"There are no more Liberal senators," Trudeau told reporters outside the House of Commons in January 2014.
The move stunned Liberal senators, who were told just before Trudeau made the decision public. It came as the 
auditor general was preparing to audit individual senators after Mike Duffy, Patrick Brazeau and Pamela Wallin 
were accused of improper expenses.
The Star's Ottawa bureau chief Susan Delacourt reported at the time Trudeau and his advisers were explicitly 
looking for a "dramatic and decisive" way to distance the Liberals from the partisan Senate, as it was mired in 
controversy.
Scott Andrews and Massimo Pacetti
Page 2 of 3
Trudeau has been swift to dole out discipline Is PM treating himself as he treated other Liberals caught up in 
scandal?
Two Liberal MPs were almost immediately suspended from Liberal caucus after two female NDP MPs accused 
them of sexual misconduct in November 2014.
Newfoundland MP Scott Andrews and Quebec MP Massimo Pacetti both denied the claims, but Trudeau moved 
swiftly to remove them from the Liberal caucus. So swiftly that it made one of their accusers uncomfortable.
"I think it was too fast for him to act like that," one told a Star reporter at the time.
After an independent investigation into the claims, neither were invited to rejoin the party. Pacetti did not run again, 
while Andrews ran as an independent in the 2015 election and lost.
Hunter Tootoo
The Liberals were fresh off their historic 2015 victory when Trudeau announced that Hunter Tootoo, his fisheries 
minister, had resigned from cabinet and Liberal caucus to seek treatment for alcohol addiction.
At the time of his resignation, May 2016, unnamed sources suggested Tootoo's resignation had something to do 
with an incident at the Liberals' convention that year in Winnipeg. But CTV News subsequently reported that Tootoo 
was dating a staff member before starting a relationship with her mother.
Tootoo told reporters that he told Trudeau everything and that the prime minister was supportive. But the Nunavut 
MP, who is not running again, never rejoined the Liberal benches.
Darshan Kang
Trudeau did not move as quickly in the case of Darshan Kang, a Calgary MP accused by two women of 
inappropriate conduct.
The Hill Times reported in early August 2017 that Kang was under investigation for inappropriate advances 
toward a female staffer. A second woman, who worked for Kang when he was an Alberta MLA, also came forward 
with accusations.
The Star reported at the time that the Liberal party's deputy whip travelled to Calgary months earlier to interview 
one of the women. But Kang, who maintained his innocence, resigned from caucus at the end of August 2017.
Kent Hehr
A day after an Alberta civil servant accused then-cabinet minister Kent Hehr of inappropriate sexual comments, 
Trudeau announced the minister's resignation from cabinet.
"As a government we take any allegations of misconduct extremely seriously, and we believe that it is important to 
support women who come forward with allegations and that is exactly what our government will do," Trudeau said 
in January 2018.
While Hehr resigned from cabinet, he was not removed from Liberal caucus. Hehr is running again for the Liberals 
in Calgary Centre in this October's election.
Raj Grewal
The Brampton MP told the Prime Minister's Office in late November 2018 that he had a gambling addiction, 
borrowing millions from friends and family to finance his problem. Three days later, Grewal announced he was 
resigning his seat for personal reasons. The following day, Trudeau's office revealed Grewal's addiction problems.
Grewal was also the subject of a conflict of interest investigation by the federal ethics commissioner.
Page 3 of 3
Trudeau has been swift to dole out discipline Is PM treating himself as he treated other Liberals caught up in 
scandal?
Trudeau praised Grewal's decision to step down as "the right call," but when Grewal suggested he had changed his 
mind the following week, Trudeau's office quietly reiterated the prime minister's statement. On Wednesday, CBC 
News reported Grewal will not seek re-election in Brampton East.

title: Trudeau resists calls to fire Bennett over 'hurtful' text, says he knows her 'heart'
body:
OTTAWA - Prime Minister Justin Trudeau is resisting calls to fire Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Carolyn 
Bennett over a text message he acknowledges was "wrong" and "hurtful" and harmed his government's progress on 
reconciliation.
Bennett apologized Thursday for texting "Pension?" to Jody Wilson-Raybould in response to the Independent MP's 
tweet urging Trudeau to quit "jockeying" for an election in light of the discovery of what are believed to be 715 
unmarked graves of Indigenous children in Saskatchewan.
Members of Parliament must serve for six years before becoming eligible for a pension, so Bennett appeared to be 
suggesting that Wilson-Raybould, who is Indigenous, was only concerned about losing her pension if she were 
voted out before she hits the six-year mark in October.
"Of course, I'm deeply disappointed. She did the right thing by apologizing because it was the wrong thing to do," 
Trudeau told a news conference Friday.
"As a government, as ministers, as Canadians, we need to be focused on the work that needs to happen for 
Indigenous people across this country who have been going through extremely difficult times, not just in these past 
weeks but over years and generations."
He added: "Mistakes like this are hurtful and nudge us in the wrong direction instead of steadily moving in the right 
direction."
Trudeau's government has faced intense scrutiny over its handling of Indigenous issues since the discovery of an 
unmarked burial site at a former residential school in British Columbia last month. Thursday's news of more 
graves at a Saskatchewan institution has magnified the public concern.
Wilson-Raybould tweeted a screenshot of Bennett's text message on Thursday. The Vancouver Granville MP said it 
was racist, misogynistic and reflected the stereotype that Indigenous people are "lazy & only want $."
Bennett issued a swift apology on her Twitter account, saying she let "interpersonal dynamics" get the better of her 
and had apologized directly to Wilson-Raybould for the "insensitive and inappropriate" comment.

Page 2 of 3
Trudeau resists calls to fire Bennett over 'hurtful' text, says he knows her 'heart'
Trudeau said he spoke with Bennett Friday morning and he knows her "heart" and how hard she has worked for 
years on improving Canada's relationship with Indigenous Peoples.
"We both understand that there is now even more work for her to do and I know we will do it together," he said.
Charlie Angus, NDP critic for Indigenous youth, continued to call for Bennett's firing on Friday.
"On a day when Canadians were grappling with the discovery of hundreds of more bodies in unmarked graves, the 
minister took a cheap, derogatory stab at an Indigenous leader grieving for these lost lives," Angus said in a 
statement. 
"You can't say reconciliation is a priority while tolerating this kind of behaviour from your minister. If anything, 
Prime Minister Trudeau highlighted the fact that he will say one thing and act in a completely different way."
The Union of BC Indian Chiefs has also called on Bennett to resign, saying it is "deeply disturbed and disgusted by 
the extreme callousness, spite, and ignorance you have shown through the racist message."
"With a single word — 'pension' — you not only decided to perpetuate a damaging racial stereotype, that 
Indigenous peoples are lazy and only financially motivated — but dismissed the pressing, overarching issue of 
residential schools, missing and murdered children, and Indigenous rights.''
Wilson-Raybould was appointed by Trudeau as Canada's first Indigenous justice minister. In 2019, she resigned 
as a cabinet minister and was later booted from the Liberal caucus after she called out the prime minister for 
pressuring her to secure a deferred prosecution agreement for SNC-Lavalin.
In August 2019, the federal ethics commissioner concluded that Trudeau violated the Conflict of Interest Act by 
improperly pressuring Wilson-Raybould to halt a criminal prosecution of the Montreal engineering giant on 
corruption charges related to contracts in Libya.
Wilson-Raybould was re-elected as an Independent MP in October 2019.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published June 25, 2021.

title: Trudeau to unveil new cabinet Oct. 26, Parliament to return Nov. 22
body:
OTTAWA - Prime Minister Justin Trudeau will unveil on Oct. 26 the roster of cabinet ministers who will shepherd 
his government into a third mandate focused on finishing the fight against COVID-19 and rebuilding the pandemic-
ravaged economy.
His ministers will then have about a month to settle into their jobs before Parliament is recalled on Nov. 22 — just 
over two months after the Sept. 20 election returned Trudeau's Liberals with a second consecutive minority.
The timing of Parliament's return, announced Friday by the Prime Minister's Office, was slammed by opposition 
parties who accused Trudeau of being uninterested in getting back to work.
In a written statement, Trudeau's office said the prime minister plans to talk by phone with opposition leaders early 
next week to discuss Canadians' priorities and how the House of Commons should resume operations as the 
fourth wave of the pandemic continues to rage.
Among the first orders of business, the statement said, will be working with opposition leaders to ensure all 
members of Parliament are fully vaccinated before setting foot in the Commons — an issue on which the Liberals, 
Bloc Québécois and NDP are in agreement.
But it creates a potential conflict with Conservative Leader Erin OToole, who has refused so far to disclose how 
many of his MPs have had two shots and who continues to defend the right of individuals to make their own 
personal health choices.
At the same time, the Conservatives want the Commons to resume normal, in-person operations and are 
adamantly opposed to any continuation of the hybrid model — with only a small number of MPs physically in the 
chamber and the rest participating virtually — used during the earlier waves of the pandemic.
Mandatory vaccination was a central pillar of the Liberals' election campaign and, since the Sept. 20 vote, Trudeau 
has moved quickly to deliver on his promise to require proof of vaccination for federal employees and anyone 
planning to board a plane or train.
His office said requiring MPs in the Commons to be fully vaccinated is a matter of showing leadership.

Page 2 of 4
Trudeau to unveil new cabinet Oct. 26, Parliament to return Nov. 22
"Canadians expect their elected representatives to lead by example in the fight against this virus, and the Prime 
Minister will be raising this with other leaders," the statement said.
Once Parliament is back, the statement suggested, extending pandemic support benefits will be high on the 
agenda.
"One of the immediate areas of focus for the next Parliament will be the COVID-19 support benefits that many 
Canadians and businesses still rely on, and the government will work collaboratively with other parliamentarians to 
continue to have Canadians’ backs," it said.
Emergency rent and wage subsidy programs are set to end later this month but can be extended to the end of 
November. New legislation would be required to extend them beyond that — a process that the Canadian Chamber 
of Commerce fears could stretch into the new year, with benefits cut off in the meantime.
While it welcomed the priority placed on extending business support programs, the chamber said the Nov. 22 start 
date for Parliament is too late for small businesses in the hardest-hit sectors.
“Extending these programs through November needs to be an immediate priority, followed by legislation to 
introduce programs for the hardest-hit sectors as soon as the House returns,” said Alla Drigola Birk, the chamber’s 
director of parliamentary affairs.
Businesses need "support and certainty now, not a retroactive payment months from now," she added.
NDP Leader Jagmeet Singh said the delay in recalling Parliament shows that the Liberals "are not interested in 
helping struggling families and small businesses in this fourth wave of COVID-19."
Conservative House leader Gerard Deltell said it demonstrates that "the $600-million ‘urgent’ election was nothing 
more than a power grab for Justin Trudeau trying to secure a majority government, and that he is in no rush to get 
back to work."
“It’s wrong that in the middle of the fourth wave of the COVID-19 pandemic, Justin Trudeau is waiting 63 days to 
return to work. That’s 63 days that Members of Parliament should be working in the House of Commons to address 
the pandemic, inflation, labour shortages, and a number of other issues important to Canadians," Deltell said.
According to the statement from Trudeau's office, other "early priorities" will include reintroducing legislation to ban 
conversion therapy, the practice of forcing individuals to undergo therapy aimed at altering their sexual orientation 
or gender identity. A bill to criminalize the practice was passed by the Commons in June but did not make it to a 
vote in the Senate before the summer break and ultimately died when Trudeau called the election.
The government will also move quickly on the promise of 10-day paid sick leave for federally regulated workers and 
work with the remaining provinces and territories that have not yet signed on to the federal plan to create $10-a-day 
child care across the country.
Just one week after the election, Trudeau announced that Chrystia Freeland will retain her crucial dual roles as 
deputy prime minister and finance minister.
But whether he'll opt to leave most other ministers in their current portfolios or conduct a major shakeup remains to 
be seen. He is under pressure to at least shuffle Harjit Sajjan out of the Defence portfolio, where he's been widely 
criticized for his handling of serial sexual misconduct allegations among the senior ranks of the military. 
Trudeau has said gender parity will be the "base starting point" for any regionally balanced cabinet he puts 
together.
Trudeau lost three female ministers in the election — Fisheries Minister Bernadette Jordan, Gender Equality 
Minister Maryam Monsef and Seniors Minister Deb Schulte. A fourth, Infrastructure Minister Catherine McKenna, 
did not seek re-election.
Page 3 of 4
Trudeau to unveil new cabinet Oct. 26, Parliament to return Nov. 22
While only Trudeau and a handful of his closest advisers know who the prime minister will choose to fill those 
vacancies, speculation has centred on rookie Halifax West MP Lena Metlege Diab, a former provincial justice 
minister, to fill Jordan's Nova Scotia slot.
McKenna's Ottawa slot could be filled by Orleans MP Marie-France Lalonde, a former Ontario cabinet minister, or 
newly elected Kanata-Carleton MP Jenna Sudds, a former deputy mayor of Ottawa.
Other women who could be promoted into cabinet include newly elected London West MP Arielle Kayabaga, a 
refugee from Burundi and former city councillor; Harvard-educated businesswoman Leah Taylor Roy, newly 
elected in Ontario's Aurora-Oak-Ridges-Richmond Hills; and Pascale St-Onge, a former union leader in Quebec's 
cultural sector who eked out a slim victory over the Bloc in Brome-Missisquoi.
Trudeau could also choose to promote more experienced, re-elected female MPs who've already proven 
themselves to be strong performers, including Pickering-Uxbridge MP Jennifer O'Connell, Brampton North MP 
Ruby Sahota and Toronto Centre MP Marci Ien.
Randy Boissonnault, elected in Edmonton Centre in 2015, defeated in 2019 and re-elected last month, would seem 
a shoo-in for cabinet as one of only two Liberals from Alberta.
The second Albertan, Calgary Skyview MP George Chahal, was also initially considered a lock for cabinet. But his 
ambitions may be thwarted by the fact that he was caught on a doorbell camera removing a campaign brochure left 
by his Conservative rival, who has asked the elections commissioner to investigate.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2021.

be seen. He is under pressure to at least shuffle Harjit Sajjan out of the Defence portfolio, where he's been widely 
criticized for his handling of serial sexual misconduct allegations among the senior ranks of the military. 
Trudeau has said gender parity will be the "base starting point" for any regionally balanced cabinet he puts 
together.
Trudeau lost three female ministers in the election — Fisheries Minister Bernadette Jordan, Gender Equality 
Minister Maryam Monsef and Seniors Minister Deb Schulte. A fourth, Infrastructure Minister Catherine McKenna, 
did not seek re-election.

While only Trudeau and a handful of his closest advisers know who the prime minister will choose to fill those 
vacancies, speculation has centred on rookie Halifax West MP Lena Metlege Diab, a former provincial justice 
minister, to fill Jordan's Nova Scotia slot.
McKenna's Ottawa slot could be filled by Orleans MP Marie-France Lalonde, a former Ontario cabinet minister, or 
newly elected Kanata-Carleton MP Jenna Sudds, a former deputy mayor of Ottawa.
Other women who could be promoted into cabinet include newly elected London West MP Arielle Kayabaga, a 
refugee from Burundi and former city councillor; Harvard-educated businesswoman Leah Taylor Roy, newly 
elected in Ontario's Aurora-Oak-Ridges-Richmond Hills; and Pascale St-Onge, a former union leader in Quebec's 
cultural sector who eked out a slim victory over the Bloc in Brome-Missisquoi.
Trudeau could also choose to promote more experienced, re-elected female MPs who've already proven 
themselves to be strong performers, including Pickering-Uxbridge MP Jennifer O'Connell, Brampton North MP

ambitions may be thwarted by the fact that he was caught on a doorbell camera removing a campaign brochure left 
by his Conservative rival, who has asked the elections commissioner to investigate.

title: Trudeau's legacy under fire in Liberal memoirs
body:
Former Liberal environment minister Catherine McKenna just released a new book, and attention has focused 
immediately on how it reserves harsh words for her former boss, Justin Trudeau.
And this has happened several times already: A retired Trudeau cabinet minister releases a memoir, and the book 
contains condemnations of Trudeau. What's more, the criticisms are different. Some slam Trudeau's grasp of 
economics. Others blame him for detonating Canada's global reputation. Others blast him as a hypocrite and a 
tokenist.
Below, a cursory guide to Liberal memoirs and their explicitly anti-Trudeau passages.
RUN LIKE A GIRL:
CATHERINE McKENNA McKenna served as Trudeau's environment minister during the years when the party's 
climate policy was still quite popular. Climate change regularly ranked as one of Canadians' top political concerns 
upon the Trudeau government first coming to power in 2015, and the carbon tax was initially greeted with acclaim - 
in sharp contrast to the deep ire it would attract in later years. But while McKenna wrote that she and Trudeau were 
sympatico on their environmental sensibilities, she developed a problem with his constant virtue signalling. She 
wrote that she particularly objected to his regular boasts about a cabinet that was 50 per cent female. "By making it 
such a big deal, Trudeau put the spotlight on his own virtue rather than the hard work and expertise of the women 
around him," she wrote, adding that this would become a "recurring issue."
"The prime minister liked to remind people that he was a feminist. Inevitably, when issues arose with strong 
women in cabinet or caucus, his commitment would then be called into question," she wrote. McKenna also 
accused Trudeau of existing in a "fortress" in which he ignored cabinet ministers to the exclusion of ones he had 
personally known as children. "The prime minister was aloof and just didn't seem interested in his ministers or 
caucus members beyond his childhood friends, Dominic LeBlanc and Marc Miller," she wrote.
The result? Wrote McKenna, Canada under Trudeau lacked "leadership" and the prime minister never built a "true 
team." INDIAN IN THE CABINET: JODY WILSON-RAYBOULD Given the circumstances of her departure from 
cabinet, it was clear that Jody Wilson-Raybould's 2021 memoir was not going to be kind to Trudeau. Wilson-
Raybould was the central figure in the 2019 SNCLavalin scandal. Wilson-Raybould, then the attorney general, 
objected to Trudeau's attempt to intervene in a bribery-related prosecution of SNC-Lavalin, a prominent Quebec 
engineering firm. In response, Wilson-Raybould was pushed out of both cab- inet and the Liberal caucus.
Page 2 of 3
Trudeau's legacy under fire in Liberal memoirs
Her book gets into pointby-point detail about her heated final meetings with Trudeau, and is among the most poetic 
about highlighting his alleged character flaws.
Wilson-Raybould wrote that Trudeau betrayed "her deep desire to believe in people" and that "this man was not the 
leader I had thought him to be." His tone is described as "aggressive and condescending," and Wilson-Raybould 
alleges that he attempted to coach her into participating in a coverup. "In that moment, I knew he wanted me to lie - 
to attest that what had occurred had not occurred," she wrote.
WHERE TO FROM HERE: A PATH TO CANADIAN PROSPERITY: BILL MORNEAU As its title suggests, Bill 
Morneau's 2023 book is mostly policy prescriptions and doesn't delve too much into the interpersonal details of his 
time as finance minister during Trudeau's first five years. But Morneau describes how he ultimately lost faith in 
Trudeau's leadership during the chaotic first months of the COVID-19 pandemic. Morneau complained that he had 
often been up against a government where "policy rationales were tossed aside in favour of scoring political points," 
and that this became untenable during the pandemic. As Morneau described it, his people presented COVID relief 
measures that were moderate and fiscally responsible, only to have them discarded in favour of policies that were 
more expensive and less protected from abuse.
"During the period when the largest government expenditures as a portion of GDP were made in the shortest time 
since the advent of the Second World War, calculations and recommendations from the Ministry of Finance were 
basically disregarded in favour of winning a popularity contest," he wrote.
As for Trudeau personally, his "management and inte -r personal communication abilities were sorely lacking," 
wrote Morneau. The ex-finance minister also accused Trudeau's office of orchestrating a series of leaks designed 
to undermine him, writing that they seemed to grow in "both number and degree of malice."
It wasn't the first time Morneau had publicly slammed Trudeau as an economic illiterate. The year prior, he had told 
a gathering of the C.D. Howe Institute that the Trudeau government had mostly been concerned about redistributing 
wealth rather than creating it.
"There was little attention given to the importance of increasing our collective prosperity - let alone dev -el oping a 
disciplined way of thinking and acting on the problem," he said. A MOST EXTRAORDINARY RIDE: SPACE, 
POLITICS AND THE PURSUIT OF A CANADIAN DREAM:
MARC GARNEAU After a working life that included becoming the first Canadian in space, Marc Garneau capped it 
off with six years in the Trudeau cabinet, including five years as minister of transport and nine months as minister 
of foreign affairs. As such, Garneau only briefly touched on his political career in this memoir published just seven 
months before his death in June, at age 76.
But those chapters included Garneau's view that Trudeau's foreign policy had prioritized style over substance, 
causing the rest of the world to increasingly ignore Ottawa's input on international issues.
"Unfortunately Canada's standing in the world has slipped, in part because our pronouncements are not always 
matched by a capacity to act or by actions that clearly demonstrate that we mean what we say," Garneau wrote.
The ex-astronaut singled out Trudeau's disastrous 2018 trip to India, which would become widely mocked for the 
prime minister's flamboyant outfits and diplomatic gaffes.

title: Trudeau's nightmarish week continues with byelection loss
body:
OTTAWA - The Liberals suffered a crushing loss in the Cloverdale-Langley City, British Columbia byelection to 
close out an already nightmarish Monday( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/reaction-to-chrystia-freeland-
resignation ) for Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.
Conservative Tamara Jansen will be returning to Ottawa as the riding's MP after cruising to victory, beating Liberal 
runner-up Madison Fleischer by 50 points. Jansen previously held the seat from 2019 to 2021, before losing it to 
Liberal John Aldag.
The byelection loss comes on the heels of the shocking resignation of former finance minister Chrystia Freeland on 
Monday, who announced her decision on social media just hours before the government was set to unveil its fall 
economic statement. At a fundraiser on Monday evening, Trudeau called the day "eventful" and "not easy."
The House of Commons will adjourn on Tuesday until the last week of January and the Liberals will gather for a 
holiday party on Tuesday evening. Trudeau is scheduled to give remarks at what promises to be one of the stranger 
gatherings in the party's history.
On Parliament Hill on Tuesday, some Liberals MPs encouraged Trudeau to reflect on whether he is the right person 
for the job.
"I think what the prime minister has to think about is does he have the right vision for the country?" said Liberal MP 
Francis Scarpaleggia. "I would like to see the drama dialled down a bit, actually."
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre( https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/poilievre-demands-election-before-
trump-inauguration ) and Bloc Québécois leader Yves-François Blanchet( https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/bloc-
leader-blanchet-pushes-for-january-election-call-after-freeland-resignation-1.7148107 ) are both calling for an 
election to be held in early 2025, to allow a rejuvenated Parliament to deal with incoming U.S. President Donald 
Trump.
Trump, who's antagonized both Trudeau and Freeland( 
https://x.com/TrumpDailyPosts/status/1868866668753297801 ) on social media, has threatened to slap a 25-per-
cent tariff( https://nationalpost.com/news/trump-threatens-to-impose-25-per-cent-tariff-on-canada-and-
mexicohttps://nationalpost.com/news/trump-threatens-to-impose-25-per-cent-tariff-on-canada-and-mexico ) on all 
Canadian goods shortly after he takes office on Jan. 20.
Page 2 of 3
Trudeau's nightmarish week continues with byelection loss
Poilievre called this week's events a "circus" during a Tuesday appearance in Mississauga, Ont., but stressed the 
Liberal dysfunction is no laughing matter.
"The real consequences of yesterday's clown show are playing out in tragedies right across this country," said 
Poilievre.
Blanchet said that there was no moral justification that, through his personal ambition to stay in power, the prime 
minister could "allow himself to be so harmful, dangerous and malignant for the entire population of Quebec and 
Canada" rather than face the electorate in an election.
"We must put an end as quickly as possible to the very bad spectacle that we are giving internationally about the 
way Canada is preparing to face discussions with the Americans," said Blanchet.
The blowout Conservative win in the B.C. byelection marks a departure for the usually competitive Metro Vancouver 
riding, which was decided by less than five points in the last two elections.
It was also the Liberals' fourth straight byelection loss, closing out a winless 2024 for the historically unpopular 
governing party( https://nationalpost.com/opinion/liberal-party-may-never-recover ).
Three of these losses, including last night's, came in ridings that were last held by a Liberal MP.
Fleischer, a first-time Liberal candidate, was dogged by questions( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/liberal-
candidate-metis-indigenous-heritage ) about her past claims to Indigenous heritage and was conspicuously absent 
from campaign photos( https://x.com/christyclarkbc/status/1866203479041363976 ) posted by ex-B.C. premier 
Christy Clark.
Liberal Party officials were criticized for green-lighting Fleischer's nomination on Nov. 10, while a scandal over 
similar ancestral claims( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/randy-boissonnault-indigenous-claims-2 ) made by 
then-cabinet minister Randy Boissonnault raged in Ottawa.
One silver-lining for the Liberals is that it was also a bad night for the NDP, which has failed to capitalize( 
https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/while-provincial-ndp-parties-rise-in-western-canada-federal-ndp-support-
drops-poll ) on the recent Liberal missteps.
NDP candidate Vanessa Sharma finished in a distant third with 12.5 per cent of the vote, seven points down from 
the party's nominee in 2021.
NDP Leader Jagmeet Singh called on Trudeau to step down on Monday, after the surprise departure of Chrystia 
Freeland( https://nationalpost.com/news/politics/reaction-to-chrystia-freeland-resignation ) from cabinet, but 
wouldn't commit to bringing down the prime minister in the next non-confidence vote( 
https://x.com/globalnews/status/1868772620029591719 ).
Singh helped the Liberals survive three Conservative non-confidence motions( 
https://www.ctvnews.ca/politics/liberal-government-survives-third-conservative-non-confidence-vote-1.7138316 ) in

title: Trudeau's strange Carney obsession
body:
With all due respect to the MPs who spent many mortifying minutes last week batting the idea back and forth across 
the House of Commons, I don't think Justin Trudeau's public undermining of his as-of-Monday-morningex finance 
minister, Chrystia Freeland, just days before she was to deliver a fiscal update, was about her being a woman - or 
about Trudeau being a "fake feminist." I think it was more about a prime minister, and his retinue, who believe that 
communications and celebrity (of a sort) are ninetenths of politics.
No question, for a man who as recently as last Tuesday described himself as "a proud feminist," Trudeau has 
treated notable female ministers appallingly.
He fired Canada's first Indigenous justice minister, Jody Wilson-Raybould, for not intervening on SNC-Lavalin's 
behalf in its Libyan-related legal troubles; fired highly regarded health minister Jane Philpott for supporting Wilson-
Raybould; lumbered Maryam Monsef with an electoral-reform file on which he had no intention of following through. 
Now there's Freeland, who in her public resignation letter claims Trudeau said Friday he was planning to dump her 
from the finance portfolio ... with a fiscal update to come Monday.
And no question, he seems to have (or to have had) much more time for perennial liabilities like Bill Blair, Harjit 
Sajjan, Marco Mendicino, Steven Guilbeault ... hmm. Do you know what, maybe there is something about strong 
women he can't stand.
Still, that wouldn't explain Trudeau's strange obsession with luring former Bank of Canada and Bank of England 
governor Mark Carney into the Liberal fold - to replace Freeland, reports suggest, despite Carney not being an 
elected MP. And despite the rather delicate matter of Brookfield Asset Management, of which Carney is chair, trying 
to set up a $50-billion investment fund using Canadian pensioners' money. (It also wouldn't explain the always-
fireable Mélanie Joly's continued presence in cabinet.)
Most Canadians have probably never given any thought to the notion of a cabinet minister not being an elected 
MP. I'm not sure that now, when many Canadians (including many Liberal voters) are sick to death of the sight and 
the sound of this government, is the best moment to test them - or to add yet another conflict-of-interest 
controversy to the pile.
The Liberals were certainly not pleased last time we had an unelected cabinet minister, when Stephen Harper 
appointed then Senator Michael Fortier as minister of public works in 2006 to ensure Montreal had a seat at the 
table. "Mr. Harper ran a campaign which emphasized accountability and ethical behaviour by parliamentarians. I 
have to say that I am concerned, given Mr. Harper's past statements, he put into his cabinet a non-elected minister 
Page 2 of 3
Trudeau's strange Carney obsession
of public works," interim Liberal leader Bill Graham said at the time. "This portfolio is vital to the functioning of the 
federal government ... is responsible for all government purchasing and contracting and, therefore, spends billions 
of taxpayers'dollars per year."
That concern would have gone double, presumably, had Harper appointed Fortier as finance minister. And as a 
senator Fortier was, at least, a parliamentarian. And he didn't have that $50-billion toilet seat hanging around his 
neck. And that was Harper's first cabinet; he had some capital to burn among his supporters, and he spent it 
making his ministry geographically representative. Trudeau has no extra political capital left. His line of credit is 
maxed out, and the bank is calling several times a day.
For months we heard reports suggesting the Prime Minister's Office is concerned Freeland lacks the "ability to 
communicate the government's economic message." The PMO has precisely zero standing to be judging bad 
communications, but they're right: Freeland isn't a good communicator. Carney, on the other hand, has a reputation 
as a master communicator.
But let's take a look at who has bestowed that reputation upon him: Paul Martin, who was prime minister while 
Carney was associate deputy finance minister; former Treasury Board president Scott Brison, who's a personal 
friend of Carney's; left-wing economist Armine Yalnizyan, of the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives; 
Scotiabank economist Derek Holt; former National Post columnist Andrew Coyne (though he also dubbed Carney 
"a master of jargon") ... you take my point. It's a fairly elite audience, and all these reviews concern Carney's 
performance as governor of a central bank ... not as a minister of the Crown.
Carney's attempts at communicating his regular-bloke bona fides have thus far included a photo of him wearing his 
hometown Edmonton Oilers jersey and holding a can of Budweiser as if it were an obscure local delicacy.
It has been said so many times by now, but as terrible as Trudeau's Liberals are at communicating, communicating 
is not even close to their main problem. Housing, immigration, out-ofcontrol spending, Trudeau's refusal to resign, 
his caucus's refusal to make him resign - until Monday, perhaps? - those are among their main problems, and there 
is no communicating them away.
Notably absent from this whole conversation has been what exactly Carney would do differently than Freeland as 
finance minister, or indeed, any indication that he would have more freedom from the PMO to act on his 
preferences than Freeland has now. If Carney is really willing to donate his body to this lost cause, I can see why 
Trudeau and Co. would want to take a chance on him. But it's easy to imagine it ending in nothing but further woe.

title: Trump sends letter to Herzog requesting pardon for Netanyahu, calls corruption trial a 'political prosecution'
body:
U.S. President Donald Trump has sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog requesting a full pardon for Israeli 
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in his corruption trial, Herzog's office said on Wednesday.
The letter reads in part, "As the Great State of Israel and the amazing Jewish People move past the terribly difficult 
times of the last three years, I hereby call on you to fully pardon Benjamin Netanyahu, who has been a formidable 
and decisive War Time Prime Minister and is now leading Israel into a time of peace, which includes my continued 
work with key Middle East leaders to add many additional countries to the world changing Abraham Accords."
The letter continues: "Prime Minister Netanyahu has stood tall for Israel in the face of strong adversaries and long 
odds, and his attention cannot be unnecessarily diverted."
Trump wrote that, while he respects the independence and requirements of the Israeli judicial system, he believes 
the case against Netanyahu is a "political, unjustified prosecution." He added that "it is time to let Bibi unite Israel by 
pardoning him, and ending lawfare once and for all."
??President Isaac Herzog received a letter this morning from Donald Trump, calling on him to grant a pardon to 
Benjamin Netanyahu in his criminal trial. pic.twitter.com/6vkQLbsc7e( https://t.co/6vkQLbsc7e )
- Amit Segal (@AmitSegal) November 12, 2025( 
https://twitter.com/AmitSegal/status/1988555210386559025?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw )
Herzog, for his part, responded to the letter, with his office noting that a formal request for a pardon must be 
submitted:
"President Herzog holds President Trump in the highest regard and continues to express his deep appreciation for 
President Trump's unwavering support for Israel, his tremendous contribution to the return of the hostages, to 
reshaping the situation in the Middle East and Gaza especially, and to ensuring the security of the State of Israel," 
the statement reads.
"Alongside and not withstanding this, as the Office of the President has made clear throughout, anyone seeking a 
Presidential pardon must submit a formal request in accordance with the established procedures," it added.
Page 2 of 3
Trump sends letter to Herzog requesting pardon for Netanyahu, calls corruption trial a 'political prosecution'
The letter follows Trump's Nov. 2 comments on CBS News' "60 Minutes," in which he said his administration would 
"help out" with Netanyahu's trial.
During an interview at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, Trump told journalist Norah O'Donnell: "I don't think they 
treat him [Netanyahu] very well. He's under trial for some things and I don't think they treat him very well. We'll be 
involved in that to help him out a little bit because I think it's very unfair."
Netanyahu faces corruption charges in three separate cases-Cases 1000 and 2000 (the charge is "breach of 
trust" in both instances), and Case 4000 (bribery, fraud and breach of trust).
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump hold a joint news conference in the 
State Dining Room at the White House on September 29, 2025 in Washington, DC.
Trump made similar remarks during his address to the Knesset in Jerusalem on Oct. 13, saying, "Hey, I have an 
idea. Mr. President [Herzog], why don't you give him a pardon? Give him a pardon. Come on."
He called Netanyahu "one of the greatest wartime presidents," mocking the charges against him: "And cigars and 
champagne, who the hell cares about that?" The comment referred to Case 1000, in which the prime minister is 
accused of accepting gifts from two wealthy businessmen.

title: Two more Alberta petitions get green light to collect signatures to oust politicians
body:
EDMONTON - Recall petitions aiming to oust two opposition members of Alberta's legislature have been approved 
by Elections Alberta.
One targets Pete Guthrie, a former United Conservative Party cabinet minister who stepped down over the 
government's handling of a government contracts scandal.
Guthrie, representing Airdrie-Cochrane, now sits in the legislature as the leader of the Progressive Tory Party.
The other petition is against Marie Renaud, the NDP member for St. Albert.
They bring the total to 28 recall petitions initiated since last fall.
Twenty of the 24 against members of Premier Danielle Smith's UCP caucus, including Smith, have so far fallen 
short or been withdrawn.
Those petitioning Guthrie and Renaud have until June 10 to collect signatures equal to 60 per cent of votes cast in 
their ridings in the 2023 provincial election.
In Airdrie-Cochrane, that means just over 18,000 signatures are needed, and in St. Albert, 15,000.
Petitioner Lawrence Martini, in a statement published by Elections Alberta, cites legal proceedings that appear to 
date back to 2014. Martini says Guthrie refused to communicate with him and at an open house and called the 
police to have him removed.
"We did nothing wrong, punished, lost everything. This is a scam. Public Inquiry," the statement says.
Guthrie, in a statement also posted on the Elections Alberta website, says he respects the process and wishes 
Martini well in exercising his rights under the law.
"As an MLA, there are limits to my role, particularly with respect to private legal matters and court proceedings. 
While we were unable to resolve this individual's concerns, we approached the situation in good faith and remain 
focused on serving the people of Airdrie-Cochrane," he writes.

Page 2 of 3
Two more Alberta petitions get green light to collect signatures to oust politicians
Lilo Forsyth, who is seeking to unseat Renaud, says the politician "represents an ideology — not St. Albert," and 
accuses Renaud of "pushing gender ideology" into classrooms.
"She treats parents like the problem, deliberately shutting them out — along with anyone who disagrees with her," 
Forsyth's statement reads.
Renaud says in her statement to Elections Alberta that her constituents have said accessible public education is 
vitally important to them.
"I will endeavour to do all I can in my role as MLA for St. Albert to ensure every student has access to quality 
education regardless of their race, religion, ability or gender."
Many who started the earlier petitions said they were motivated by the UCP government’s use of the Charter’s 
notwithstanding clause to force striking teachers back to work last fall. Others have said their representatives were 
hard to reach or dismissive of local concerns.
The results of two remaining petitions seeking to recall NDP members are not yet available.
If a petition is successful, a constituency-wide vote would be held on whether the politician keeps their seat. If the 
member loses, a byelection would be held.
The next provincial general election is scheduled for next October.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published March 12, 2026.

title: U.S. Consulate home to Calgary ICE office; Controversial policing force not armed or making any arrests on
body:
Amid rising tensions and deadly confrontations linked to immigration enforcement in the United States, some 
Calgarians are asking: What is ICE doing in Calgary?
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operates field offices in five Canadian cities - including one in 
downtown Calgary.
The Calgary office of ICE's Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) team - the agency's criminal investigative arm - 
opened in 2019 and operates out of the U.S. Consulate General at Rocky Mountain Plaza, along Macleod Trail in 
downtown. The consulate is heavily secured and only accessible by appointment.
The U.S. Consulate in Calgary handles consular affairs for Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and the Northwest 
Territories.
ICE's website states that its Homeland Security Investigations department has more than 90 international offices in 
more than 50 countries, staffed by roughly 500 special agents, analysts and support personnel.
In Canada, HSI has staff at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa and consulates in Calgary, Vancouver, Toronto and 
Montreal.
Three HSI agents are assigned to the Calgary office, according to the U.S. Consulate General in Calgary.
In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for ICE said HSI special agents work closely with Canadian partners to 
investigate serious transnational crimes and threats.
"These skilled and highly trained special agents focus on a wide variety of serious crimes, like drug trafficking, child 
exploitation, weapons smuggling, human smuggling, financial fraud and more," the spokesperson said.
"They also help track and detain known and potential terrorists before they can carry out attacks against the United 
States and her allies."
The agency stressed HSI agents do not conduct enforcement operations on Canadian soil, such as making arrests 
or executing search warrants. They also don't carry firearms in Canada.
Page 2 of 4
U.S. Consulate home to Calgary ICE office; Controversial policing force not armed or making any arrests on 
Canadian soil
The U.S. Consulate General in Calgary said about 27 victims of child exploitation were rescued during the 2024 
fiscal year due to "co-operation between Calgary's DHS-HSI office and Canadian law enforcement."
At the nearby City Hall CTrain station, just steps from the U.S. consulate, hearing about ICE's Calgary presence 
sparked unease among some commuters.
"It's concerning," said Red Deer resident Michael Serrano. "Because of what's happening in the U.S."
Serrano pointed to widely publicized ICE raids and recent fatal shootings involving immigration enforcement in the 
U.S.
According to The Associated Press, at least six people have died during the U.S. government's immigration 
enforcement sweep. That includes two in Minneapolis last month - a 37-year-old man who was shot by a border 
patrol officer, and the fatal shooting of a woman in her vehicle by an ICE officer.
Calgary resident Lia Rojas said she was unsettled by the idea of ICE operating in her city.
"It's upsetting to see what's happening in the States and the fact that (ICE) is coming to Calgary now - it's weird," 
she said. "It doesn't really matter what side you lean politically. Objectively, it's wrong.
"Like, why are they here?" Rojas asked.
Last week, Edmonton Strathcona MP Heather McPherson released an open letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney 
calling for the closure of ICE offices in Canada.
"Over many months, Canadi- ans have watched in horror as the Trump administration has stripped Americans and 
non-citizens of some of their constitutional rights," McPherson wrote.
In response to rising backlash on social media, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa issued a public statement on social 
media clarifying HSI's mandate.
"Let's be clear: HSI operates in close partnership with Canadian law enforcement to combat transnational crime 
and protect communities on both sides of the border," the embassy said in a post on X.
Doug King, a criminal justice professor at Mount Royal University, said he understands the alarm but said 
Calgarians don't need to be worried.
"I can appreciate why some people would be thinking it's concerning - because they're reacting to what they're 
seeing in the media about the use of ICE in Minneapolis and other cities," said King.
King said U.S. immigration and customs enforcement have long-standing partnerships with Canadian law 
enforcement agencies.
He compared ICE's presence in Canada to the RCMP's presence in the U.S., with both sides co-operating on 
transnational criminal investigations, he said.
"I don't think people need to be worried that the ICE contingent here in Calgary is going to be, you know, storming 
the streets and trying to pull people out of homes," he said. "Things like what they're doing in the United States.
"First of all, they have no legal jurisdiction to do that and, secondly, that's not what their role is."
King said calling for ICE's ouster from Canada "(ignores) the fact that there's been really good law enforcement 
partnerships with (ICE) and Canadian authorities" for decades.
"I think saying ICE shouldn't have a presence in Canada is cutting off our nose to spite our face," he said.
Page 3 of 4
U.S. Consulate home to Calgary ICE office; Controversial policing force not armed or making any arrests on 
Canadian soil
"That partnership is producing benefits to Canadian society."
Another expert said ICE's pres- ence in Canada poses a "political problem" at a time when the agency faces 
allegations of operating outside the rule of law in the U.S., and when Canada-U.S. relations are anything but 
"business as usual."
Rob Huebert, a political science professor at the University of Calgary and director of the university's Centre for 
Military, Security and Strategic Studies, noted Canada allows foreign law enforcement agencies to pursue criminal 
investigations in the country, but only under strict conditions.
What makes ICE problematic for Canada, Huebert said, is how the agency has come to be perceived by 
Canadians.
"There's a growing consensus that ICE seems to be appearing to operate beyond the Americans' rule-based 
system," he said, fuelling what he described as "a very strong political distaste" toward the agency.
"The concern is more related to the political view of them as rogue actors within the U.S."

exploitation, weapons smuggling, human smuggling, financial fraud and more," the spokesperson said.
"They also help track and detain known and potential terrorists before they can carry out attacks against the United 
States and her allies."
The agency stressed HSI agents do not conduct enforcement operations on Canadian soil, such as making arrests 
or executing search warrants. They also don't carry firearms in Canada.
Page 2 of 4
U.S. Consulate home to Calgary ICE office; Controversial policing force not armed or making any arrests on 
Canadian soil
The U.S. Consulate General in Calgary said about 27 victims of child exploitation were rescued during the 2024 
fiscal year due to "co-operation between Calgary's DHS-HSI office and Canadian law enforcement."
At the nearby City Hall CTrain station, just steps from the U.S. consulate, hearing about ICE's Calgary presence 
sparked unease among some commuters.
"It's concerning," said Red Deer resident Michael Serrano. "Because of what's happening in the U.S."
Serrano pointed to widely publicized ICE raids and recent fatal shootings involving immigration enforcement in the 
U.S.
According to The Associated Press, at least six people have died during the U.S. government's immigration 
enforcement sweep. That includes two in Minneapolis last month - a 37-year-old man who was shot by a border 
patrol officer, and the fatal shooting of a woman in her vehicle by an ICE officer.
Calgary resident Lia Rojas said she was unsettled by the idea of ICE operating in her city.
"It's upsetting to see what's happening in the States and the fact that (ICE) is coming to Calgary now - it's weird," 
she said. "It doesn't really matter what side you lean politically. Objectively, it's wrong.
"Like, why are they here?" Rojas asked.
Last week, Edmonton Strathcona MP Heather McPherson released an open letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney 
calling for the closure of ICE offices in Canada.
"Over many months, Canadi- ans have watched in horror as the Trump administration has stripped Americans and 
non-citizens of some of their constitutional rights," McPherson wrote.
In response to rising backlash on social media, the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa issued a public statement on social 
media clarifying HSI's mandate.
"Let's be clear: HSI operates in close partnership with Canadian law enforcement to combat transnational crime 
and protect communities on both sides of the border," the embassy said in a post on X.
Doug King, a criminal justice professor at Mount Royal University, said he understands the alarm but said 
Calgarians don't need to be worried.
"I can appreciate why some people would be thinking it's concerning - because they're reacting to what they're 
seeing in the media about the use of ICE in Minneapolis and other cities," said King.
King said U.S. immigration and customs enforcement have long-standing partnerships with Canadian law 
enforcement agencies.
He compared ICE's presence in Canada to the RCMP's presence in the U.S., with both sides co-operating on 
transnational criminal investigations, he said.
"I don't think people need to be worried that the ICE contingent here in Calgary is going to be, you know, storming 
the streets and trying to pull people out of homes," he said. "Things like what they're doing in the United States.
"First of all, they have no legal jurisdiction to do that and, secondly, that's not what their role is."
King said calling for ICE's ouster from Canada "(ignores) the fact that there's been really good law enforcement 
partnerships with (ICE) and Canadian authorities" for decades.

Canadian soil
"That partnership is producing benefits to Canadian society."
Another expert said ICE's pres- ence in Canada poses a "political problem" at a time when the agency faces 
allegations of operating outside the rule of law in the U.S., and when Canada-U.S. relations are anything but 
"business as usual."
Rob Huebert, a political science professor at the University of Calgary and director of the university's Centre for 
Military, Security and Strategic Studies, noted Canada allows foreign law enforcement agencies to pursue criminal 
investigations in the country, but only under strict conditions.
What makes ICE problematic for Canada, Huebert said, is how the agency has come to be perceived by 
Canadians.
"There's a growing consensus that ICE seems to be appearing to operate beyond the Americans' rule-based 
system," he said, fuelling what he described as "a very strong political distaste" toward the agency.
"The concern is more related to the political view of them as rogue actors within the U.S."

title: Under pressure, Smith opts for distraction
body:
No premier has ever gone into an election campaign under investigation for a possible ethics violation.
This will likely stick with Danielle Smith to voting day in Alberta, May 29, unless commissioner Marguerite Trussler 
breaks her long record of taking months to produce a report.
The subject is far more serious than the usual look into whether some MLA voted for a personal benefit.
The probe is about "whether or not the premier has interfered with the administration of justice in relation to a 
COVID prosecution," according to Smith's office.
She has some of her of her own MLAs in a constant state of dread.
One said Tuesday, asking for anonymity, "I cannot even begin to comment on how she can keep stepping on our 
message like this, time after time."
The UCP is running a meat-and-potatoes campaign based on health care and affordability. But Smith constantly 
smothers the banquet with her own peculiar political toppings.
The odd thing is, we only have her word that she's under investigation.
Even the NDP, which demanded the inquiry, has no formal notice.
The initial request for an investigation came from NDP justice critic Irfan Sabir. On Tuesday, he finally got a note 
from Trussler's office. It said: "The office of the ethics commissioner cannot provide any comment to any person 
unless authorized or required to do so by law.
"As such, this office cannot provide the confirmation that you have requested." Media got similar notices.
That's some transparent government we've got here in Alberta. But don't blame Trussler for the smokescreen. She 
just follows the legislation they gave her.
At this point, it's not even clear that the inquiry covers Smith's infamous phone call with Artur Pawlowski, the 
intolerant, homophobic pastor. She talked to Pawlowski for 11 minutes about the charges against him for his 
behaviour at Coutts, and how they were, in her view, purely political.
Page 2 of 3
Under pressure, Smith opts for distraction
On her Corus radio spot Saturday, Smith made her most breathtaking claim yet. She said she was talking to 
Pawlowski as a fellow party leader, kind of an equal in that regard.
Pawlowski was briefly the leader of the Independence Party of Alberta. It doesn't even register in opinion polls.
Smith has long since spiked the real risk on the UCP's right, the Wildrose Independence Party. Its followers have 
swarmed back to the UCP because of her sovereignty pitch.
On that phone call, there was no discussion of party matters.
Very quickly after disclosing the ethics probe, Smith tried to change the channel by fiercely blasting federal Justice 
Minister David Lametti.
At a conference with First Nations leaders, Lametti had seemed to show some sympathy for their demands to 
rescind the Resource Transfer Acts of 1930.
These bills gave Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta control over development and taxation of their natural 
resources - powers other provinces had enjoyed since Confederation.
First Nations leaders want the old transfer acts gone because they fear that Alberta's Sovereignty Act, and the 
recently passed Saskatchewan First Act, will be used to interfere with their treaty rights.
They say that nobody asked their opinion in 1930, and the same thing happened with the new provincial laws.
Lametti said the action he was asked to take "won't be uncontroversial, is the only thing I would say, with a bit of a 
smile."
Smith and Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe jumped on this vague comment as proof of federal atrocity. Smith 
called it "an unprecedented risk to national unity."
Lametti responded on Twitter: "To be clear, at no point did I commit our government to reviewing areas of provincial 
jurisdiction, including that over natural resources."
The powers in those old acts have been enshrined since 1982 in section 92a of the Constitution. They can't be 
removed or changed without support of seven provinces that include 50 per cent of the national population. Ottawa 
whittles away at resource control with its own new legislation and friendly court rulings. Laws like Bill C-69 are 
backdoor challenges to the constitutional protections.
But the 1930 transfer acts have been irrelevant to those battles for decades - unless you're anxious to paper over 
an ethics investigation.
Don Braid's column appears regularly in the Calgary Herald. Twitter: @DonBraid !@COPYRIGHT=© 2023 
Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

possible ethics violation because of a phone call with a COVID protester.;
