title: Zelenzkyy's Betrayal; $100-Million Kickback scandal ensnares Ukrainian president's allies
body:
Ukraine's top anticorruption agencies revealed this week that a high-powered clique, led by a close friend of 
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, was caught embezzling US$100 million from the country's energy sector. The 
investigators further suggested that this scheme compromised the wartime security of the national electrical grid 
and indirectly allowed Russia to plunge much of the country into prolonged blackouts this autumn.
This is undoubtedly the largest corruption scandal Zelenskyy has ever faced. Not only did his allies orchestrate 
the plunder of strategically vital funds, it appears that the Ukrainian president himself may have tried to protect them 
from investigation and prosecution.
The clique - which consisted of several ministers, energy officials and a notable businessman - took control of 
Energoatom, Ukraine's state-owned nuclear energy provider, and demanded that suppliers pay kickbacks worth 
10-15 per cent of any contracts signed with the company. Those who failed to remit these bribes risked losing their 
supplier status and having their payments frozen.
The scheme took advantage of the fact that, under martial law, contractors are banned from suing strategically-
important companies, including Energoatom, for outstanding debts.
These conspirators apparently delayed the wartime fortification of critical energy infrastructure, either because they 
were not paid kickbacks quickly enough or because they believed that suppliers could be extorted for greater 
gains. They also attempted to funnel related contracts to companies they controlled, so they could make more 
money.
This left the country's electrical substationswhich connect Ukraine's nuclear power plants to the national grid 
vulnerable to Moscow's strikes. Many were subsequently damaged or destroyed by missiles and drones, especially 
after a massive attack last weekend that left millions of Ukrainians in the dark.
The Russians appear to have been involved in the scheme to some degree, as the illicit kickbacks were apparently 
laundered through a secret Kyiv-based office owned by the notorious Derkach family.
The family's patriarch, Leonid Derkach, is a former KGB officer who briefly led Ukraine's main intelligence agency in 
the late 1990s before stepping down due to his alleged ties with the Russian mafia. His son later became a 
Ukrainian parliamentarian, was identified as a Kremlin intelligence asset and then fled to Russia in 2022 after it was 
discovered that he had set up spy networks throughout Ukraine to aid Moscow's full-scale invasion. The two 
Page 2 of 4
Zelenzkyy's Betrayal; $100-Million Kickback scandal ensnares Ukrainian president's allies
Ukrainian agencies investigating the energy embezzlement scandal - the National Anti-Corruption Bureau 
(NABU) and Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) - conducted over 70 raids throughout Ukraine 
last Monday morning, confiscating several large bags of cash. They then immediately went public with their core 
findings and announced that their probe, code-named "Midas," had lasted 15 months and involved the collection of 
over 1,000 hours of wiretapped conversations.
NABU has since published a series of slickly-produced videos on YouTube featuring damning wiretap excerpts 
lasting roughly 10 to 20 minutes each. Although the interlocutors used pseudonyms and were not named, local 
Ukrainian media outlets have been able to identify most of them.
"It'll be total f--king chaos for the whole line of companies. You'll just end up on the blacklist. You'll be wiped out 
completely, and all your employees will be conscripted into the army," said one conspirator in a recording, 
describing the effects his tactics could have on disobedient contractors.
The interlocutors further discussed halting the defensive reinforcement of electrical transformers, which they 
derided as a "waste of money," and claimed that some embezzled funds went to Energy Minister Svitlana 
Hrynchuk. One even alleged that the Security Service of Ukraine, the Office of the Prosecutor General and "other 
forces" were informed of, or even involved in, the corruption scheme.
Hrynchuk submitted her resignation last Wednesday - as did her predecessor, who was appointed justice minister 
last July. Both have denied any wrongdoing.
NABU also named seven main suspects last Monday, which did not include some of the individuals implicated in 
the published recordings. All were formally charged the following day. Of these suspects, the most important by far 
is Timur Mindich.
Mindich is a close ally of Zelenskyy's and a co-owner of Kvartal 95, a production company the Ukrainian president 
founded when he still worked in entertainment. The friendship between the two men is so deep that, in 2021, 
Zelenskyy was thrown a surprise birthday party in Mindich's apartment, despite COVID-era quarantine restrictions.
Although Mindich is primarily known as a film producer, he maintains an eclectic set of business interests ranging 
from Russian diamond production to Ukrainian banking. Before this week's corruption scandal, he was allegedly 
already being investigated for a US$48-million embezzlement case linked to a fertilizer company.
At some point last decade, Mindich introduced Zelenskyy, then still an entertainer, to Israeli-Ukrainian billionaire 
Ihor Kolomoisky, who would later become a leading patron of Zelenskyy's successful 2019 presidential campaign. 
The president eventually turned on the oligarch and, in 2022, stripped him of his Ukrainian citizenship as 
punishment for international fraud and money laundering.
This would not be Mindich's only controversial intervention into Zelenskyy's life.
After Zelenskyy's election, Mindich reportedly recommended that he appoint Oleksiy Chernyshov, a prominent 
businessman, to important political positions. Chernyshov became a close ally of Zelenskyy's and was made 
governor of the Kyiv region in 2019. He was eventually appointed as one of Ukraine's Deputy Prime Ministers in 
2024 (the country typically maintains three such positions).
Last June, NABU alleged that Chernyshov significantly undervalued plots of public land at the cost of $24 million to 
the state - to benefit developers who paid him $345,000 in kickbacks. He was then fired, barred from leaving the 
country and hit with a US$2.9-million bail until his future trial.
Chernyshov was implicated in this week's embezzlement scandal, and allegedly received US$1.2 million and 
100,000 euros from the conspirators. Some Ukrainian investigative journalists now believe that these funds were 
used to construct a collection of luxury villas in Kyiv's suburbs, which were allegedly to be used by allied elites.
"A stupid a--hole," said Mindich in one of the wiretap excerpts released this week, apparently referencing 
Chernyshov. "If he exposes (other suspects) in the case, we're f--ed."
Page 3 of 4
Zelenzkyy's Betrayal; $100-Million Kickback scandal ensnares Ukrainian president's allies
Although Zelenskyy has tried to publicly distance himself from Mindich, Ukrainian investigative journalists have 
reported that Mindich's influence only grew after Russia's full-scale invasion, especially after a 2024 cabinet shuffle 
allowed Mindich to insert two more of his proteges into cabinet. After that point, three ministers - including the two 
that resigned last week - were allegedly under Mindich's sway.
This influence persisted despite the obvious criminality emanating from Timur Mindich's life. In June, for example, 
NABU charged one of his relatives with embezzling US$3 million from a major energy company based in Kharkiv, a 
front-line Ukrainian city.
Not only did Zelenskyy fail to curtail Mindich's informal power, he even seemed prepared to sabotage the 
anticorruption investigations closing in on his friend's schemes.
NABU and SAPO were both created in 2015 as a condition of the European Union's financial and political support, 
and were vested with a high degree of political independence. Last summer, though, Zelenskyy abruptly passed a 
law which would have placed these agencies under his indirect control, giving him the power to shut down, or 
otherwise thwart, inconvenient cases.
Zelenskyy quickly reversed course after thousands of protesters took to Kyiv's streets and major international allies 
expressed concerns but the damage to his credibility was severe.
At the time, many political commentators already suspected that Zelenskyy had attacked the anticorruption 
agencies to protect Chernyshov and Mindich. Yet, ono one understood just how deep this rot went.
The plundering of the energy sector indirectly caused millions of Ukrainians to spend long hours each day sitting 
frigidly in the dark. So, given a choice between his elite friends and his nation, Zelenskyy, in a truly inexcusable 
betrayal, seemingly chose the former.
In a final insult: attempts to detain Mindich have failed so far, as he illegally fled Ukraine hours before his properties 
were raided, having been tipped off by unknown parties.
